"Death is defined according to the body one has received; it is the cessation of the final moment of consciousness that constitutes death."
If the cessation of the mind constitutes death, then because the mind ceases moment by moment, every such cessation would be death.
If one fears death, then because the mind ceases moment by moment, one should fear at every such cessation.
One should not only fear the cessation of the final moment of mind, but one should also fear the exhaustion and cessation of preceding moments of mind. Why is this?
Because there is no difference between the cessation of preceding and succeeding moments of mind.

If it is argued that one fears falling into the evil realms and fears the cessation of the final moment of consciousness, then a person of merit should not fear falling into the evil realms, as previously stated.
"Since I shall undergo moment-to-moment cessation, when the final mind ceases, there should be no fear of death.
He further thought:
"Throughout beginningless worlds, as I have wandered through birth and death, I have undergone immeasurable and boundless *asaṃkhyeya* deaths; there is no place where one can escape death."
The Buddha said:
"Birth and death have no beginning.

If one were to die throughout a single kalpa, the accumulated bones would rise higher than the Snowy Mountains. Such deaths as these do not bring benefit to oneself nor benefit to others. Now that I have resolved upon the vow for the Unsurpassed Way, desiring to benefit both myself and others, and because practicing the Path with a diligent mind brings great benefit, why should I be startled or afraid?
In this way, the bodhisattva abandons the fear of death.
Furthermore, they reflect:
"This phenomenon of death must inevitably be experienced; there is no one who can escape it. Why is this?"

"At the beginning of the kalpa, there were great kings such as Mūrdhaja, Roca, and Roca-rāja, whose bodies were adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man. Followed by the seven treasures, they were revered and loved by devas and humans; they ruled over the four continents and constantly practiced the ten paths of wholesome action. Yet all these great kings eventually succumbed to death."

Furthermore, there were minor universal monarchs such as Śaṅkha, who, by their own power, ruled over Jambudvīpa; their physical forms were upright and handsome like those of devas, and they enjoyed themselves at will with forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and textures without lack.
Wherever he turned, all were subdued; none retreated, for he was highly proficient in the art of archery.
Yet these kings, who ruled as sovereigns over the world with their subjects and retinues, could not all escape death.

"Furthermore, the various sages and saints—such as Kāśyapa, Kauṇḍinya, and others—who practiced various ascetic austerities, attained the five supernormal powers, and composed scriptures, all nonetheless failed to escape death."

"Furthermore, the Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Arhats—who have attained mastery over the mind, who are free from defilement and have realized the Way—are all nonetheless worn away by the law of death; there is no sentient being whatsoever who can transcend it."
"I have resolved to attain the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment; I should not fear death.
Furthermore, in order to destroy the fear of death, I shall resolve with diligence to eliminate my own fear of death and likewise that of others."
"Therefore, having resolved to set forth on the path, why should one feel alarm and fear toward death?
When a bodhisattva contemplates impermanence in this way, they immediately eliminate the fear of death.
Furthermore, because a bodhisattva constantly cultivates the dharma of emptiness, he should not fear death. As it is said:
Apart from death there is no dying; apart from the dying there is no death.
Through death there is a dying; through the dying there is death.

If death were established by means of a dying person, then at the time prior to death, when [the dying person] was not yet established, there would be no determinate characteristic; thus, there would be neither death nor one who dies.
If the dying person were distinct from death, then the dying person should be established independently.
In reality, one is detached from death, and there exists no "one who dies" that is established.
Yet the world discriminates, saying, "This is death" and "this is the one who dies.
Not knowing the coming and going of death, for this reason one is ultimately unable to escape it.
By means of such causes and conditions, one contemplates the characteristics of all phenomena;
with a mind that remains unwavering, one ultimately has no fear of death.
Regarding "having no fear of the evil realms":
Because Bodhisattvas constantly cultivate merit and virtue, they do not fear falling into the evil realms.
They form this thought:
"It is the transgressors who fall into the evil realms, not those who possess merit."

From this moment until even a single thought arises, I shall not allow any evils to enter; rather, I shall constantly give rise to pure actions of body, speech, and mind. Therefore, I have attained the accomplishment of immeasurable and boundless merit.
"Since he is such a mass of great merit, why would he fear falling into the evil realms?

Furthermore, because a bodhisattva has once resolved his mind for the sake of benefiting and bringing peace to all sentient beings, and because he is protected by great compassion, he abides in the four bases of merit and attains immeasurable virtue, thereby crossing over all evil realms. Why is this so?
This mind surpasses all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, as stated in the *Viniścaya-viśuddhi-sūtra*, where Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How rare!..."
“Excellent is the teaching of the World-Honored One!
By means of this mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*), a bodhisattva is able to surpass all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Having accomplished such great merit and abiding in such a Great Dharma, how could I fear falling into the evil realms?
Again, he reflects:
"Since beginningless time, I have wandered through birth and death, falling into the various evil realms and undergoing immeasurable suffering, neither benefiting myself nor benefiting others."
I now make this supreme and great vow for the sake of my own benefit and also for the benefit of others.
Previously, having fallen into the evil realms, I gained no benefit; now, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, even if I were to fall into the evil realms, I should have no fear.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva practicing the true path gives rise to this thought:
"Even if I must suffer in the Avīci Hell for one kalpa before being able to emerge from it, I shall cause even a single person to give rise to a single wholesome mind;
by accumulating such immeasurable wholesome minds, I shall become capable of transforming them, causing them to resolve upon the three vehicles."

"If I were to thus teach the Śrāvaka vehicle to beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle to beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and inspire the Mahāyāna in beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and only thereafter attain the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, even then I should not fall back; how much less so now, when I am cultivating and accumulating immeasurable and boundless merit and remaining far removed from the evil realms!"
When a bodhisattva reflects in this way, how could there be any fear of the evil realms?
Furthermore, as it is said in the *Raurava-niraya-sūtra*:
"The Bodhisattva replied to Māra:"
"Because of my practice of giving, I fell into the Raurava Hell;
yet all those who received my gifts were reborn in the heavens."
"If this were so, I should still constantly practice giving;
while sentient beings dwell in the heavens, I endure the suffering of wailing.
Through various causes and conditions such as these, the Bodhisattva is able to ward off the fear of the evil realms.
"Being without fear of the great assembly" means that because he has accomplished the wisdom of hearing,

the wisdom of reflection, and the wisdom of cultivation, and because he is free from the faults of various disputations, this Bodhisattva establishes his discourse such that what he says is without error.
He is able to employ causes, conditions, parables, and concluding verses—neither too many nor too few—without any doubt.
His speech is never devoid of meaning; it is free from flattery and deception.
He is upright, gentle, and harmonious, adorned with all manner of refinements.
It is easy to understand and easy to uphold; its meaning and sequence are clear.
It can illuminate one's own practice and refute the arguments of others.
It is free from the four false causes and possesses the four great causes.
With such adorned speech, he speaks amidst the great assembly without any fear.
Regarding "fear of ill repute" and "fear of being reviled":
because he does not crave gain and offerings, and because his conduct of body, speech, and mind is pure.
Regarding the phrase "there is no fear of confinement, shackles, fetters, or torture":

because there are no offenses; because of compassion for all sentient beings; because of enduring all sufferings and afflictions; and because one relies upon the retribution of karmic results—namely, that what was previously committed by oneself is now being experienced as its own retribution.
Because of such causes and conditions as these, this bodhisattva has no fear regarding livelihood or other such matters.
Furthermore, because they joyfully contemplate that all phenomena are without self, they are free from all fears.
All fears arise from the view of self; this view of self is the root of all decline, sorrow, and suffering.
Because this bodhisattva possesses sharp wisdom and penetrates deeply into the true nature of all phenomena as they truly are, there is no self.
Since I do not exist, from what could fear arise?
[The questioner] asks:
How does this bodhisattva lack the notion of a self?
Answer: Because they delight in the dharma of emptiness;
when a bodhisattva contemplates the body, they are detached from the notions of "self" and "what belongs to self."
As it is said:
"The self arises because of 'mine,' and 'mine' arises because of the self;
therefore, both the self and 'mine' are empty of inherent nature."
"I" is the master, and "mine" is the property of the master;
if there were no master, there would be no property of the master.
If there were no property of the master, then there would likewise be no master.
"I" is the view of self; "mine" is the view of what belongs to self.
Through observing reality, there is no self; since there is no self, there is no non-self.
Because of sensation, there is a feeler; yet where there is no sensation, there is no feeler.
Apart from the feeler, there is no feeling; how then could it be established by means of feeling?
If the feeler were established by means of feeling, then feeling itself would not be established;
because feeling is not established, the feeler cannot be established.
Because the recipient is empty, one cannot say it is "I";
because the recipient is empty, one cannot say it is "mine.
Therefore, there is neither self nor non-self, and neither both self and non-self.
Neither "self" nor "non-self"— these are all heterodox doctrines. "Mine" and "not mine," as well as "I" and "not mine," and "neither I nor mine"—
these too are heterodox doctrines.
Because Bodhisattvas thus constantly delight in cultivating emptiness and selflessness, they are free from all fears.
Why is this? It is because the dharmas of emptiness and selflessness enable one to leave behind all fears.
The Bodhisattva on the Stage of Joy possesses such characteristics as these.
Chapter Four: The Pure Stages. Question:
Having attained the first stage, how should the Bodhisattva cultivate and purify it?
The answer is:
The power of faith increases further; practicing the mind of great compassion deeply, one feels pity for all classes of sentient beings and cultivates a virtuous mind without weariness.
Rejoicing in all sublime dharmas, always drawing near to virtuous friends,
possessing shame and modesty with a respectful mind, and keeping the heart supple and harmonious;
observing the Dharma with joy and non-attachment, seeking much learning with a single-minded focus.
Not coveting gain or offerings, free from guile, deceit, and flattery;
not defiling the family of the Buddhas, nor violating the precepts or deceiving the Buddha;
deeply delighting in *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), as immovable as a great mountain.
Constantly delighting in the practice of cultivation, They turn toward the sublime Dharma that transcends all;
Delighting in the supramundane Dharma, They take no pleasure in worldly dharmas.
Thus they govern the Stage of Joy, A stage difficult to govern, yet they are able to govern it.
Therefore, with constant single-mindedness, diligently practice these various dharmas.
When a bodhisattva is able to accomplish such sublime and wondrous dharmas,
they are then said to be securely established within the first stage of a bodhisattva.
By means of these twenty-seven dharmas, the Bodhisattva purifies and cultivates the first stage (*bhūmi*).
Regarding "the predominance of the power of faith" (*śraddhā-bala-adhimātra*):
faith (*śraddhā*) refers to that which, having been heard or seen, is accepted with certainty and without doubt.
"Adhipati" means "superior. Question:
There are two kinds of adhipati:
The first is "abundant" and the second is "superior.
Which one is being discussed here?
The answer is:
In this context, two matters are explained together.

Because a bodhisattva entering the first stage (*prathamā bhūmiḥ*) attains the flavor of all meritorious qualities, the power of their faith increases further; by means of this power of faith, they weigh the qualities of the Buddhas and are able to believe in and accept them as immeasurable, profound, and sublime. Therefore, this mind is both vast and superior.
Regarding "profoundly practicing great compassion":
it is called "profound" because his compassionate concern for sentient beings penetrates to the very marrow of his bones;
it is called "great" because he seeks the Buddha-way for the sake of all sentient beings.
"Kindness of mind" (maitrī-citta) means constantly seeking beneficial matters to bring peace and security to sentient beings.
There are three types of kindness, which shall be explained in detail later.
Regarding "cultivating wholesome states of mind without weariness":
wholesome dharmas are called those that should be approached and practiced, for they can yield desirable fruits.
When practicing such dharmas, the mind does not become lax or indolent.

The causes and conditions for wholesome dharmas refer to the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*), the ten paths of wholesome action (*daśakuśalakarmapatha*), the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), the ten stages of the bodhisattva (*bodhisattvabhūmi*), and so forth, as well as all other meritorious qualities.
"Delighting in the sublime Dharma" means:
by constantly contemplating and practicing it, one deeply attains the flavor of the Dharma; after a long time, joy arises.
It is like a person in a flower grove, enjoying themselves with its lovely forms and colors.
Regarding "always remaining close to spiritual friends" (*kalyāṇamitra*):
there are four kinds of spiritual friends for a bodhisattva, which shall be explained in detail later.
In this context, the spiritual friends are the Buddhas and bodhisattvas.
One should always approach [the teacher] with a correct mind, which can cause them to rejoice.
"Shame and remorse" (hrī-apatrāpya) means being joyful in one's sense of shame.
"Reverence": it means to keep in mind one's virtues and to hold that person in high esteem. "Gentleness":
It is called "the harmony and joy of the mind" and "dwelling together in peace and happiness.
Regarding "joyfully contemplating the dharmas":
"dharmas" refers to the five aggregates (skandhas), the twelve bases (āyatanas), the eighteen elements (dhātus), emptiness (śūnyatā), signlessness (animitta), wishlessness (apraṇihita), and so forth.
With right mindfulness, one should constantly contemplate this Dharma.
Regarding "non-attachment":
attachment refers to the mind’s inclination toward an object.
The three realms of existence are where sentient beings take refuge. Some say:
"The five desires and various false views are what they resort to."
Why is this? Because the minds of sentient beings are constantly bound by attachment.
Bodhisattvas possess sharp wisdom, and their minds are free from greedy attachment.
“Single-mindedness” means valuing the Buddha-dharma and having no other thoughts in the mind.
Regarding “seeking great renown”:
it refers to being able to exhaustively investigate the ninefold scriptures taught by the Buddha, practicing and studying them until they are clearly understood, leaving nothing incomplete.
Regarding "not coveting gain and support":
"gain" refers to obtaining food, drink, wealth, and so forth;
"support" refers to receiving respect and prostrations, being provided with beds and seats, and being welcomed and seen off.
A bodhisattva should bestow these things upon sentient beings without being greedily attached to them themselves.
"Deceitful fraud" refers to the falsification of measures such as bushels and scales, or the use of counterfeit clothing and goods.
“Flattery” (*śāṭhya*) refers to a mind that is not upright.
“Deceit” (*māyā*) refers to the five modes of wrong livelihood:
first, hypocrisy; second, self-familiarization; third, incitement; fourth, exaggeration and disparagement; and fifth, seeking profit from profit.
Regarding "pretending to be eccentric":

there are those who, out of greed for gain and offerings, adopt such ascetic practices (*dhūta-guṇa*) as dwelling in the forest (*āraṇyaka*), wearing rag-robes (*pāṃsukūlika*), always begging for food (*piṇḍapātika*), eating at a single sitting (*ekāsanika*), always sitting (*naiṣadyika*), or not drinking liquids after midday; they then think:
"Others perform these practices and receive offerings and respect; if I perform these practices, perhaps I too shall obtain them."
To alter one’s deportment for the sake of gain and honor is called "feigning eccentricity.
As for "befriending oneself":
there are those who, out of greed for gain and honor, go to the homes of donors and say:
"They are no different from my own parents, brothers, sisters, and relatives.
If they have anything they require, I can provide it for them;
if they wish to do anything, I can do it for them."
"I do not consider distance; I am able to come to inquire after your health.
My staying here is solely for your sake.
For the sake of seeking offerings, they are greedily attached to their patrons and can entice people's hearts with their words; those such as these are called "intimates."
"Agitation" refers to someone who disregards the offense of greed and, desiring to obtain material goods, creates the mental image of acquiring them, saying:
"This bowl is excellent; or this robe is excellent; or this door-latch is excellent; or this sitting mat (niṣīdana) is excellent. If I were to obtain these, I would be able to make use of them."
Furthermore, he says:
"A person who can give according to their own inclination is difficult to find.
He also goes to the house of a donor and speaks these words:

“The soup, rice, cakes, and meat in your home are fragrant and delicious, and your clothing is also fine; you have always made offerings to me, and because of our long-standing friendship, I shall certainly give it to you.”
Manifesting such signs of greed in this manner is called "agitation.
Regarding "exaltation and disparagement":
there are those who, out of a desire for gain and offerings, say to a donor:
"You are so extremely stingy that you cannot even give to your parents, brothers, sisters, wife, children, or relatives; who then could possibly obtain your property?"
The donor felt ashamed and, with a mixture of reluctance and compliance, made the offering.
He then went to other households and said:
"You possess great merit; your human existence is not in vain, for Arhats constantly enter and leave your home. You should offer them a seat and engage them in conversation."
He formed this thought: "The donor might think:
'There is no one else entering or leaving my house; they must surely be referring to me.'"
This is called "exalting and disparaging.
Regarding "seeking profit through profit":
there is someone who takes up articles for the necessities of life—such as robes, an alms bowl, a saṃghāṭī, or a sitting mat—and shows them to others, saying:
"If a king, one like a king, or other nobles give this object to me," he thinks:
"The donor might perhaps give rise to [this] thought:"
"If even those kings and nobles are able to provide offerings, how much more so should I not give to such a person?
Because one seeks further gain by means of this initial gain, it is called "seeking gain through gain."
Therefore, one should remain far removed from such flattery and hypocrisy.
Regarding the phrase "not defiling the family of the Buddhas":
what constitutes defiling the family of the Buddhas?

Some say: "If a person has already resolved to seek the unsurpassed path, yet later turns toward the paths of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, they will be unable to remain in the world to continue the lineage of the Triple Gem; this is called defiling the family of the Buddhas."
This interpretation is not correct.

Why? Because this person is able to cross over birth and death, and has further attained the various untainted faculties (*indriya*), powers (*bala*), factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*), and the path (*mārga*); they are also a child of the Buddha. How, then, can it be said that they defile the family of the Buddhas?
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
'You are my sons; you are born from my mind and born from my mouth, having obtained a share of the Dharma.'"
Furthermore,
the śrāvakas say:
"The foundations of truth, relinquishment, cessation, and wisdom are called the family of the Buddhas."
Why is this? Because it is from these four matters that all Buddhas are born.
If one defiles these four dharmas, it is called defiling the family of the Buddhas.
Therefore, if a person is false, stingy and greedy, deranged, or deluded, they defile the family of the Buddhas.
If one correctly practices these four [opposites], then one does not defile the families of all Buddhas.
Some say: "The six pāramitās are the family of all Buddhas, for it is from these that all Buddhas are born;
if one violates these six matters, one defiles the Buddha-family."
Some say: "Prajñāpāramitā is the mother of all Buddhas, and skillful means (upāya) is the father; this is called the family of the Buddhas.
Since these two dharmas give birth to all Buddhas, to contravene these dharmas is to defile the Buddha-family."
Furthermore, the verse itself explains the characteristics of defilement and non-defilement, namely: "not violating the precepts" and "not deceiving the Buddha.
If one receives the Buddha’s precepts but is unable to guard and uphold them, one then deceives all Buddhas; this is to defile the Buddha's household.
Why is this? When one receives the precepts, one is born into the family of the Buddhas; to break the precepts is to deceive all the Buddhas, which is called defiling the Buddha-family.
Question:
"Does it follow that a bodhisattva must necessarily break the precepts?
He replied:
"The failure to sever the afflictions is what is truly to be feared."
Not long after entering the state of certainty (*niyāma*), some bodhisattvas may break the precepts.
As it is said in the *Mahāvaipulya-buddha-dharma-sūtra*: "Nanda intentionally broke the precepts.
Even when I speak of such matters, I still regard them with apprehension.
"However, because this scripture contains such a teaching and because one has faith in the Buddha's words, the mind accepts it with conviction.
If one receives the precepts without breaking them and does not deceive the Buddhas, this is called 'not defiling the Buddha-family.'"

Furthermore, the name "precepts" refers to the three trainings—the training in morality, the training in mind, and the training in wisdom. To violate these trainings is called defiling the Buddha’s family;
to receive the precepts according to the Dharma and subsequently destroy them is called deceiving the Buddha.
These two phrases each have their own specific meaning.
"Deceiving the Buddha" means to make vows in vain while failing to act according to one's words, thereby deceiving sentient beings; this is called deceiving the Buddha.
Furthermore, among all dharmas, to act contrary to what has been taught is called "deceiving the Buddha.
Regarding the phrase "firmly abiding in *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), immovable like a great mountain":
this means that in all the vows the bodhisattva makes to seek *sarvajñā*, through various causes and conditions—even unto the sufferings of the great hells—their mind does not waver.
Like Sumeru, the king of mountains, it cannot be moved by the wind.
"Constantly practicing the ever-surpassing dharmas" means:

from the first generation of the mind of enlightenment, one constantly seeks the superior dharma; upon entering the first stage (*bhūmi*), one further practices the higher dharmas; thus progressing step by step, the mind never knows satiety.
Regarding the phrase "delighting in supramundane dharmas and not delighting in mundane dharmas":
mundane dharmas refer to things that conform to worldly affairs and increase birth and death.

The six destinies, the three realms of existence, the five aggregates, the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, the twelve links of dependent origination, all afflictions, and contaminated karma, and so forth.
Supramundane dharmas:

these are named according to the dharmas employed that enable one to transcend the triple world. They are: the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold path, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power; the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; the restraint of the precepts, extensive learning, the roots of goodness consisting of non-attachment, non-hatred, and non-delusion, the mind of wearying detachment, and heedfulness, among others.
Because this bodhisattva possesses sharp faculties, he does not delight in the false dharmas of the world, but delights only in the true dharmas that transcend the world.
Regarding the phrase "he treats the Stage of Joy, which is difficult to treat, yet is able to treat it":
"treats" (治) means to penetrate with unimpeded mastery.
It is like a person splitting bamboo: the first section is difficult, while the remaining ones are all easy.
The first stage (*bhūmi*) is difficult to cultivate; once it has been cultivated, the rest become easy by themselves. Why is this?

When a bodhisattva is on the first stage (*bhūmi*), their power is not yet sufficient, their roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) are not yet deep, and they have not long practiced the wholesome dharmas; therefore, the eye and other faculties still follow after sensory objects, the mind is not yet tamed, and thus the various afflictions (*kleśa*) are still able to cause harm.
It is like a person whose strength is insufficient; going against the current is difficult.

Furthermore, because Māras and their followers create many obstacles within this stage, one must practice with diligence through the power of skillful means; for this reason, this stage is called "Difficult to Master."

Thus, beginning with "the power of faith becomes increasingly superior" and concluding with "not delighting in worldly dharmas," one cultivates these twenty-seven dharmas to remedy the first stage of the bodhisattva, the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*); therefore, it is said that a bodhisattva should constantly practice these dharmas.
Cultivation means single-minded heedfulness;
because one constantly practices and constantly contemplates to eliminate all faults and evils, it is called "treatment.
It is like a person who treats a traveled road to make it clean and clear.
These dharmas are not only for cultivating the first stage; all stages are cultivated by means of these dharmas.
Question: You have already explained the skillful means for attaining the first stage and the methods for its purification.
How does a bodhisattva abide so as not to fall back?
The answer is:
constantly practicing and accomplishing such dharmas as "the power of faith further increasing," this is called abiding in the first stage (bhūmi).
*Bodhi* is called the supreme path;
*sattva* is called the profound mind.
Because one deeply delights in *bodhi*, one is called a *bodhisattva*.

Furthermore, "sentient beings" (sattva) refers to those who are called *sattva*. Because they cultivate and accumulate enlightenment (*bodhi*) for the sake of sentient beings, they are called Bodhisattvas.
Regarding "supreme dharmas":
because dharmas such as faith and the like can cause a person to attain the Buddha-way, they are called supreme dharmas.

5. Commentary on the Chapter on Vows (Praṇidhāna-viniścaya). The "expedient means for entering the first stage" (*prathamabhūmi-praveśopāya*) and the "purification of the dharmas" have already been explained.

Because of their vows, bodhisattvas are able to enter the various stages; furthermore, by accomplishing qualities such as the increase of the power of faith (*śraddhā-bala*), they abide securely within those stages. Now, these vows shall be analyzed in detail.
I vow to provide offerings and serve all Buddhas with reverence;
I vow to protect and uphold all the teachings of the Buddhas.
This is the first vow of all Bodhisattvas.

From the first generation of the mind of enlightenment until the attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, one shall fully make offerings to, serve, and revere all the Buddhas who appear during that interval.
"Offering" refers to such things as "flowers, incense, necklaces, banners, canopies, lamps, and the construction of stupas and temples.
"Providing" refers to "robes, bedding, and all necessary articles."
Reverence means "to honor, prostrate, welcome and see off, join the palms, and serve with devotion.
Furthermore, to teach and transform sentient beings by means of the Dharma of the Śrāvakas is called making offerings;
to teach and transform sentient beings by means of the Dharma of the Pratyekabuddhas is called providing service.
To teach and transform sentient beings by means of the Mahāyāna Dharma is called "reverence";
this is the first vow.
Regarding the protection and upholding of all the Buddhas' teachings, the bodhisattva reflects as follows:
"I should protect all the dharmas of the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time—past, future, and present.
He asked: "The past Buddhas have already passed away, and their dharmas have likewise ceased with them."
When future Buddhas have not yet appeared and the Dharma does not yet exist,
there is not even the first turning of the Wheel of Dharma, let alone other teachings!
How, then, could it be protected?
One can indeed protect the dharmas of all Buddhas of the present, because all Buddhas are currently present.
The answer is:
the dharmas of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present are all of one essence and one characteristic.
Therefore, if one protects a single Buddha-dharma, one protects the Buddha-dharmas of all Buddhas of the three periods of time. As it is said in a sutra:
"The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

'The dharma of Vipaśyin Buddha—his renunciation, receiving the precepts, wearing robes, holding the alms bowl, meditative concentration, wisdom, preaching the Dharma, and teaching and transforming others—was also like mine.'"
Therefore, your objection is not valid;
this is the second vow.
Furthermore: The Buddhas descend from Tuṣita And come into this world.
Until the work of teaching and transforming all beings is complete, they shall forever enter the realm of nirvana without remainder.
Whether dwelling in the womb or at the time of birth, when leaving home to proceed to the site of enlightenment,
when subduing Māra and attaining the Buddha-way, and when first turning the wondrous Wheel of Dharma— [in all these stages, they remain ever present].
May I always welcome all Tathāgatas, as well as during other times;
may I fully attain the opportunity to serve and make offerings to them with all my heart,
from the moment the Buddhas descend from Tuṣita Heaven into the world until their final entry into *nirvāṇa* without remainder.

During that interval, they made grand offerings when he entered the womb, as well as at his birth, his renunciation and journey to the site of enlightenment, his subduing of the Māra king, his attainment of the Buddha-way, and his turning of the Wheel of Dharma, welcoming the Tathāgata on each occasion.
As for "other times":
when one manifests great supernormal powers at a great assembly of humans and devas to extensively deliver sentient beings;

at such times, one should employ flowers, incense, banners, canopies, music, songs, praises, leaving the household life to receive the Dharma, and practicing according to the teachings, using these foremost articles of offering to make offerings to the Buddhas.
This is the third vow.
Furthermore— I vow to teach and transform sentient beings, causing them all to enter the various paths.
"Teaching" means instructing others in wholesome dharmas.
Transformation is defined as being far removed from unwholesome dharmas.
By means of these two dharmas, I shall cause immeasurable, incalculable sentient beings to abide in the paths of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
This is the fourth vow.
Furthermore—may all sentient beings achieve the Bodhi of the Buddhas;
as for those who incline toward the paths of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.

If there are persons who cultivate and accumulate the dharmas of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas but have not yet entered the stage of certainty (*niyāma*), I shall teach and transform them, causing them to advance toward the Buddha-way.
If there are persons who do not incline toward the paths of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, I shall teach and transform them, causing them to incline toward the unsurpassed Buddha-way.
To those who are directed toward the unsurpassed path of the Buddha, I shall instruct, benefit, and gladden them, so that their merit may increase even further.
In this manner, I shall teach and transform all sentient beings.
This is the fifth vow.
Furthermore— May all phenomena be entered into with faith and understanding as equal.
"All phenomena" refers to whatever phenomena there may be:
Dharmas that lead to liberation and dharmas that do not lead to liberation;
dharmas that encompass the factors of enlightenment and dharmas that do not encompass the factors of enlightenment;
dharmas that assist the path and dharmas that do not assist the path.
Dharmas subsumed under the noble path and dharmas not subsumed under the noble path;
dharmas to be cultivated and dharmas not to be cultivated;
dharmas to be approached and dharmas not to be approached.
Dharmas that should arise and dharmas that should not arise;
dharmas that have arisen and dharmas that have not arisen;
present dharmas and non-present dharmas.
Phenomena arising from causes and conditions; phenomena not arising from causes and conditions.
Phenomena that are causal; phenomena that are non-causal.
Phenomena arising from mental reflection; phenomena not arising from mental reflection.
Coarse phenomena and subtle phenomena;
phenomena that are grasped and phenomena that are not grasped;
internal phenomena and external phenomena.
Dharmas included within the internal bases; dharmas not included within the internal bases.
Dharmas included within the external bases; dharmas not included within the external bases.
Dharmas included within the five aggregates; dharmas not included within the five aggregates.
Phenomena subsumed under the five aggregates of clinging and phenomena not subsumed under the five aggregates of clinging;
phenomena subsumed under the four noble truths and phenomena not subsumed under the four noble truths;
worldly auxiliary phenomena and non-worldly auxiliary phenomena.
Dharmas based on attachment and dharmas based on renunciation;
inverted dharmas and non-inverted dharmas;
changing dharmas and unchanging dharmas.
Dharmas involving remorse and dharmas not involving remorse;
great dharmas and small dharmas;
dharmas pertaining to a proper basis for acceptance and dharmas not pertaining to a proper basis for acceptance.
Dharmas that can be abandoned and dharmas that cannot be abandoned;
dharmas that are known and seen and dharmas that are not known and seen;
tainted dharmas and untainted dharmas.
There are bound phenomena and unbound phenomena.
There are pure phenomena and impure phenomena.
There are superior phenomena and unsurpassed phenomena.
There are dharmas with vitarka and dharmas without vitarka;
dharmas with vicāra and dharmas without vicāra;
dharmas that are agreeable and dharmas that are disagreeable.
Associated phenomena and dissociated phenomena;
differentiated phenomena and undifferentiated phenomena;
conditioned phenomena and unconditioned phenomena.
There are dharmas with conditions and dharmas without conditions.
There are dharmas that follow a sequence and dharmas that do not follow a sequence.
There are visible dharmas and invisible dharmas.
There are dharmas with resistance and dharmas without resistance;
dharmas visible and with resistance, and dharmas invisible and without resistance;
dharmas with signs and dharmas without signs.
Dharmas that may be practiced and dharmas that may not be practiced;
conditioned dharmas and unconditioned dharmas;
perilous dharmas and non-perilous dharmas.
There is the fundamental dharma and there is no fundamental dharma.
There is the dharma of emergence and there is no dharma of emergence.
There are the dharmas of sentient beings and the dharmas that are not sentient beings.
Phenomena that are suffering and phenomena that are not suffering;
phenomena that are afflictive and phenomena that are non-afflictive;
phenomena that exist and phenomena that do not exist.
Factors contrary to the Dharma and factors not contrary to the Dharma;
factors leading to pleasant retribution and factors not leading to pleasant retribution;
factors leading to painful retribution and factors not leading to painful retribution.
Dharmas born of recollection and dharmas not born of recollection;
dharmas whose practice is headed by wisdom and dharmas whose practice is not headed by wisdom;
dharmas whose practice is headed by faith and dharmas whose practice is not headed by faith.
Dharmas preceded by reflection and dharmas not preceded by reflection;
dharmas preceded by aspiration and dharmas not preceded by aspiration;
material dharmas and non-material dharmas.
Teachings and non-teachings;
transformative phenomena and non-transformative phenomena;
phenomena of wondrous travel and non-phenomena of wondrous travel.
Dharmas that are subject to desire and dharmas not subject to desire;
dharmas that have wholesome factors as their cause and dharmas that do not have wholesome factors as their cause;
dharmas that have roots of goodness as their cause and dharmas that do not have roots of goodness as their cause.
Determined phenomena and undetermined phenomena;
bodily phenomena and non-bodily phenomena;
vocal phenomena and non-vocal phenomena.
Mental phenomena and non-mental phenomena;
phenomena produced by contact with resistance and phenomena not produced by contact with resistance;
phenomena produced by mental contact and phenomena not produced by mental contact.
Unwholesome dharmas and non-unwholesome dharmas;
wholesome dharmas and non-wholesome dharmas;
productive dharmas and non-productive dharmas.
Dharmas that perish moment by moment and dharmas that do not perish moment by moment;
dharmas that are accumulative and dharmas that are not accumulative;
dharmas that pertain to the side of clarity and dharmas that do not pertain to the side of clarity.
Causes and non-causes;
conditions and non-conditions;
causes-and-conditions and non-causes-and-conditions.
Phenomena arising from causes and phenomena not arising from causes;
phenomena possessing causes and phenomena not possessing causes;
identical phenomena and distinct phenomena.
Dharmas subject to cessation and dharmas not subject to cessation;
dharmas included within the faculties and dharmas not included within the faculties;
dharmas associated with the mind and dharmas not associated with the mind.
Mental phenomena and non-mental phenomena;
mental concomitants and non-mental concomitants;
the five factors associated with contact and the five factors not associated with contact.
The sixteen dharmas shared with others and the sixteen dharmas not shared with others;
subtle dharmas and coarse dharmas;
dharmas dedicated toward enlightenment and dharmas not dedicated toward enlightenment.
Wholesome phenomena, unwholesome phenomena, and indeterminate phenomena;
phenomena to be abandoned by seeing the truths, phenomena to be abandoned by cultivation, and phenomena not to be abandoned;
phenomena of those in training, phenomena of those beyond training, and phenomena of neither training nor beyond training.

—All these immeasurable tens of millions of kinds of dharmas are made to enter the gates of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; they are equal and non-dual by virtue of the power of faith and understanding.
This is the sixth vow.
*Daśabhūmivibhāṣā-śāstra*, Scroll 20 (also titled *Daśabhūmivibhāṣā-śāstra*, Scroll 3).
Composed by the Holy Nāgārjuna;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty.
Furthermore: "In order to purify the Buddha-fields, may all various evils be extinguished."
Killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, divisive speech, harsh speech, frivolous chatter, greed, anger, wrong livelihood, drinking alcohol, and so forth—
such evils as these are called impurity.
Furthermore, within a land, the presence of various evil realms such as the hells, animals, and hungry ghosts is termed "impure."

Furthermore, sentient beings who lack faith, are indolent, have distracted minds, are ignorant, deceitful, stingy, envious, heavy with anger and resentment, hold wrong views, and are characterized by pride, arrogance, great pride, self-pride, false pride, affectation, self-familiarity, agitation, fluctuation, seeking profit from profit, valuing worldly pleasures, being heedless and unrestrained, having many desires, evil desires, perverse greed, perverse lust, not recognizing their parents, śramaṇas, or brāhmaṇas, lacking forbearance, violating dignified conduct, being difficult to speak with, having perverse thoughts and reflections, and being shrouded by covetousness, malice, sloth, restlessness, and doubt—these are called impure.

Furthermore, malignant birds and beasts, numerous enemies and bandits, the lack of water and grain, famine and pestilence, fear of humans and fear of non-humans, internal rebellion and external invasions, excessive rain or severe drought, various forms of decay and affliction, and all the sufferings at the end of a minor kalpa—these are called impurities.

Furthermore, sentient beings who have short lifespans, ugly complexions, and lack strength; who experience much sorrow and suffering; who have little courage or capability, many illnesses, little majesty, few followers, or followers who are wicked or easily corrupted; who live in small households, are weak and inferior, or have left the home life in a heterodox manner—these are called impure.
Furthermore, [there were] the followers of Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Ulūka-rāja, Nappātaka, Vikhaṇa,
Piṅgala-rāja, the ṛṣi Nāgila, the elephant-ṛṣi, the one who has severed lust, the superior disciple-practitioner,
the shepherd, the one of great mind, the one of patience, and Garga...
Dharmika, Kūlaṇḍaka, Jīvakas, Tarukāśikas, Ambuvāsikas, Pārasīkas,
Pāṭaliputrakas, Āvarāṇakas, Nirvastrakas, Vairambhakas, Carmavāsakas, Tṛṇasaṃvṛtikas, Adhovastrikas, and Śikhaṇḍilakas.
Those who wear garments of tree bark, those who have washed three times, those who follow [the path],
those who serve Brahmā, those who serve Kumāra, those who serve piśācas, those who serve garuḍas,
those who serve the king of the yamas, those who serve Vaiśravaṇa, and those who serve the Secret One.
Those who worship the deity Traces, those who worship the deity Arbuda, those who worship Nāgas,
naked ascetics (nirgrantha), white-robed ascetics, dyed-robed ascetics, Māgandiya ascetics, followers of Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, followers of Maskarin Gośālīputra,
followers of Sañjayin Vairaṭīputra, followers of Ajita Keśakambalin, and those who observe the cow-vow.
The precepts of dogs, the precepts of horses, the precepts of elephants, the precepts of mendicants,
the precepts of *kumāras*, the precepts of the various devas, the higher precepts, the precepts of celibacy, the precepts of purity, the fire-precepts,
those who claim that the cessation of form is nirvāṇa, and those who claim that the cessation of sound is nirvāṇa.
those who teach that the cessation of fragrance is nirvāṇa; those who teach that the cessation of flavor is nirvāṇa; those who teach that the cessation of touch is nirvāṇa;
those who teach that the cessation of vitarka and vicāra is nirvāṇa; those who teach that the cessation of joy is nirvāṇa; those who teach that the cessation of suffering and pleasure is nirvāṇa;
those who wear water-moss as garlands; those who practice water-purity; and those who practice food-purity.
Those who believe in birth as pure, those who hold to the pestle and mortar, those who strike stones, those who delight in washing, those who float and sink, those who dwell in empty spaces,
those who lie upon thorns, those who hold to the primordial nature (*prakṛti*), those who hold to the Great One (*mahat*), those who hold to the Self (*ātman*),
and those who hold to form (*rūpa*) and so forth, sound (*śabda*) and so forth, fragrance (*gandha*) and so forth, taste (*rasa*) and so forth, and touch (*spraṣṭavya*) and so forth.
...the knower of earth, the knower of water, the knower of fire, the knower of wind,
the knower of space, the knower of combination, the knower of transformation, the knower of the eye, the knower of the ear,
the knower of the nose, the knower of the tongue, the knower of the body, the knower of the mind, and the knower of the spirit.
Such various wrong views and wrong practices among householders and renunciants are called impure.
Furthermore, the ground is uneven, with pits, hollows, mounds, and hillocks; it is thick with brushwood and thorny brambles, presenting many obstacles;
it is covered in dust and filth, mired in mud and bogged down in pits, and features treacherous, jagged mountains with winding clefts and obstructed recesses.
The heavy mountain ranges are obstructive and steep, making them difficult to ascend; the soil is saline and alkaline, parched, and strewn with sand, gravel, shards, and stones.
The various fruits have little flavor and lack both color and fragrance; medicinal herbs are of poor quality, possessing meager potency.
Rare are those things of exquisite color, sound, fragrance, taste, and texture.
Gardens, groves, towers, and pavilions; flowing streams and bathing pools; small hills and earthen mounds from which one may ascend and gaze afar—all such places of recreation were exceedingly few.
Districts, counties, and villages were not situated close to one another; the land was largely overgrown with mounds and wasteland, and the population was sparse.
One frequently beheld cities that were meritless, impoverished, and lowly.
Ministers, herdsmen, high officials, nobles, various merchants, hosts and guests, skilled artisans, master craftsmen, and those who study and recite are likewise very few;
furthermore, clothing, bedding, medicine, and other articles for bodily comfort are extremely difficult to obtain, and even when obtained, they are not of fine quality.
It is called impurity.
Briefly stated, there are two kinds of impurity:
first, that which arises from the conditions of sentient beings; second, that which arises from the conditions of karmic actions.
Regarding the causal conditions of sentient beings, they arise from the faults and evils of sentient beings.
Regarding the causal conditions of formative actions (*saṃskāra*), they arise from the faults and evils of all formations (*saṃskāra*).
These two matters have already been explained above.
When these two matters are transformed, there arise the merit of sentient beings and the merit of karmic actions.
These two merits are called the Pure Land; this pure land should be understood as following the causal conditions of the original vows of the various bodhisattvas.

Because these bodhisattvas are able to practice various forms of great diligence, their vows are immeasurable and cannot be fully described; therefore, I shall now briefly explain them, merely indicating the general outline of the matters.
All other matters should be understood in this same way. To briefly describe the characteristics of the Pure Land, they are as follows:

the Bodhisattvas have well attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; the Buddha’s power of merit; the perfection of the Dharma; the perfection of the Śrāvakas; the perfection of the Bodhi tree; the adornment of the world; the excellent benefit for sentient beings; the great number of those capable of being saved; the assembly of the great multitude; and the perfection of the Buddha’s powers.
Those who well attain Bodhi are adorned with ten things:

first, being free from all ascetic practices; second, having no mind of weariness or inferiority; third, attaining it with swiftness; fourth, not seeking teachers of external paths; fifth, the perfection of the bodhisattvas; sixth, the absence of Māra’s enmity; seventh, the absence of all obstacles; eighth, the great assembly of devas; ninth, the perfection of rare and marvelous events; and tenth, the perfection of the time.
Regarding "being free from all ascetic practices":
if a bodhisattva has left the household life for the sake of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they do not engage in various ascetic practices, namely:
fasting for four days, six days, eight days, half a month, or one month; or even consuming only a single sesame seed, a single grain of rice, or a single fruit.
Some drink only water, while others practice only the cultivation of vital energy (*vāyu*).
Without seeking the Way through such ascetic practices, he sat peacefully at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and attained Buddhahood.
He was one who possessed no weary or inferior mind.
If a bodhisattva attains even a slight degree of the mind of weary detachment, they immediately leave the household life.
Regarding "attaining it swiftly":
if a bodhisattva, having already left the household life, immediately attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Not seeking teachers of external paths" means that once a bodhisattva has gone forth, even if there are renowned masters of external paths at that time, they do not go to them to inquire:
"What dharma do you teach?"
"What matter does he discuss?
What is his benefit?
He likewise does not seek it out in the four directions.
Regarding the "Bodhisattva Endowed with Fulfillment":

when a bodhisattva desires to attain the Buddha-way, all the bodhisattvas within the trichiliocosm, as well as those from other directions, each bring offerings and arrive to surround him in full assembly.

They shall await the Buddha’s attainment of enlightenment; when he emits great radiance, they will together make offerings to him, hear the Dharma from the Buddha, and all become non-retrogressive bodhisattvas in their final birth before Buddhahood.
"Being free from the Māra-enemy" means that when a Bodhisattva is on the verge of attaining Buddhahood, no demonic host is able to come and destroy [the path].
"Being free from all obstacles" means:
When a Bodhisattva is on the verge of attaining Buddhahood, not even a hair’s breadth of affliction enters his mind.
As for the great assembly gathered there:

when the Bodhisattva is on the verge of attaining Buddhahood, there are the gods of the Four Great Kings, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, the Brahmā Heaven, and so on up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.
All the various deities, including the nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and so forth.

From the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions, each brings the most supreme and wondrous articles of offering to make offerings to the Bodhisattva; this is called the "Gathering of the Great Assembly."
Furthermore, the śrāvakas say:
"When all the devas from the ten worlds have come together, it is called the Great Assembly of Devas.
One who is endowed with rare and marvelous practices is [a true assembly]."
When a Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, the earth shakes in six ways.

Throughout the immeasurable trichiliocosm worlds of the ten directions, the palaces of all the Māra kings undergo transformation and decay; they become colorless, and their radiance no longer appears.

Immeasurable Mount Sumerus all shook, and immeasurable great oceans all trembled; in all worlds, untimely flowers appeared, and sandalwood powder incense and various celestial named flowers rained down—these were rare and wondrous events.
As for "endowed with the right time":
at that time there will be no epidemics, famine, warfare, displacement, or flight.
Rainfall will occur according to the seasons, and there will be no calamities or misfortunes.
The various kings and rulers govern according to the Dharma; the people are peaceful and happy, and their lifespans are prolonged.
There are no enemies, bandits, predatory birds or beasts, venomous insects, or malevolent spirits to afflict or harm sentient beings.

Regarding the power of the Buddha’s merit: the majestic power, merit, wisdom, and immeasurable profound dharmas of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present are equal and without distinction. However, according to the causal conditions of each Buddha’s original vows, some have an immeasurable lifespan;

some cause those who see them to immediately attain the stage of certainty (*niyāma*), and those who hear their names likewise attain certainty; some cause women who see them to immediately become male bodies, and those who hear their names likewise transform their female bodies;
and some cause those who hear their names to immediately attain rebirth [in his land].
There may be immeasurable lights such that sentient beings who encounter them are freed from all hindrances and obscurations;
or by means of these lights they immediately enter the state of certainty (*niyāma*);
or by means of these lights all suffering and affliction are extinguished.
"Immeasurable lifespan" means that his life span lasts for immeasurable kalpas,

exceeding all calculations— whether one kalpa, a hundred kalpas, a thousand kalpas, ten thousand kalpas, a hundred million kalpas, or hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas of asaṃkhyeya kalpas;
he abides thus for such a long time for the sake of benefiting and having compassion for sentient beings.
Although all Buddhas possess immeasurable power and lifespan, by virtue of their original vows, some abide in the world for a long time while others do not.
Regarding those who attain entry into the stage of certainty upon seeing [a Buddha]:
there are sentient beings who, upon seeing a Buddha, immediately abide in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and the stage of *avaivartika*. Why is this?
When these sentient beings behold the Buddha’s body, their hearts are filled with great joy, purity, and delight; their minds immediately attain such a bodhisattva samādhi.
By the power of this samādhi, they penetrate the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena and are able to enter directly into the stage of certainty (*niyama-bhūmi*) of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

These beings have cultivated deep-seated roots of goodness over a long night, planting the seeds for seeing the Buddha and entering the stage of certainty; with great compassion as their primary motivation, they are virtuous, wondrous, and pure. Because they seek to penetrate all Buddha-dharmas and to deliver all sentient beings, the time has now arrived for these roots of goodness to reach fulfillment; therefore, they are able to encounter this Buddha.
Furthermore, through the causal conditions of the original vows of all Buddhas, and by the convergence of these two factors, this matter is accomplished.
Regarding those who hear the Buddha’s name and enter the stage of certainty (*niyāma*):
the Buddha possesses an original vow that if anyone hears his name, they shall immediately enter the stage of certainty.
As it is with seeing the Buddha, so it is with hearing him.
Regarding women who see the transformation of their female form:
if there is one who single-mindedly seeks to transform her female form, deeply loathing it herself, possessing the power of faith and understanding, and vows for a male body—
If such a woman should behold the Buddha, she will immediately transform her female form.
If a woman lacks such karmic causes and conditions, or if the karma of her female body has not yet been exhausted, she shall not encounter such a Buddha.
Regarding women who, upon hearing the name of the Buddha, transform their female forms:
the causes and conditions for this matter are as explained in the "Seeing the Buddha" chapter.
Regarding those who, by hearing the name of the Buddha, attain rebirth [in the Pure Land]:
If a person possesses great power of faith and understanding, has perfected their various roots of goodness, and has exhausted all karmic obstacles, such a person shall hear the names of the Buddhas.
Furthermore, by virtue of the causal conditions of the original vows of those Buddhas, they will immediately attain rebirth there.
Regarding "immeasurable radiance":
it is that which is illumined by the radiance of all Buddhas, extending far or near according to one's will.
This so-called "immeasurable" refers to their constant radiance.
Its constant radiance cannot be measured by the distance of *yojana*s; it fills hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions,
and billions of *yojanas* in the eastern direction to such an extent that it cannot be measured,
and it is likewise in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below.
One merely knows its immeasurability, yet cannot know its limits.
As for those who encounter the light and are able to eliminate all hindrances:

this is brought about by the power of the fundamental vows of the Buddhas; having removed these obstructive hindrances—namely, sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and regret, and doubt—sentient beings who encounter the light are immediately able to practice mindfulness of the Buddha.
"Because of the causal conditions of mindfulness of the Buddha, one is mindful of the Dharma; because of mindfulness of the Dharma, the various hindrances are removed.
When light touches the body, all suffering and affliction are extinguished":
this refers to when sentient beings fall among those in the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, or among non-humans, where there is much suffering and affliction.
By the power of the Buddha’s original vows and his supernormal abilities, light touches their bodies, and they immediately attain liberation from suffering.
Regarding the "perfection of the Dharma":

all the dharmas of the Buddhas are entirely perfected; there is nothing that is either perfected or unperfected, for since the teachings of all Buddhas are identical, the Dharma is fully perfected in all of them.
It is only because of the causes and conditions of their original vows that there are differences; some may remain for a long time, while others do not!
What is meant by the perfection of the Dharma?
The Dharma has a brief exposition, an extensive exposition, and a brief-and-extensive exposition.
There are those who are fully endowed with the Śrāvaka-yāna, those fully endowed with the Pratyekabuddha-yāna, and those fully endowed with the Mahāyāna.
By means of various supernormal powers, they shall be protected so that they are not destroyed by non-Buddhists nor defeated by Māras, and may long abide in the world.
Brief exposition means that by means of few words,
many meanings are encompassed, so that those of sharp faculties attain awakening upon hearing them.
Extensive exposition means:
Regarding a single matter or a single meaning, he expounds and explains it through various causes and conditions for the sake of those with dull faculties who delight in analytical discrimination.
As for what is taught both concisely and extensively:
even with a single word, he encompasses a vast range of meanings.
Furthermore, there are various ways in which a single meaning is expounded and disseminated.
There are those who fully possess the Śrāvaka vehicle, those who fully possess the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, and those who fully possess the Mahāyāna;
this matter shall be explained later.
Regarding "protecting the Dharma through spiritual power":
this Dharma is protected and kept in mind by the spiritual power of the Buddhas, and it is sealed with the seals of all Buddhas.
The seal of all Buddhas refers to the four great causes, which are free from the four dark causes.
"Being uncorrupted by non-Buddhists" means that all śramaṇas,
brahmins, and non-Buddhist teachers hold various false views regarding arising, cessation, gratification, peril, and escape.
Furthermore, regarding the realization of all that is wholesome and the teaching on the causes and conditions for its destruction,
one who is not destroyed by any māras does so because the Buddhas possess immeasurable and boundless merit, wisdom, skillful means, and supernormal powers.
Although Māra possesses power, he cannot destroy it.
Furthermore, by the power of the bodhisattvas, Māra is unable to destroy it.
Regarding "the Dharma abiding for a long time":
Whether for one kalpa, or less than a kalpa;

or for more than hundreds of kalpas, thousands of kalpas, tens of thousands of kalpas, hundreds of thousands of kalpas, millions of kalpas, ten million kalpas, hundred million kalpas, or immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of nayutas of asaṃkhyeya kalpas, even unto immeasurable and boundless kalpas.
Regarding the fulfillment of the śrāvakas:

all Buddhas are fully endowed with a community of śrāvakas; however, due to the causes and conditions of their respective original vows, there are differences in the smallness or greatness [of these communities].
What is meant by "endowment"?

It refers to the Tathāgata’s assembly of śrāvakas, who are fully endowed with ethical discipline, meditative concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; they are equally pure, all possess sharp faculties, benefit all bodhisattvas, and are of majestic and pure appearance.

One who is fully endowed with the observance of precepts is one who stays far removed from all unwholesome dharmas, such as killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, frivolous speech, drinking intoxicants, and wrong livelihood.
Furthermore, they remain entirely remote from all that is prohibited by the Vinaya, and because they are able to accomplish the untainted precepts (*anāsrava-śīla*).
As for "being fully endowed with meditative concentration" (*dhyāna-samādhi*):

it refers to the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables (*catur-apramāṇa*), the four formless attainments (*catasra ārūpya-samāpattayaḥ*), the eight liberations (*aṣṭau vimokṣāḥ*), the eight stages of transcendence (*aṣṭau abhibhvāyatanāni*), the ten totalities (*daśa kṛtsnāyatanāni*), and so forth, as well as the attainment of various untainted meditative concentrations.
One who is endowed with wisdom:
they have accomplished four kinds of wisdom—
wisdom born from extensive learning, wisdom born from reflection, wisdom born from cultivation, and wisdom born from the karmic retribution of causes and conditions in previous lives.
One who is fully endowed with liberation:
one who has attained liberation from all afflictions and has also attained liberation from all hindrances.
One who is fully endowed with the knowledge and vision of liberation:
"Name" refers to knowing the matter; "seeing" refers to clearly understanding that matter. Within liberation, one knows and sees with perfect clarity, free from doubt.
Furthermore, "name" refers to the knowledge of the exhaustion [of outflows] (*kṣayajñāna*);
"seeing" refers to seeing the Four Noble Truths.
"Equal" means that all those who have entered the fruit of *srotāpanna* are entirely equal, and this remains so up to the *arhat*.
"Pure" means:
They have accomplished the three kinds of purity: purity of body, purity of speech, and purity of mind.
As for those of sharp intelligence:
merely hearing a few words, they are able to extensively understand and penetrate their meaning and intent.
To condense the extensive and expand the concise, and to make subtle and hidden meanings easy to understand.
To benefit bodhisattvas means:

to never treat with contempt even those bodhisattvas who have only recently resolved to attain enlightenment, but rather to cherish and respect them deeply; and to constantly reveal what is wholesome and unwholesome, explaining for them the causes and conditions that serve as skillful means for the Buddha-way.
Regarding the purity of physical form:
his body is exquisite and his features are complete; endowed with the primary and secondary marks of excellence, all who behold him rejoice.

Like a pratyekabuddha, whether walking or staying, advancing or halting, sitting or reclining, waking or sleeping, eating or bathing, dressing or holding his almsbowl, his majestic deportment is orderly and lacks nothing.
If anyone sees it, their mind becomes pure.
As for the Bodhi tree being fully endowed with [all trees]:

it includes all great trees—such as the śāla tree, tāla tree, tilaka tree, tamāla tree, bakula tree, campaka tree, aśoka tree, sahakāra tree, punnāga tree, nāga tree, nāgavṛkṣa tree, śirīṣa tree, nyagrodha tree, aśvattha tree, plakṣa tree, and udumbara tree.
Among these great trees, take any one that stands upon level ground, possessing full height and breadth;
its roots, trunk, branches, and leaves are lush and flourishing, and its flowers are brilliant in color, free from any blemish or defect.
The tree rises fifty yojanas high, straight and smooth without knots;
its bark is fine and soft, white and bright in color;
it is free of thorns or obstructions, and its interior is not decayed or rotten.
Furthermore, there are no insects or scorpions to sting or bite within its hollows;
its roots are deep and firm, growing in continuous, interconnected succession,
while its flowers are exquisitely adorned like floral wreaths and necklaces.
The branches and leaves are luxuriant and dense, like a circular canopy.
Their orderly distribution is far superior to human craftsmanship.

The leaves are fresh and verdant, with the hue of precious gems; the branches are free from twisting or contortion, and there are no withered, yellowed, or decayed leaves. They are entirely devoid of insects, ants, mosquitoes, gnats, or flies.

Beneath it, pure golden sand was spread, with various radiances shining all around; the ground was sprinkled with sandalwood scented water, level, soft, cool, and pleasant, and covered with fine powder of gośīrṣa sandalwood.

The devas constantly rained down mandārava flowers, and the fragrance of black agarwood burned everywhere, overflowing with its scent. Five-colored celestial silks were interlaced and hung in rows; a pure breeze stirred gently, causing them to sway in harmonious grace, while birds and beasts roamed nearby in silent stillness.

On both sides of that tree, the devas constantly rain down flowers of various exquisite colors, naturally interspersed and hanging like necklaces resembling the bodies of dragons; from time to time, golden flower garlands are suspended upon them, and from the great branches on all four sides hang jeweled nets.
Adorned with various jewels, it was like a mountain of purple gold; towering and exquisitely beautiful, it resembled the banner of Śakra.
This was brought about by the merit of virtuous conduct accumulated by the Bodhisattva over hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
Various exquisite jewels transformed into lion kings; upon the heads of these four lions were great jeweled couches spread with celestial silks.

The gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, the Brahma Heavens, and even up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, riding in palaces made of various jewels—lapis lazuli, musāragalva, agate, mahānīla, indranīla, diamond, and crystal—their colors incomparable and their radiance shining afar, gathered together and surrounded the jewel tree to offer worship.

Furthermore, the assemblies of bodhisattvas from the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions, in accordance with their original vows, prepared all manner of offerings and rained down various precious objects, flowers, incense, banners, canopies, and diverse kinds of music.
This is called being fully endowed with the Bodhi tree.
Regarding "the adornment of the world":
the Bodhisattva observes the most supreme and wondrous pure lands in the ten directions and makes a great vow.
The land I shall attain through the accumulation of merit will be even more excellent than this, supreme and peerless.
As for the virtuous benefit of sentient beings:

they will be handsome, free from all ailments, and without aging or illness; their lifespan will be immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas; they will all be born by transformation; their bodies will be free from all impurities and endowed with the thirty-two marks; their radiance will be immeasurable, their afflictions will be slight, and they will be easy to transform and deliver.
Regarding those who are capable of being fully delivered:

while a single Buddha preaches the Dharma from one seat, sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are simultaneously delivered. In contrast, when other Buddhas preach the Dharma, they deliver only one or two people at a time. This is because these sentient beings have planted roots of goodness in past lives and their fetters and afflictions are so subtle that they attain awakening upon hearing the teaching.
Regarding the assembly of the great multitude:

there are great assemblies of Buddhas that fill one yojana, or ten yojanas, or hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, millions, billions, or trillions of yojanas, even filling a triple-thousand great thousandfold world system.
Regarding this "Great Assembly":
the assemblies of worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions constitute the great gathering;

furthermore, within that assembly are only those of merit and virtue, as well as the eight classes of celestial beings, and bodhisattvas from the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the tenth abode (*vihāra*), all having come together in this assembly, with the sole exception of the Buddhas.
Regarding "endowed with the power of the Buddhas":
the forty unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma) practiced by all Buddhas—the sphere of activity for each and every one of these dharmas—is entirely immeasurable and boundless.
This is the seventh vow.
Furthermore: May they act together toward a single purpose, and may there be no resentment or rivalry.
Whether it be the merit performed by a bodhisattva—be it through giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom;
Regarding the four bases of meritorious virtue—truthfulness, relinquishment, cessation, and wisdom—if one seeks the path of the Buddha by means of various great vows, one should make this aspiration:

"If there are other persons who, like myself, practice these six pāramitās and the four bases of meritorious virtue while seeking the path of the Buddha, may I, through the causal conditions of this merit, not give rise to resentment or rivalry toward them. Why is this?"
"Regarding the matter of traveling together":
those who possess wisdom speak of the characteristics of enmity, and such things are indeed currently manifest in the world.
To eliminate this fault, one makes this great vow.
This is the eighth vow:
May I practice the bodhisattva path, turn the irreversible wheel,
cause all afflictions to be eliminated, and enable beings to enter the purity of faith.
The "wheel" refers to the Wheel of Dharma.
As for "irreversible," no one can destroy it.
A bodhisattva should make a vow in this manner:

"I shall practice the path as it has been taught; I will surely turn the irreversible wheel of Dharma. By turning this wheel of Dharma, I shall eliminate the afflictions of the three poisons in all sentient beings.
I shall turn away from birth and death and enter the Sangha of the Buddha's Dharma, attaining purity within the truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path."
This is the ninth vow.
Furthermore: "I vow that in all worlds, I shall manifest the attainment of enlightenment.

In whatever world there should be a place for the Buddha-work to be performed, I shall, throughout it all, manifest the attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. This is for the sake of bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings and for the sake of leading all sentient beings to final liberation (*parinirvāṇa*); because *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is supreme, it is mentioned alone."

Furthermore, [he manifested] entering the womb, emerging from the womb, growing up in the household, leaving home to receive the precepts, practicing asceticism, subduing the hosts of Māra, being exhorted by the Brahma King, and turning the Wheel of Dharma; he gathered great assemblies to extensively deliver sentient beings, manifesting great supernormal powers and displaying his great parinirvāṇa.
All such matters should be performed in this manner.

One should know that there exists such immeasurable power capable of benefiting immeasurable and boundless sentient beings; therefore, one should not manifest the attainment of the Buddha-way in only a single land.
Some say: "Within a single Buddha-field, all the four continents—each Jambudvīpa constitutes one Buddha-land; beyond this, only a Buddha can know."
Yet in reality it is not so.
This is the tenth vow.
Thus, for all bodhisattvas, these ten great vows are the foremost.
Vast as space, extending to the limits of the future;
And other immeasurable vows— These too shall each be explained in detail.
The names of these vows are:
Whatever the mind covets and delights in, its desires will surely be fulfilled.
The tenth [section] consists of ten gates.
"Vast as space" means:
in whatever direction the object of the vow extends, just as there is space in that place,
so too is the vow.
"Until the end of the future" means:
the duration for which one dwells in aspiration, reaching to the limit of the future births and deaths of all sentient beings. Some say:
Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi is the limit of birth and death in future lives; when all Buddhas enter nirvana without remainder, that is the subsequent limit of birth and death.
The vows of Bodhisattvas are inexhaustible, yet they truly cease upon attaining Buddhahood; all the great Bodhisattvas throughout the worlds of the ten directions possess such vows.
Regarding the remaining immeasurable vows:
because all bodhisattvas have accomplished immeasurable and rare merits, all their vows cannot be fully described.
Furthermore—The Bodhisattva brings forth these ten great vows to ultimate fulfillment.
These ten great vows have ten matters of ultimate fulfillment. What are the ten?
The answer is:
The nature of sentient beings and the nature of the world, The nature of empty space and the nature of phenomena (dharmatā),
The nature of nirvāṇa and the nature of the Buddha’s birth, And the ultimate nature of the wisdom of all Buddhas—

The nature of all objects of mental focus, the wisdom regarding the sphere of action of all Buddhas, and the turning of the wisdom regarding worldly phenomena—these are called the ten ultimate consummations:

first, the consummation of the nature of sentient beings; second, the consummation of the nature of the world; third, the consummation of the nature of space; fourth, the consummation of the nature of phenomena; fifth, the consummation of the nature of nirvana; sixth, the consummation of the nature of the birth of Buddhas; seventh, the consummation of the nature of the wisdom of all Buddhas; eighth, the consummation of all objects of mental focus; ninth, the consummation of the wisdom regarding the sphere of action of all Buddhas; tenth, the consummation of the turning of the wisdom regarding worldly phenomena.
These are called the ten culminations (*niṣṭhā*). Question:
You speak of "culmination" (*niṣṭhā*); what constitutes "culmination"?
This meaning should be analyzed.
The answer is:
When the nature of sentient beings is exhausted, my vows shall likewise be exhausted.
Just as the nature of sentient beings is ultimate, so too are these vows ultimate.
The meaning of "ultimate" is called "non-ultimate"; my roots of goodness are non-ultimate.
As for the ultimacy of the nature of sentient beings:
If all sentient beings were to be completely extinguished, my vows would then come to rest.

However, until the nature of the world is exhausted, the nature of space is exhausted, the nature of all phenomena is exhausted, the nature of nirvana is exhausted, the nature of the birth of all Buddhas is exhausted, the nature of the wisdom of all Buddhas is exhausted, the nature of the objects of mind for all sentient beings is exhausted, the nature of entering the wisdom of the Buddha-dharma is exhausted, and the revolutions of the world, the revolutions of the Dharma, and the revolutions of wisdom are all exhausted—only then will these ten vows of mine come to an end.
But as long as these ten realities, such as the nature of sentient beings, are not exhausted, my merit and roots of goodness shall likewise never be exhausted nor cease.
The meaning of "unceasing" (*aksaya*) is as follows:
it is immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable; because it transcends all calculation, it is called unceasing.
Just as this trichiliocosm and the infinite, boundless worlds of the ten directions transcend all calculation, they are called the "boundlessness of the world."
Because the sentient beings within these worlds across the three realms and six destinies are infinite, it is called the "infinite nature of sentient beings.
Because the two kinds of space—internal and external—within all these worlds are infinite, it is called the "infinite nature of space."

Because within these worlds, the conditioned phenomena subsumed under the nature of the outflow-free (anāsrava)—namely those of the desire, form, and formless realms—are infinite, it is called the "infinity of the dharma-nature" (dharmatā).
