When the people of that land reach the end of their lives, even if they were destined to undergo various sufferings, they do not fall into the evil hells; therefore, I take refuge in and pay homage to him.
If one is born in that land, they shall never fall into the three miserable realms, nor among the asuras;
I now take refuge in and pay homage to them.
Their human and celestial bodies are identical, resembling the summit of a mountain of gold.
The place to which all victors return; therefore, I prostrate with head and face.
Those born in that land possess the supernormal powers of the divine eye and ear, unimpeded throughout the ten directions;
I bow my head to the Honored One among Sages.
The sentient beings in that land possess supernormal transformations and mental mastery, as well as the wisdom of recollecting past lives;
therefore, I take refuge in them and pay homage.
Those born in that realm are free from the notion of self and the notion of "mine."
Free from the mind of self and other, I therefore prostrate in homage.
Having transcended the prison of the three realms, with eyes like lotus petals and an immeasurable assembly of śrāvakas, I therefore prostrate in homage.
The sentient beings of that land are all gentle by nature;
they spontaneously practice the ten wholesome deeds and prostrate before the assembly of holy kings.
From goodness arises pure radiance, in measureless and boundless numbers.
Foremost among those with two feet, I therefore take refuge in you.
If anyone aspires to become a Buddha and calls Amitābha to mind, he manifests his body at that very moment; I therefore take refuge in you.
By the power of that Buddha’s original vow, bodhisattvas from the ten directions come to make offerings and listen to the Dharma; for this reason, I prostrate.
The bodhisattvas of that land are fully endowed with all the primary and secondary marks of excellence.
Adorning their own bodies, I now take refuge and pay homage to those great Bodhisattvas;
for they daily, at the three periods of the day,
make offerings to the Buddhas of the ten directions, and thus I bow my head in reverence.
If a person plants roots of goodness, yet harbors doubt, the flower will not open;
for one whose mind of faith is pure, the flower opens and they see the Buddha.
The Buddhas of the ten directions, present now, through various causes and conditions, [reveal this].
Praising the virtues of that Buddha, I now take refuge and pay homage.
His land is most magnificently adorned, surpassing even the palaces of the various devas;
its merit is exceedingly profound and vast, and for this reason I bow at the Buddha’s feet.
The Buddha’s feet have wheels with a thousand spokes, Soft and the color of lotuses;
All who see them rejoice, Bowing their heads to worship the Buddha’s feet.
The white tuft of hair between his brows Is like the pure, bright moon.
Increasing the radiance and color of his countenance, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet.
When he first sought the path of the Buddha, he performed all manner of wondrous deeds as described in the various sūtras;
thus, with his head bowed low, he paid homage.
The words spoken by that Buddha destroy all roots of evil;
his beautiful speech brings manifold benefit, and I now prostrate in worship.
By means of these beautiful words, he rescues all who suffer from the disease of attachment to pleasure.
Having already crossed over and still crossing others, I therefore bow my head in worship.
Most honored among gods and humans, to whom the various devas pay homage with their heads and faces;
you who wear a crown of seven jewels and mani-gems, I therefore take refuge in you.
All the assemblies of worthy sages, as well as the multitudes of humans and devas, all together take refuge; therefore, I too pay homage.
Riding upon that boat of the Eightfold Path, they are able to cross the sea that is so difficult to cross.
Having crossed over myself, I also deliver others; I pay homage to the Sovereign One.
Even if all Buddhas were to praise his merits for immeasurable eons, they could not exhaust them; I take refuge in the Pure One.
I now do likewise, extolling your immeasurable virtues;
by the causal conditions of this merit, may the Buddha always keep me in mind.
Whatever merits I have possessed in this life or in past lives, whether great or small—
May my mind always attain purity in the presence of the Buddha;
by the causal conditions of this merit, may all classes of sentient beings likewise obtain the supreme and wondrous virtues that I have gained.
Furthermore, one should also bring to mind:
the Buddha Vipaśyin, the Buddha Śikhin, the Buddha Viśvabhū, the Buddha Krakucchanda, the Buddha Kanakamuni, the Buddha Kāśyapa, the Buddha Śākyamuni, and the future Buddha Maitreya.
All should recollect and pay homage, praising him with these verses:
"Vipaśyin, the World-Honored One, Beneath the tree of the Way free from sorrow,
Has attained all-encompassing wisdom And all subtle, wondrous virtues."
Rightly contemplating the world, his mind attained liberation;
I now, with my five limbs prostrate, take refuge in the Unsurpassed Honored One.
The World-Honored Buddha Śikhin was dwelling in Piṇḍola.
Sitting beneath the tree of the site of enlightenment, you have accomplished bodhi;
your physical form is peerless, like a blazing mountain of purple gold.
I now take refuge in you, the Unsurpassed Honored One of the three realms.
The World-Honored One Viśvabhū, sitting beneath a śāla tree,
naturally attained mastery over all sublime wisdom;
among all humans and devas, he is supreme and without peer.
Therefore, I take refuge in the most supreme among all,
the Buddha Kākuṭstha, who attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* beneath the śirīṣa tree.
Having achieved great wisdom, Forever liberated from birth and death,
I now take refuge and pay homage To the foremost, peerless Honored One.
Kanakamuni, The Great Sage, the Unsurpassed Honored One.
Beneath the Udumbara tree, you attained the path of Buddhahood;
you have mastered all dharmas, which are immeasurable and boundless.
Therefore, I take refuge in you, the foremost and unsurpassed Honored One.
The World-Honored One Kāśyapa Buddha, His eyes like twin lotus flowers,
Attained the Way of the Buddha Beneath a young *kubjaka* tree;
Fearless throughout the three realms, His gait like that of a king of elephants.
I now take refuge and bow my head in homage to the Infinite Honored One,
Śākyamuni Buddha; beneath the Aśvattha tree,
he subdued the hosts of Māra and his enemies, and accomplished the Unsurpassed Way.
Your countenance is like the full moon, pure and free from the dust of blemish;
I now prostrate in homage to you, the foremost among the valiant.
In the future, when Maitreya Buddha sits beneath the Nāga tree, [I shall likewise pay homage].
Having accomplished the vast mind, you naturally attained the Buddha-way;
your merit is exceedingly firm and solid, such that none can surpass it.
Therefore, I take refuge in myself in the peerless and wondrous Dharma King.

Furthermore, there are the Buddhas Guṇavara, Samantaprabha, Jetāri, Rājanimitta, Nimittarāja, Aparimitaguṇaprabhāsvareśvararāja, Bhaiṣajyarāja-anāvaraṇa, Ratnacaṅkrama, Ratnakusuma, Sthitika, and Śailendra-rāja; these too should be recollected, honored, and prostrated to, and praised with verses:
In the world-system Anabhibhūta, There is a Buddha named Guṇavara;
I now bow my head in homage To him, and to the Dharma Jewel and the Saṃgha Jewel.
In the world of Yathāśayasukha, there is a Buddha named Samantaprabhā;
I now take refuge in him, as well as in the Jewel of the Dharma and the Jewel of the Saṃgha.
In the world of Samantabhadra, there is a Buddha named Vijayavikrāmin.
I now take refuge and pay homage to the Buddha, the Dharma Jewel, and the Sangha Jewel.
In the world-system of Well-Purified Accumulation, the Buddha’s name is King Banner Sign;
I now bow my head in prostration to him, as well as to the Dharma Jewel and the Sangha Jewel.
In the world Vimalasaṃcaya, the Buddha Anantaguṇaprabha reigns with mastery throughout the ten directions; therefore, I bow my head in homage.
In the world Akṣobhya, the Buddha Bhaiṣajyarāja is unimpeded.
I now prostrate with my head at the feet of the Buddha, the Dharma Jewel, and the Sangha Jewel.
In the world-system Jambudhvaja, there is a Buddha named Ratnacārin;
I now prostrate with my head at his feet, and at the Dharma Jewel and the Sangha Jewel.
In the realm of beautiful sounds, adorned with jeweled flowers, The Buddha King of Mountains resides;
I now prostrate my head in worship, As well as to the Jewel of the Dharma and the Jewel of the Saṅgha.
Now these Tathāgatas dwell in the realms of the eastern direction.
With a heart of reverence, I praise, take refuge in, and pay homage.
I pray that all Tathāgatas, out of profound compassion,
will manifest their forms before me, so that I may behold them with my own eyes.
Furthermore, one should collectively recollect, revere, and prostrate to all Buddhas of the past, future, and present, praising them with these verses:
The Buddhas of the past, Who have subdued the hosts of Māra’s enemies,
By the power of their great wisdom, Have extensively benefited all sentient beings.
At that time, all sentient beings offered worship with their whole hearts;
they honored him and praised him, and for this reason, they prostrated themselves before his head.
Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, there are immeasurable Buddhas.
Their number exceeds the sands of the Ganges, immeasurable and without limit;
out of compassion for all sentient beings, they constantly turn the wondrous Wheel of Dharma.
Therefore, I pay homage with reverence, taking refuge and prostrating myself before them.
The Buddhas of future ages, their bodies golden in color,
with immeasurable radiance and adorned by the primary marks,
shall appear in the world to deliver sentient beings and eventually enter into nirvana.
To all such World-Honored Ones, I now pay homage with my head at their feet.
Furthermore, one should call to mind the great Bodhisattvas:

Bodhisattva Good Intention (Kalyāṇamati), Bodhisattva Good Eye (Sudarśana), Bodhisattva Moon of Hearing (Śruticandra), Bodhisattva King Śibi, Bodhisattva All-Victorious (Sarvavijaya), Bodhisattva Knower of the Great Earth, Bodhisattva Great Medicine (Mahauṣadhi), Bodhisattva Kauśika, Bodhisattva Aranemin, Bodhisattva King Mūrdhaja, Bodhisattva Joyful Sight (Priyadarśana), Bodhisattva Uttara, Bodhisattva Sahadatta, Bodhisattva King Long-Life (Dīrghāyu), Bodhisattva Kṣānti, Bodhisattva Veḷama, Bodhisattva Śyāma, Bodhisattva Moon Canopy (Candracchattra), Bodhisattva Bright Head (Prabhāśiri), Bodhisattva Dharma Head (Dharmasiri), Bodhisattva Accomplished Benefit (Siddhārtha), and Bodhisattva Maitreya.
Furthermore, there were:
Vajragarbha Bodhisattva, Vajramukha Bodhisattva, Vimalagarbha Bodhisattva, Vimalakīrti Bodhisattva,
Vimatisamudghātin Bodhisattva, Vimalaguṇa Bodhisattva, and Jālinīprabha Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva Amitābha, the Bodhisattva Mahāprabha, the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati, the Bodhisattva Cittarāja,
the Bodhisattva Anantamati, the Bodhisattva Sūryaghoṣa, the Bodhisattva Candraghoṣa, the Bodhisattva Manojñaghoṣa,
the Bodhisattva Manojñasvara, the Bodhisattva Mahāsvara, and the Bodhisattva Dṛḍhavīrya.
...the Bodhisattva Constant Firmness, the Bodhisattva Firm Resolve, the Bodhisattva King of Adornments, the Bodhisattva Constant Compassion,

Chapter Ten: Eliminating Karma. Question:
Is it only by recollecting Amitābha and other Buddhas, as well as mindfulness of other bodhisattvas, that one attains the stage of *avaivartika*, or are there further skillful means?
The answer is:

One who seeks the stage of *avaivartika* should not merely practice mindfulness, recite the names [of the Buddhas], and pay homage; they must further, in the presence of all Buddhas, perform confession, entreaty, sympathetic joy, and dedication.
Question: What does this matter mean? Answer:
The Buddhas of the ten directions, whose knowledge is exhaustive and leaves nothing unknown,
before them all I now confess and reveal all my dark and evil deeds.
These consist of nine types— three groups of three— all arising from the three afflictions.
Whether in this present life or in previous lives, I now repent of all these transgressions.
Should there be any karmic retribution due to me within the three evil realms,
may I repay it in this present body and not enter those evil paths to suffer.
"The Buddhas of the ten directions" refers to all currently existing Buddhas whose life-faculties are perfected and who have not yet entered nirvana.
"Ten directions" means the four cardinal directions, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.
"Buddha" refers to the objects that ought to be known; he knows them all without exception.
"To disclose" means, in the presence of the Buddhas, to disclose all transgressions without concealment, and not to commit them again, just as a dam holds back water.
The "black and evil" refers to those who, due to the absence of wisdom, insight, and clarity, frequently commit various evils—whether unwholesome dharmas or obscured-unspecified states.
Regarding the "three types of three," these are: the arising of evil through body, speech, and mind;
retribution in the present life, retribution in the next life, and retribution in subsequent lives.
One performs it oneself, instructs others to perform it, or rejoices in its performance.
It arises from three kinds of afflictions; these three kinds of afflictions are those bound to the desire realm, those bound to the form realm, and those bound to the formless realm;
whether they assist the affliction of greed, assist the affliction of hatred, or assist the affliction of delusion.
Whether they be superior afflictions, middling afflictions, or inferior afflictions—

regarding those committed in this life or in previous lives— if one repents them all, then all the various evils committed in this world and in past worlds shall be fully repented of, leaving nothing behind.
As for the hells, there are eight kinds of hot hells and ten kinds of cold hells.
As for animals, they are those born on land, those born in water, those with no feet, those with two feet, or those with many feet.
As for the hungry ghosts (*preta*), they eat saliva, vomit, wash-water, pus, blood, excrement, urine, and the like.
If the karmic results of my own actions should be experienced within these three evil realms, may this transgression be experienced by this very body;
if it must be experienced in a future body, may it not be experienced among the denizens of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.
Furthermore, the Buddha himself taught the method for repentance.
If a bodhisattva wishes to repent of their transgressions, they should speak as follows:

"In the worlds of the ten directions at this present time, there are Buddhas who have attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; they turn the wheel of Dharma, rain down the rain of Dharma, beat the drum of Dharma, blow the conch of Dharma, and erect the banner of Dharma."
By bestowing the gift of Dharma, I satisfy sentient beings, providing them with great benefit and great peace, out of compassion for the world to enrich devas and humans.
"With my body, speech, and mind, I now prostrate with my head at the feet of all present Buddhas—the Buddhas who know and see, the eyes of the world, the lamps of the world."

"Throughout the beginningless cycle of birth and death, whatever sinful karma I have generated—driven by greed, hatred, and delusion—I have either failed to recognize the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha;
or failed to recognize sin and merit;
or committed many transgressions through body, speech, and mind."
Either drawing blood from the body of a Buddha with an evil mind;
or destroying the True Dharma, disrupting the Sangha, or killing a true person who is an Arhat;
or practicing the ten unwholesome paths oneself, or teaching others to practice them, or further rejoicing in such acts.
If one speaks unpleasant words to sentient beings;
if one deceives and encroaches upon others by using false measures and scales; if one afflicts and disturbs sentient beings through various wrongful conducts;
or if one is unfilial toward one's parents;
Or they may steal the property of a stūpa or the belongings of the Saṅgha from the four quarters;
they may violate the sūtras or precepts taught by the Buddha, or act in opposition to their upādhyāyas and ācāryas;
or they may utter malicious words to insult and humiliate those who have set out in the Śrāvaka-yāna, the Pratyekabuddha-yāna, or the Mahāyāna, treating them with contempt, disdain, and resentment.
Because my mind was shrouded by stinginess and envy, I may have uttered harsh words toward the Buddhas;
or I may have declared that which is the Dharma to be non-Dharma, and that which is non-Dharma to be the Dharma.

Now, regarding these transgressions, before all the present Buddhas—who know, who see, and who realize—I openly confess them all and dare not conceal them. From this day forward, I shall not commit them again.

If I have committed any transgressions that would cause me to fall into the realms of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, or asuras, or to fail to encounter the Triple Gem and be born amidst the various difficulties, I pray that these offenses may be experienced in this very life.

"Just as the bodhisattvas of the past who sought the Buddha-way repented of their evil karma and offenses, I likewise reveal and repent, not daring to conceal them, and shall not commit them again hereafter."
"If all the bodhisattvas who now seek the Buddha-way repent of their evil karmic offenses, I likewise confess and reveal them; I dare not conceal them, and shall never commit them again."

"Just as the bodhisattvas of the future who seek the Buddha-way repent for their evil karmic offenses, I likewise confess and reveal my own transgressions, not daring to conceal them, and vowing never to commit them again."

"Just as all Bodhisattvas of the past, future, and present who seek the Buddha-way have repented their evil karmic offenses—having repented, now repenting, and about to repent—I too likewise repent my evil karmic offenses; I dare not conceal them, and shall never commit them again."
Question: You have already explained the method of repentance; what is the practice of exhortation? Answer:
To all Buddhas of the ten directions, those currently attaining enlightenment,
I entreat you to turn the wheel of Dharma to bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings;
to all Buddhas of the ten directions, should you wish to relinquish your life-span, [I entreat you to remain].
I now prostrate with my head at his feet, entreating him to remain for a long time.
As for the turning of the Wheel of Dharma, it refers to the teaching of the meaning of the Four Noble Truths through three turnings and twelve aspects:

"This is the truth of suffering," "This is the origin of suffering," "This is the cessation of suffering," and "This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering"—this is called one turning and four aspects.

"This is the truth of suffering, which should be known; this is the origin of suffering, which should be abandoned; this is the cessation of suffering, which should be realized; this is the path leading to the cessation of suffering, which should be cultivated. This is called the second turning of the four aspects.

"This is the Truth of Suffering, which has been known; this is the Origin of Suffering, which has been abandoned; this is the Cessation of Suffering, which has been realized; this is the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering, which has been cultivated. This is called the third turning of the four aspects.
Regarding the four characteristics, it is said that within the Four Noble Truths, there arises vision, knowledge, clarity, and awakening.
Some say that the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the Mahāyāna are called the Wheel of Dharma.
To explain the meaning of these three vehicles is called "turning the wheel of Dharma.

Regarding the phrase "bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings": the pleasures of the five desires are not called peace and happiness; rather, it is the attainment of pure peace and happiness in both this life and future lives through entry into the three vehicles that is called peace and happiness.

This person exhorts and entreats all Buddhas to turn the wheel of Dharma, causing all sentient beings to receive the bliss of nirvana; if they have not yet attained nirvana, he causes them to receive worldly happiness. For this reason, it is called "peaceful bliss."

"Life-span" refers to the continuity of the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) that persists due to the causes and conditions of karmic retribution; it abides like a magical creation, following the karma of the mind, and ceases when the mental karma stops.
"Exhortation" (*adhyeṣaṇā*) means "earnestly seeking and praying.
All Buddhas regard all sentient beings without distinction between great and small; therefore, one prays and entreats them, hoping that their wishes may be fulfilled:
"Do not relinquish your life-span, but remain for immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas to deliver and liberate sentient beings."
Furthermore, the Buddha himself taught the method for exhortation: a bodhisattva should speak these words:

"I pay homage to all the Buddhas currently residing in the ten directions who have newly attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* but have not yet turned the wheel of Dharma. I now entreat you: may you turn the wheel of Dharma, beat the drum of Dharma, blow the conch of Dharma, raise the banner of Dharma, establish the great sacrifice of Dharma, and kindle the great torch of Dharma. By means of this gift of Dharma, satisfy all sentient beings; bring about great benefit and great peace and happiness. Out of compassion for the world, to enrich devas and humans—I therefore now exhort you."
—This is called exhorting all Buddhas to turn the wheel of Dharma.
Regarding their remaining for a long time, one should also say:

"I entreat the present Buddhas of the ten directions to remain for a long time, as these Buddhas intend to relinquish their life-span; may they do so for the sake of great benefit and great peace, out of compassion for the world to bring profit to devas and humans."
Question: You have already explained confession and entreaty; what is meant by sympathetic joy? Answer:
All merit from giving, The observance of precepts and the practice of dhyāna,
Arising from body, speech, and mind— Whatever has existed in the past, future, and present;
Those who practice the three vehicles And those who are fully endowed with the three vehicles—
All the merit of ordinary beings is followed with joy.
The merit of giving arises from abandoning the dharma of stinginess;
the merit of upholding the precepts arises from being able to subdue the karma of body and speech.
Meditative practitioners refer to the various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna-samādhi*).
Those arising from body and speech include giving, observing precepts, welcoming and seeing off others, and so forth, which are caused by the body and speech.
Those arising from the mind include meditative concentration, loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), and so forth.
"Whatever exists in the past, future, and present" refers to the merit of all sentient beings throughout the three periods of time.
"Practitioners of the three vehicles" refers to those who seek the vehicle of the śrāvaka, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddha, and the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna).
"Endowed with the three vehicles" means achieving the vehicle of the arhat, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddha, and the vehicle of the Buddha.
"All" means that they are entirely exhausted without exception.
An ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is one who has not yet attained the Four Noble Truths.
Merit (*puṇya*) consists of two kinds of karma:
wholesome karma and non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) karma.
Regarding rejoicing (*anumodanā*): when others perform meritorious deeds, one gives rise to a heart of joy and praises them as virtuous.
It is asked:
"You have spoken of repentance (*pāpadeśanā*), entreaty (*adhyeṣaṇā*), and rejoicing."
What is dedication?
The answer is:
May all the merit that I possess, entirely combined together, [be dedicated].
For the sake of all sentient beings, one correctly dedicates [merit] toward the Buddha-way.
"I" refers to one's own person.

"All merit" refers to that which arises from the body, that which arises from speech, or that which arises from the mind; that which arises from giving, that which arises from maintaining the precepts, that which arises from practicing meditation, that which arises from sympathetic joy, or that which arises from making requests—such as these and all other virtues are called "all merit."
"All are in harmony" means that one contemplates all merits with the mind, collects and weighs them together, and realizes their vastness.
"All sentient beings" refers to the sentient beings within the three realms.
"Correct" means, for example, the dedication of all Buddhas, which is the true dedication, dedicating toward bodhi.
To dedicate toward bodhi means to direct all merits and virtues toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Furthermore, regarding these two matters—rejoicing (*anumodana*) and dedication (*pariṇāmanā*)—the Buddha himself has said:

"There is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who, wishing to rejoice and dedicate, should bring to mind all Buddhas who have severed the continuity of the three realms, extinguished all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), dried up the mire of afflictions (*kleśa*), eliminated all thorns, laid down all heavy burdens, attained their own benefit, and through right knowledge and liberation, have gained mastery over the mind and exhausted all fetters of existence."

In immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and incalculable worlds of the ten directions, in each and every world, there have appeared immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and incalculable Buddhas who have passed into parinirvāṇa;

from their first generation of the mind of enlightenment until they attained Buddhahood, entered nirvana without remainder, and until their Dharma has not yet vanished—in the interval between these times, all the roots of goodness and merit of these Buddhas corresponding to the six pāramitās, as well as all the roots of goodness of those for whom they have received the prediction of becoming pratyekabuddhas;

furthermore, the roots of goodness of śrāvakas, whether through giving, observing precepts, or practicing dhyāna, as well as the untainted (anāsrava) roots of goodness of those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).

Furthermore, there are the Buddhas’ categories of morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, as well as their immeasurable merits such as great loving-kindness and great compassion;

and all the teachings spoken by the Buddhas, wherein certain people have faith and understanding, receive and study them, and thereby obtain the benefits of these dharmas—the roots of goodness possessed by all such persons within these teachings, as well as the roots of goodness planted by ordinary worldlings;

and the various devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas who, having heard the Dharma, give rise to wholesome minds, even down to animals who hear the Dharma and give rise to wholesome minds.
And when all Buddhas are about to enter parinirvāṇa, there are the roots of goodness planted by sentient beings;

may all these roots of goodness and merit be combined and weighed together without exception, and be rejoiced in with the highest, most wondrous, most supreme, unsurpassed, unequaled, and peerless rejoicing.
Having rejoiced, one dedicates the merit arising from this rejoicing toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The same applies to all Buddhas of the future and the present.

One rejoices in all the merit of the Buddhas of the three periods of time, as well as the merit arising from those Buddhas, with a mind that fully approves, and dedicates it toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Therefore, the verse says:
"Sins should be confessed in this manner; likewise, one should likewise perform the acts of exhortation, sympathetic joy, and dedication toward the unsurpassed path."
As the Buddhas have taught, my confession of transgressions, entreaties, sympathetic joy, and dedication are all likewise.

From beginningless worlds, there have been immeasurable transgressions that obstruct the Buddha-way; one should repent before the Buddhas of the ten directions, entreat the Buddhas, rejoice, and dedicate in this very same way.
Just as the Buddha knows, sees, and permits this repentance, so do I likewise repent.
My exhortation of the Buddhas, my sympathetic joy, and my dedication of merit are likewise performed in this same manner.
If one performs confession, entreaty, sympathetic joy, and dedication in this manner, it is called "right dedication. Question:
What are the "confession, entreaty, sympathetic joy, and dedication" that are known, seen, and permitted by all Buddhas?
Answer: Repentance and entreaty are as previously explained.
Regarding sympathetic joy and dedication, they are as described in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*:
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

Regarding the merit and roots of goodness possessed by all Buddhas of the past, future, and present, as well as their disciples and all sentient beings—as spoken of—[the Bodhisattva] unites and weighs them all together, and rejoices in them with the highest degree of sympathetic joy."
“World-Honored One!
What is called the supreme rejoicing?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

If a bodhisattva, regarding all phenomena of the past, future, and present, does not grasp them, does not dwell upon them, does not perceive them, does not acquire them, and does not discriminate them, yet is able to reflect thus:
"All these phenomena arise from conceptualization and discrimination; they exist through the conjunction of various conditions."
All phenomena are in truth unarisen and have no place from which they come.
Within this, there is not even a single phenomenon that has arisen, is arising, or will arise; nor is there any that has ceased, is ceasing, or will cease.
"The characteristics of all dharmas are thus; I rejoice in accordance with the characteristics of all dharmas.
Having rejoiced, I also accord with the true nature of all dharmas and dedicate [the merit] toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
This is called "the supreme rejoicing and dedication.
Furthermore, Subhūti,
a son of good family or daughter of good family seeking the Buddha-way who does not wish to slander the Buddha should dedicate their roots of goodness in this manner.
One should form this thought:
"Just as the minds, wisdoms, and eyes of all Buddhas know and see these roots of goodness and merit—their origin, their culmination, and their essential characteristics—from what do they arise?"

I am likewise; I rejoice in accordance with the knowledge and vision of all Buddhas. Just as all Buddhas have authorized, I also dedicate these roots of goodness in this manner. If a bodhisattva dedicates in this way, they do not slander the Buddhas and remain free from fault.
To dedicate with deep-seated faith and understanding according to reality is called the "Great Dedication" and the "Complete Dedication.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
Good sons and good daughters, you should dedicate all roots of goodness and merit in this manner:

Just as the aggregates of morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation of the noble ones are not bound to the desire realm, not bound to the form realm, and not bound to the formless realm; and as they do not exist in the past, do not exist in the future, and do not exist in the present—because they are unbound to the three realms, so too is this dedication unbound, and the place to which it is dedicated is likewise unbound.

If a bodhisattva can attain such a mind and believe and understand it as it truly is, this is called "non-wasteful dedication," "poison-free dedication," and "dedication according to the nature of phenomena (dharmatā)."
"If a bodhisattva, regarding this dedication, grasps at signs and becomes attached to them, this is called 'wrong dedication.

Therefore, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should dedicate by means of the characteristics of dharmas as known by the Buddhas; being able to reach unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment through such dedication is called 'right dedication.'"
*Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle 50;
*Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle 6.
Composed by the Holy One Nāgārjuna.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty.
Chapter Eleven: Distinguishing Merit. Question:
How should one perform repentance, exhortation, sympathetic joy, and dedication?
"At what times during the day and night does one practice?
He replied:
"With the right knee touching the ground and the right shoulder bared."
With palms joined in a heart of reverence, three times each day and night;

because of this posture of reverence—kneeling with the right knee on the ground, baring the right shoulder, and joining the palms—one should perform worship to all Buddhas during one period of the first watch of the night.
One should likewise perform confession, exhortation, sympathetic joy, and dedication during the middle watch and the final watch of the night.
One should do the same during the first, middle, and last divisions of the day.
Dividing one day and one night into six periods, one should single-mindedly contemplate all Buddhas as if they were present before one.
Question:
Having performed such practice, what fruit or retribution is obtained?
The answer is:
If the merit accumulated from practicing for even a single moment were to have a physical form,
the worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges would not be sufficient to contain it.

If the merit obtained by one who performs this deed for even a single moment were to take form, it would not be contained within as many immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable trichiliocosm world-systems as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River.
As it is said in the *Tri-lakṣaṇa-sūtra*, in the chapter "Eliminating Karmic Obstacles":
"The Buddha told Śāriputra:
'If a son or daughter of good family were to offer as alms to the Buddhas the seven treasures filling as many trichiliocosm worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River;'"
"If there were another person who exhorted the Buddhas to turn the wheel of Dharma, this merit would be superior.
Furthermore, in the "Chapter on Rejoicing and Dedication" of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, the Buddha said:
"Excellent!"
Excellent,
Subhūti! You are able to perform the work of a Buddha by teaching the method of dedication to the bodhisattvas.
If a bodhisattva forms this thought:
"Just as the Buddhas know and see the fundamental nature, beginning, end, and characteristics of these roots of goodness and merit, and by what causes and conditions they exist;
I too shall likewise dedicate them in accordance with what the Buddhas know and see."
The merit obtained by this person is vast.
For example, suppose all sentient beings within as many trichiliocosms as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River were to fully accomplish the ten paths of wholesome action;
the bodhisattva’s dedication of merit is supreme, most wonderful, most excellent, incomparable, peerless, and equal to the unequaled.
“Subhūti! Setting aside these sentient beings in as many trichiliocosm worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges who have accomplished the ten paths of wholesome action;

if sentient beings in as many trichiliocosm worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges were all to attain the four dhyānas, their merit would be even more supreme, most wonderful, and most excellent than this.”

The same applies to the four immeasurable minds, the four formless absorptions, the five supernormal powers, and the attainment of the fruits of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, and arhat, as well as the path of the pratyekabuddha.
The merit dedicated in accordance with the Dharma is most supreme, most wondrous, and most excellent.

"Subhūti! Let alone all the sentient beings in as many trichiliocosm worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, were they all to become pratyekabuddhas; [the merit of dedication would still surpass it]."
Suppose there were sentient beings in as many trichiliocosm world systems as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, and all of them had resolved their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Furthermore, suppose there were another set of sentient beings in as many trichiliocosm world systems as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, and a single bodhisattva, with a mind that grasps at signs, were to provide these sentient beings with clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicine;

for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, he were to provide them with every article of pleasure, honoring, respecting, revering, and praising them—and let every such bodhisattva do likewise.
Subhūti, what do you think?
By means of these causes and conditions, would those bodhisattvas acquire much merit?
“Very much, World-Honored One!
Such merit cannot be reached by calculation or analogy.
If this merit had form, even worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges could not contain it.”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Excellent! Excellent!”

Subhūti! This bodhisattva is protected by the perfection of wisdom; the merit obtained from dedicating roots of goodness in accordance with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) cannot be matched by the merit of previous bodhisattvas who practiced giving while grasping at signs—even by a hundredth part, a thousandth, a ten-thousandth, a hundred-thousand-millionth, or even by any calculation or analogy. It is utterly beyond reach.
Why is this? Because previously, when bodhisattvas practiced giving while grasping at signs and making conceptual distinctions, it was all limited and quantifiable.
Furthermore, it is said in the "Dedication Chapter" (*Pariṇāmanā-parivarta*) of the *Prajñāpāramitā*:
The Buddha told the devaputra of the Śuddhāvāsa heaven:

"Setting aside these sentient beings of a trichiliocosm as numerous as the sands of the Ganges who have all resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, suppose there were other sentient beings of trichiliocosms as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and each bodhisattva were to provide these sentient beings with clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and all necessities of life—with a mind that grasps at signs—making offerings according to their wishes for as many eons as there are sands in the Ganges."
"O sons of the gods!

Suppose as many sentient beings as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River in a trichiliocosm were to resolve their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and furthermore, as many sentient beings as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River in other trichiliocosms likewise resolved their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. If a single bodhisattva were to provide these bodhisattvas with robes, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and all necessities of life for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, such giving would still involve the conceptualization of signs."

If these bodhisattvas were each, for as many eons as there are sands in the Ganges, to provide these bodhisattvas with clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and all necessities of life, making offerings of them according to their wishes and honoring, respecting, and praising them—all such acts would still be giving with attachment to signs.

“If a bodhisattva, being protected by the *prajñāpāramitā*, takes all the merit from the categories of morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation of the Buddhas of the past, future, and present; and the five categories of the śrāvakas; and the roots of goodness planted, currently being planted, or yet to be planted therein by ordinary worldlings—all of these combined and weighed together without exception—and with the most supreme, most exquisite, most excellent, peerless, unequaled, and inconceivable merit of sympathetic joy, dedicates it toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
If one forms this thought:

"I am a person of merit who can reach the path of Buddhahood," such merit does not equal even a hundredth part of the merit previously gained from grasping at signs; it does not equal a thousandth, ten-thousandth, or a hundred-millionth part, nor can it be reached by any calculation or analogy.
Why is this? It is because these bodhisattvas practice giving by grasping at signs and making conceptual distinctions.

Furthermore, there are sentient beings in as many trichiliocosm world systems as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River who have all resolved their minds toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, practicing wholesome deeds of body, wholesome deeds of speech, and wholesome deeds of mind.
Furthermore, suppose there are sentient beings in as many trichiliocosm worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, all of whom have resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
and suppose a person is able to endure being reviled with harsh speech by them for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River.
"Even if one were to exert oneself with body and mind throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, eliminating all laziness;

and even if one were to collect the mind in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) free from all distracted thoughts—yet if these were all performed while grasping at signs—this would not be as superior as when a Bodhisattva dedicates that merit in accordance with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*)."
Therefore, regarding what you previously asked—"What benefit is gained by performing such acts?"—one gains such a vast accumulation of merit.

Consequently, if anyone wishes to obtain such an immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable accumulation of merit, they should practice this confession, entreaty, sympathetic joy, and dedication; disregarding body, life, gain, and fame, they should always practice diligently throughout the day and night.
Question:
You have spoken only of the merit within exhortation, sympathetic joy, and dedication; why do you not speak of the merit within repentance? Answer:

Among all merits, the merit of repentance is the greatest, for it eliminates the transgressions of karmic obstructions, enabling one to attain virtuous practice on the bodhisattva path; its performance of exhortation, sympathetic joy, and dedication is inseparable from its harmony with emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
Furthermore, repentance is like a wish-fulfilling jewel; whatever one desires, it is obtained.
As the Buddha said:

"If a person wishes to be born into a great Brahmin clan, a great Kṣatriya clan, or a great householder family, they should repent of their karmic offenses in this manner—without concealment and vowing not to commit them again."

"If there are those who wish to be born in the heavens of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, or the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, they should likewise repent of their karmic offenses, concealing nothing and not committing them again hereafter."

"If a person wishes to be born in the Brahma world, up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, that person should likewise repent of their karmic offenses, without concealment, and not commit them again hereafter."
"If anyone wishes to attain the fruit of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, or arhat, they should likewise repent of their karmic offenses in this manner."

"If a person wishes to attain the three types of supernormal knowledge and the six supernatural powers, the sovereign power within the path of the śrāvakas, and reach the further shore of all śrāvaka merits, they too should likewise repent their karmic offenses."
“If anyone wishes to attain the path of a Pratyekabuddha, they should likewise repent of their karmic offenses.

“If anyone wishes to attain all-encompassing wisdom, inconceivable wisdom, unimpeded wisdom, and supreme wisdom, they should likewise repent of their karmic offenses, without concealment, and resolve never to commit them again.”
Therefore, one should know that repentance yields great fruit and retribution.
Question: You say, "Repentance eliminates the offenses of karmic obstructions."
Other sūtras state:
"The Buddha told Ānanda, 'Karma that has been intentionally performed must inevitably be experienced as its retribution. Furthermore, the *Abhidharma* states:
"The causal conditions of all karmas are not empty; their retributive fruits are neither lost nor extinguished."
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"Sentient beings all belong to karma; they all arise from karma; they rely upon karma.
Sentient beings each receive their retribution according to their karma—whether as retribution in the present life, retribution in the next life, or retribution in subsequent lives."
Furthermore, in the *Karmavipāka-sūtra*, King Yama says to sentient beings: "Ho!
Sentient beings!"
"This transgression of yours was not committed by your parents, nor by the gods, nor by śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas; you committed it yourself, and you must undergo its retribution yourself.
Furthermore, it is said in the verses of the Noble Ones:
"The true Dharma is like a vajra; The power of karma is unsurpassed."
"Now that I have attained the Way, I am still receiving the retribution for my evil karma.
Furthermore, the Buddha himself said:
"The great oceans and all famous mountains, the hills, mounds, trees, and forests—"
Earth, water, fire, wind, and the like, The sun, moon, and all the constellations—
When the time of the kalpa’s conflagration arrives, All are utterly consumed without remainder;
Yet karma, throughout immeasurable eons, Remains ever-present and is never lost.
Having encountered one endowed with the marks, the Teacher, the Omniscient One,
the karmic fruits of the sinful deeds you previously committed have already been requited.
Now that you have met the Buddha, your defilements are exhausted and you have realized the fruit of sainthood.
"Because of other causes and conditions, the wooden splinter still remains in the body.
Therefore, one should not say that confession eliminates karmic offenses.
The answer is:

I do not say that "through repentance, karmic offenses are completely extinguished and no retribution remains. I say that "through repentance, the offense becomes light and is experienced for only a short time. Therefore, it is said in the Verses on Repentance:
"If one is destined to fall into the three evil realms, may one instead experience this within a human body."
Furthermore, the *Tathāgatajñānamudrā-sūtra* states:
"The Buddha told Maitreya:

'If bodhisattvas who, with a profound mind, love and delight in anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, should have offenses that ought to result in retribution in the evil realms, those offenses shall be slight.'"
In future lives, they will receive an evil form, or suffer from many diseases and lack majesty and virtue;
they will be born into low-born families, impoverished families, families of wrong views, or families who subsist through wrong livelihoods;
they will be born in places contrary to their wishes, in places of much sorrow, in lands that are destroyed, villages that are destroyed, and households that are destroyed.
One’s loved ones will be separated; one will not encounter virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*); one will never hear the Dharma; one will not obtain gain or offerings.

Even if one obtains coarse and inferior things, they will never suffice for one's own sustenance. One will be able to inspire faith and respect in those of low station, yet fail to inspire faith and respect among great beings.
When cultivating and accumulating various merits, many obstacles will arise, preventing success.

Having achieved [this state], their faculties become dull and dark; though they practice meditation, their minds are distracted, and they fail to attain the merit of the untainted factors of enlightenment (*anāsrava-bodhyaṅga*).
They do not understand the teachings of the sūtras and follow whatever inclinations lead them even to bad dreams and the retribution of the evil realms.
Furthermore, the Buddha said:
"If a person commits a minor offense that could be retributed in this present life, yet that offense increases and becomes greater, they will fall into hell.
How is it that a person's minor offense in this present life increases and causes them to fall into hell?

If there are those who do not cultivate the body, do not cultivate ethical discipline, do not cultivate the mind, and do not cultivate wisdom, and who lack a great resolve, such people will fall into hell for even a minor offense.
"How is it that a person who has committed an offense should receive retribution in this present life, yet the offense does not increase and they do not fall into hell?
There is a person who cultivates the body, cultivates precepts, cultivates the mind, and cultivates wisdom; such a person possesses great resolve and their mind is free from obstruction."
When a person has committed such offenses, they no longer increase; rather, they are experienced in the present life.
It is like a person who fills a small vessel with water and puts a sheng of salt into it—the water becomes undrinkable.
If, moreover, there were a person who threw one *śoṇa* of salt into a great lake, they would not even perceive the taste of the salt, let alone be unable to drink it.
Why is this? Because the water is abundant and the salt is scant; the same applies to their transgressions.
The verse says:
If a measure of salt is cast into the great ocean, its flavor remains unchanged;
but if it is cast into water in a small vessel, its bitterness and salinity make it undrinkable.
Just as a person who has accumulated great merit, even if they commit a small evil,
does not fall into the evil realms, but experiences the retribution lightly due to other conditions;
so too for a person of meager merit, even if they commit a small evil...
Because their resolve is narrow and small, sin causes them to fall into the evil realms.
If a person’s digestive fire is weak and they eat too much, it is difficult for them to digest;
though such a person does not die, their body undergoes great suffering.
If a person’s physical strength is robust, even if they eat little, it is difficult for that food to be digested;
such a person will ultimately not die, but will suffer only slight affliction.
If one’s fire of merit, fortune, and wisdom is weak, yet possesses even a small evil offense, [the suffering will be great].
This sin is without rescue and can cause one to fall into hell.
One who possesses great merit and virtue, though they have committed sinful deeds, will not fall into hell;
rather, they will experience the retribution lightly in their present body.
For example, Aṅgulimāla, who had killed many people and even sought to harm his mother and the Buddha, attained the path of Arhatship.

He experienced the retribution for his deeds lightly in this life. Furthermore, Ajātaśatru harmed his father, the King who had attained the Way; yet, due to the causal conditions of the Buddha and Mañjuśrī, his grave offense was experienced as light.

Furthermore, it is like a person born with a venomous snake; when it first appears, it rains blood, and as it gradually grows larger, its intent is to kill people—mere sight of it causes death, and if one breathes upon it with its breath, one also dies. For this reason, the people of that time called it "the Breath-Killer" (Āśīviṣa).
When this person was about to die, Śāriputra went to his side;
though he harbored anger in his heart, the man did not die even when looked upon by him, nor did he die when exhorted by him.
Śāriputra’s own physical appearance then became even more radiant, and his mind immediately became pure as he performed the sevenfold contemplation from top to bottom.

By these causes and conditions, after his life ended, he was reborn seven times in the heavens and seven times among humans. Later, when the human lifespan was forty thousand years, he was to attain the path of a Pratyekabuddha. His body was golden in color; at that time, people thought it was a mass of gold come to be cut and taken, but he immediately passed away into parinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, King Aśoka subdued Jambudvīpa with his army and put eighteen thousand palace women to death.

Because he had previously offered land to the Buddha in a former life, he erected eighty thousand stūpas; he constantly listened to and received the sūtras and Dharma from great arhats, and later attained the stage of Srotāpanna, whereby the burden of his human body was lightened as retribution was paid.
Because such persons have committed many virtues, possess vast aspirations, and have accumulated various merits, they do not fall into the evil realms.
Therefore, your previous objection—that "if one repents, karmic offenses will be completely extinguished and there will be no retribution"—is incorrect.
Furthermore, if one says that "offenses cannot be extinguished," then the Buddha’s teaching in the *Vinaya* that "confession eliminates offenses" would be untrustworthy.
This is not the case; therefore, one must repent for the offenses that constitute karmic obstructions.
Chapter Twelve: Distinguishing Generosity. Bodhisattvas are able to perform such repentance, exhortation, sympathetic joy, and dedication.
The power of merit increases further, and the mind becomes even more supple;
one then gains faith in the Buddha’s virtues as well as the great practices of the bodhisattvas.
Because this bodhisattva practices repentance, exhortation, sympathetic joy, and dedication, the power of their merit increases and their mind becomes harmonious and supple.

Regarding the immeasurable merits of all Buddhas, which are supremely pure and beyond the belief of ordinary beings, they are able to believe and accept them; likewise, regarding the pure great practices and rare, difficult feats of the great Bodhisattvas, they are also able to believe and accept them.
Seeing that all sentient beings are afflicted by suffering and lack this profound,
pure Dharma, he gives rise to compassion for them and develops a heart of deep pity.

Having gained faith in the immeasurable, profound, pure, and supreme virtues of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, the Bodhisattva takes pity on all sentient beings who lack such virtues and, seeing that they undergo various forms of suffering due solely to their false views, gives rise to a heart of deep compassion.
"Thinking of these sentient beings, who are submerged in the mire of suffering and affliction,
I shall rescue and deliver them, causing them to dwell in a place of peace and security.
Having attained this mind of compassion, the bodhisattva forms this thought:

"These sentient beings are constantly afflicted by greed, hatred, and delusion; they undergo various physical and mental sufferings. I shall rescue them and cause them to leave the deep mire of physical and mental suffering, so that they may ultimately be free from the calamities of birth, old age, sickness, and death, and attain the state of peaceful and secure nirvana."

Therefore, one gives rise to profound compassion for these suffering sentient beings; because of this compassion, one seeks to fulfill their wishes so that they may attain peace and happiness—this is called the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
If a bodhisattva thus deeply accords with the mind of compassion,
severs all greed and attachment, and exerts diligent effort for the sake of giving—
this bodhisattva is one who seeks the Buddha-way and maintains the thought of delivering sentient beings from suffering and affliction.
"Following" means following compassion and not following other states of mind.
"Deep compassion" means pervading all sentient beings with mindfulness that penetrates to the very marrow of the bones.
"All that one possesses" refers to everything internal and external, including gold, silver, precious jewels, kingdoms, cities, wives, children, and so forth.
Greed (*lobha*) is defined as insatiable desire for acquisition.
Stinginess (*mātsarya*) is defined as attachment; it is the refusal to give to others. Severing these three evils is called detachment.
In this way, one opens the gateway to the *dānapāramitā* (perfection of giving). Therefore, one should always practice with single-minded diligence and never allow oneself to be negligent.
Why is this? The bodhisattva reflects:
"I shall now act according to my capacity to benefit sentient beings, giving rise to a firm resolve for generosity."
Whatever objects there may be, whether sentient or insentient,
even the rank of a Wheel-Turning Heavenly King— he would give them all away without seeking anything in return.
This extends even to men and women, noble clansmen, and beloved wives and concubines.
Extremely handsome in his youth, he was skillful and capable of serving others.
Reverent and compliant with a gentle heart, his affectionate feelings were most profound;
he cherished him more than his own life, giving to all who asked.
Even his own body’s flesh and blood, marrow and hands and feet, head, eyes, ears, nose, and so forth—his entire person—he is able to give.
This bodhisattva, with a concentrated mind, practices giving; whatever external things he possesses, whether animate or inanimate, there is nothing that he does not give when asked.
"Lifeless things" refers to gold,
silver, precious jewels, and even the rank of a wheel-turning sage king (*cakravartin*) or the rank of a celestial king (*devendra*).
"Living beings" refers to:
Whether they be men or women, nobles, or the young wives and concubines of noble families—

whether they be upright and dignified, gentle and mild, respectful and compliant— their love for them reaches such an extreme that it exceeds even their own lives and bodies, yet they are still able to give them away to others.
Just as the Bodhisattva Sarvāstidatta was able to give away all his external possessions, including his wife and children, so too this bodhisattva—
even his own flesh, blood, head, eyes, hands, feet, ears, and nose— cuts his flesh and extracts his bones, and breaks his bones to extract his marrow, just like Sadāprarudita.
Or they give away their entire bodies; for there is nothing more beloved than one's own body, yet they are able to give it away, as did Śakra.
For instance, when the Bodhisattva was a hare, he gave his own body to a rishi.
As when King Śibi sacrificed his own body to save a pigeon.
A question is asked:
Does this bodhisattva know through discrimination the nature of giving and the karmic retribution of giving, and for that reason is able to perform such a difficult act of giving?
Is it only because it is prompted by a mind of loving-kindness and compassion that one gives?
The answer is:
For one who gives in such a manner, they shall obtain such a retribution.
Internally, by means of the limbs and joints, as well as all external objects.
"Internal objects" refers to the head, eyes, hands, feet, and so forth.
"External objects" refers to wife and children, gold, silver, precious goods, and so forth.
This bodhisattva knows giving as it truly is, discerning each instance of what is attained and its respective retribution.
Furthermore, he has faith in what is taught in the various sūtras, or he comes to know it through his divine eye.
Question:

You previously stated that one knows the fruits of retribution obtained through the giving of one's own limbs and members as well as external objects; you may now explain what those fruits of retribution are.
Answer: In the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*, within the thirty-first chapter, "The Bodhisattva Akṣayamati," regarding the meaning of the *dānapāramitā*, it says:
"When a bodhisattva establishes a vow, they give food to those who require food, vowing: 'May I thereby obtain five kinds of retribution.'"
First, obtaining longevity; second, obtaining courage; third, obtaining happiness; fourth, obtaining strength; fifth, obtaining a beautiful complexion.
"To those who require drink, one gives drink; first they obtain fragrant and delicious beverages among human beings, and later they attain the removal of all afflictions and the thirst of craving.

To those who require a vehicle, one gives a vehicle; they then obtain the retribution of joy according to their wishes, accomplish the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), and later attain the path of the three vehicles."
"If one gives clothing to those who need clothing, one will receive the reward of the robes of shame and modesty.
If one gives lamps to those who need light, one will obtain the radiance of the Buddha-eye.
If one gives music to those who need it, one will attain the perfection of the divine ear."
"If one requires powdered incense and unguents, by giving powdered incense and unguents,
one will obtain a body free from foul odors.
If one requires liquids, by giving liquids, one will obtain a sense of taste that is fully responsive."
“If one provides dwellings, one shall become a refuge and protection for all sentient beings.
By bestowing the necessities of life, one shall assist in the merit of awakening.”
"One who gives medicine shall attain freedom from old age, illness, and death, and shall always enjoy peace and security.
One who gives servants shall attain mastery over their own will and be fully endowed with wisdom."
"By giving gold, silver, coral, musāragalva, and agate, one attains the fulfillment of the thirty-two marks.
By giving various miscellaneous objects and ornaments, one attains the eighty secondary characteristics."
"One who gives elephants, horses, and chariots shall obtain the fulfillment of the Mahāyāna.
One who gives gardens and groves shall obtain the fulfillment of the bliss of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
One who gives sons and daughters shall obtain the beloved *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
"One who gives granaries, treasures, and storehouses shall attain the fulfillment of the Dharma-treasury.
One who gives the sovereignty of a single kingdom, a single Jambudvīpa, or the four continents shall become a sovereign Dharma-king at the site of enlightenment."
"By giving various articles for play and amusement,
one obtains the joy of the Dharma.
By giving feet, one obtains the feet of the Dharma, enabling one to reach the site of enlightenment."
“Those who give with their hands shall obtain jewel-hands.
Those who can give everything, giving even their ears and noses, shall obtain a complete body.
Those who give their eyes shall obtain the complete, unobstructed Dharma-eye.”
“By giving one’s head as an offering, one attains the supreme wisdom that is uniquely honored throughout the three realms.
By giving one’s flesh and blood as an offering, one causes all sentient beings to attain firm and steadfast conduct.”
“By giving marrow as an offering, one attains a vajra-body that cannot be destroyed.
Thus should the fruits and rewards of opening the gate of giving be understood; the fruits and rewards of other forms of giving should likewise be known.”
"By giving bedding and requisites as a gift, one attains the peaceful liberation of the three vehicles.
By giving a seat for sitting, one attains the indestructible site of the bodhimanda beneath the tree of enlightenment."
"To give away one's wife is for the sake of attaining the joy and delight of the Dharma.
To give away the Way is for the sake of sentient beings who have lost the way within birth and death, so that they may enter the Right Path."
"One who gives a raft does so for the sake of crossing over the flood of desire, the flood of existence, the flood of views, and the flood of ignorance.

One who gives bone does so for the sake of attaining the firmness of precept, the firmness of concentration, the firmness of liberation, the firmness of the knowledge and vision of liberation, and the firmness regarding sentient beings."
"By giving one's retinue as a gift, one achieves immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) merit, because the people of one's retinue become unified in mind, pure, and indestructible."
"By giving 'well done,' one acts so that when the time comes to preach the Dharma, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, śramaṇas, and brahmins will rejoice and offer praise."
"To give by means of a scripture is to obtain the ninefold canon so that it may endure for immeasurable time.
To give by means of the Dharma is to obtain thorough penetration of all phenomena and the accumulation of all merits."
"This bodhisattva thus delights in practicing giving, knows the purity of giving, and knows the extent of the fruits obtained from the retribution of giving.
Therefore: "Giving of non-Dharmic wealth and so forth, up to giving censured by wisdom;"
There is no such giving; rather, one should practice giving that accords with emptiness and so forth.
"Unrighteous" refers to wealth obtained through evil conduct.
"Wealth" refers to material things that sustain life.
To speak briefly, it refers to giving away wealth obtained through unwholesome karma.
Because the Bodhisattva knows such giving is impure, he does not engage in these various other forms of illegal giving, nor even in giving that is censured by the wise.
When a bodhisattva practices giving, it is solely conjoined with emptiness, wisdom, and so forth, as well as various other merits.

Question: Regarding what was said—that giving material wealth obtained through improper means and the like, as well as giving conjoined with emptiness, wisdom, and so forth—[how are these distinguished]?
These two kinds of giving should be analyzed in detail!
The answer is:
these two kinds of giving are explained within the "Dānapāramitā" section of the "Akṣayamati-bodhisattva-parivarta."
First, the classification of the merit of giving is as follows:
namely, that all Bodhisattvas practice the giving of wealth sought through no unlawful means;
they practice the giving that does not cause affliction or distress to sentient beings.
They give without fear;
they give without attachment;
there is nothing they will not give when requested.
There is no giving that does not accord with what was promised;
there is no giving with stinginess regarding what is fine or what is not fine;
there is no giving that is not from a profound heart.
Giving without flattery or crookedness;
giving without hypocrisy or pretense;
giving without diminishing the fruit.
Giving without a crooked mind;
giving without a deluded mind;
giving without a distracted mind.
There is no giving without faith or liberation;
no giving with weariness or fatigue;
no giving out of partiality or favoritism.
Do not give with the expectation of receiving a return for your gift.
Do not give seeking a field of merit.
Do not give by disregarding any sentient being as not being a field of merit.
There is no giving with a mind of superiority or inferiority based on whether one maintains or violates the precepts;
there is no giving for the sake of seeking fame;
there is no giving with a mind of self-exaltation.
There is no giving with contempt for others;
no giving with regret;
no giving with a mind of remorse.
There is no giving out of haste;
there is no giving with contempt;
there is no giving according to the nature of things.
There is no giving with a view toward seeking karmic retribution;
there is no giving with anger;
there is no giving that leaves others thirsty or destitute.
One gives without vexing the seeker;
one gives without treating them with contempt or mockery;
one gives without deception.
One does not give with a frowning face;
one does not give by tossing [the gift];
one does not give without a single-minded heart.
There was no gift not given with one's own hand;
there was no gift not given constantly;
there was no gift given without rest.
There is no giving that is interrupted;
no giving characterized by competitiveness;
and no giving with contempt for small things.
There is no giving of light things without being invited to the *prātimokṣa* ceremony.
There is no giving that does not accord with one's capacity.
There is no giving to those who are not fields of merit.
One does not give with a weak mind regarding even a small amount;
one does not give with a conceited mind relying on a large amount;
and one does not give with improper conduct.
There is no giving performed for the sake of rebirth in the realm of pleasure;
no giving performed out of reliance on physical beauty, lineage, wealth, or nobility;
and no giving performed with the desire to be born among the Four Heavenly Kings, Śakra, or Brahmā in the heavens above.
One should not practice giving with the aim of seeking the vehicles of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha;
one should not practice giving with the aim of seeking the status of a king or prince;
and one should not practice giving with the limitation of a single lifetime.
There is no giving that is insatiable;
there is no giving that is not dedicated toward omniscience (*sarvajñā*);
there is no impure giving.
There is no giving at an improper time;
there is no giving with weapons or poison;
there is no giving that involves harassing or deceiving sentient beings.
The ignorant revile such giving.
Thus has the gateway of giving been revealed; one should likewise understand other forms of impure giving, namely:
Bodhisattvas do not give things that ought to be discarded;
they do not give with an aversion toward nirvāṇa;
and they do not give things that are abundant and easy to obtain.
Giving with immeasurable grace;
giving without expectation of gratitude;
giving without seeking a reciprocal reward.
One gives without seeking protection;
one gives without seeking auspiciousness;
one gives without a mind of pride.
There is no giving of the Dharma that lacks a household;
there is no giving that is not obtained through causes;
there is no giving that does not last a lifetime.
Giving with a stainless mind;
giving without frivolity;
giving not for the sake of a spiritual friend.
There is no giving with contempt;
there is no giving with negligence;
there is no giving that results in loss.
One does not give for the sake of praising oneself;
one does not give out of anger or abuse;
one does not give for the sake of seeking blessings or prayers.
One does not give for the sake of claiming a rare or marvelous occurrence;
one does not give for the sake of manifesting one's own faith;
one does not give out of fear.
Giving without deception;
giving without seeking followers;
giving without failing to provide guidance.
There is no giving that does not attract a multitude;
there is no giving without faith;
there is no giving without a causal basis.
There is no giving according to one's own whims;
there is no giving that displays wonders;
there is no giving accompanied by self-praise.
There is no gift that is not given according to what is requested;
there is no gift given for the purpose of subduing others;
there is no gift without affection.
There is no gift that does not employ all things;
there is no gift that is not given with reverence;
there is no inferior gift.
Do not give out of a sense of wonder at appearances;
do not give with suppression or discouragement;
do not give by using one's power to seize property.
There is no giving with an impure mind;
there is no giving with a mind of doubt;
there is no giving with a mind that rejects the seeker.
One should give without forbidden objects;
one should give without discrimination;
one should not give with alcohol.
One should not give gifts involving weapons;
one should not give gifts by seizing the property of others;
and one should not give gifts that cause people to conceive doubt in their minds.
One does not give out of intimacy;
one does not give by speaking of another's faults;
one does not give according to personal attachment.
Giving without anger.
Giving without delusion.
Giving without conceptual proliferation.
There is nothing that is not given as a gift for the sake of awakening. Question:
Regarding giving wealth sought through unrighteous means, up to and including giving that is not for the sake of awakening—does the bodhisattva possess such [giving], or does he not?

If [the merit] were to be exhausted and cease to exist, there would be faults: one would not seek fields of merit, one would have no mind of non-discrimination toward sentient beings, one would neither recognize nor repay kindness, and there would be no giving according to family law or national law.
If there are such [giving], why do all say they do not exist?
The answer is:

these are instances where wealth is acquired through unrighteous means and given as a gift, up to and including giving that is not for the sake of awakening (*bodhi*). It is not necessarily the case that Bodhisattvas lack these entirely; at times, they may indeed exist.
This giving is not subsumed within the dāna-pāramitā; it is said to be "non-existent" because it cannot fulfill the dāna-pāramitā.
Regarding the giving that is conjoined with virtues such as emptiness, it is as stated in the "Dānapāramitā Chapter" of the *Akṣayamati-bodhisattva-sūtra*:
because a bodhisattva’s giving is conjoined with the mind of emptiness, it is inexhaustible.
This giving is inexhaustible because it is practiced without signs;
this giving is inexhaustible because it is protected by the absence of longing;
this giving is inexhaustible because it is encompassed by roots of goodness.
This giving is inexhaustible because it accords with the characteristic of liberation;
this giving is inexhaustible because it can destroy all Māras;
this giving is inexhaustible because it is not intermingled with afflictions.
This giving is inexhaustible because it attains further superior benefits;
this giving is inexhaustible because it is characterized by a resolute mind;
this giving is inexhaustible because it gathers the factors conducive to enlightenment.
This giving is inexhaustible because it is correctly dedicated;
this giving is inexhaustible because it attains the fruit of liberation at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa);
this giving is inexhaustible because it is boundless.
This giving is inexhaustible because it cannot be exhausted;
this giving is inexhaustible because it is uninterrupted;
this giving is inexhaustible because it is vast.
This giving is inexhaustible because it is indestructible;
this giving is inexhaustible because it is invincible;
this giving is inexhaustible because it reaches all-encompassing wisdom.
This giving eliminates the defilements of giving, such as seeking wealth through unrighteous means; because it accomplishes various merits such as emptiness (*śūnyatā*), it is inexhaustible.

Seeking wealth through unrighteous means constitutes a defilement of giving; when giving is conjoined with such defilements, it is impure giving, whereas when it is conjoined with merits such as emptiness, it is pure.
Furthermore, I shall now further explain the purity and impurity of this giving.
The Sūtra states that there are four kinds of giving:
there is giving that is pure with respect to the giver, but not pure with respect to the recipient.
There is giving that is pure for the recipient, but not pure for the giver.
There is giving that is pure for both the giver and the recipient.
There is giving that is neither pure for the giver nor pure for the recipient.

If the donor is accomplished in wholesome actions of body, speech, and mind, while the recipient is accomplished in unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind, this is called purity on the part of the donor, not purity on the part of the recipient.

If the donor accomplishes unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind, while the recipient accomplishes wholesome actions of body, speech, and mind, this is called purity in the recipient, not purity in the donor.

If the donor accomplishes wholesome deeds of body, speech, and mind, and the recipient likewise accomplishes wholesome deeds of body, speech, and mind, this is called purity in the donor and purity in the recipient as well.

If the donor accomplishes unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind, and the recipient also accomplishes unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind, this is called being neither pure with respect to the donor nor pure with respect to the recipient.
Whether greed, hatred, and delusion are abandoned or not abandoned, they should likewise be distinguished in this manner.
Furthermore, among the four kinds of giving, there is that which is pure and that which is impure.
First, purity from the giver; second, purity from the recipient; third, mutual purity. These are called purities.
First, lack of purity from the giver; second, lack of purity from the recipient; third, lack of mutual purity.
This is called impurity.
Because the donor possesses merit, giving from such a donor results in purity.
Because the recipient possesses merit, giving to such a recipient results in purity.
Because both the giver and the recipient possess merit, the gift becomes pure through the giver and the recipient.
Because the giver possesses fault, the gift is impure through the giver.
Because the recipient has faults, the gift given to the recipient is impure.
Because both the giver and the recipient have faults, the gift given by the giver to the recipient is impure.
The merit of the giver and the merit of the recipient, as well as the fault of the giver and the fault of the recipient, have already been explained.
Question:
Among these four kinds of giving that you have described, which kind of giving should a bodhisattva practice?
The answer is:
Among the four kinds of giving, one practices two kinds of pure giving;
one does not seek fame or profit, nor does one seek karmic retribution.
This giving is of four kinds: three are pure and one is impure; the impure is entirely not practiced.
Within the pure types, two purities are observed:
first, the purity of the giver, not the purity of the recipient.
Second is shared purity.
Regarding these two forms of pure giving, one should always be diligent. Why is this?
This bodhisattva does not expect a karmic reward; for if one expected a reward, one would seek the purity of the recipient.
"Purity" refers to the adornment of the virtues of both the giver and the recipient, such that their minds are pure.
"Impurity" refers to the donor possessing a mind of stinginess and attachment.
As the Buddha said:
"Stinginess is the defilement of giving."
Although other afflictions are impure, stinginess is the most severe among them.
Question:
If a bodhisattva possesses purity regarding the giver and shared purity, they should diligently practice these two types of giving.

Avarice is a defilement of giving and is, moreover, a great defilement of giving. If a bodhisattva has not yet abandoned desire and is unable to sever avarice, how can they practice these two kinds of pure giving?
Answer: If an object can give rise to stinginess, then one does not keep that object.
If a bodhisattva knows that stinginess will arise toward any object—whether animate or inanimate—they do not keep it; therefore, whatever they give as a gift is entirely free from parsimony.
Question:
