Furthermore, regarding the four *Veda* scriptures, which are finite and limited, there are even now those who cannot know them exhaustively; how much less could anyone know all scriptures completely? Therefore, there is no such person as an omniscient one.
Furthermore, there are scriptures that increase desire, such as those concerning song, dance, and music; if an omniscient person were to know these things, they would possess desire.
These scriptures are the causes and conditions for greed; where there is a cause, there must be a result.
If an omniscient person were unaware of this matter, they would not be called omniscient.
Furthermore, there are various scriptures that can incite anger and delight in deceiving others, namely those such as the secular treatises on worldly affairs.
If one recognizes these things, then anger arises.
Why is this? Because where there is a cause, there must be an effect.
If one does not know [all things], one cannot be called an omniscient person; therefore, it is known that no omniscient person exists.
Furthermore, the Buddha does not necessarily know all future events.
For example, I am now challenging the Omniscient One; the Buddha has no scripture that pre-records:
"This person, of such a surname and such a family, at such a place, will challenge the Omniscient One with such a matter."
If it is claimed that the Buddha knows all things, why does he not speak of this matter?
If he were one who teaches the sūtras, this matter should be contained within them; yet since he does not speak of it, we know he is not an omniscient person.
Furthermore, if the Buddha were to know all future events exhaustively, he ought to have known in advance that after Devadatta had left the household life, he would cause a schism in the Sangha;
had he known this, he should not have permitted his ordination.
Furthermore, the Buddha did not know about the wooden mechanism and the flying stone.
Had the Buddha known this in advance, he would not have walked back and forth (caṅkrama) therein.
Furthermore, the Buddha did not know that the Brahmin woman Ciñcā would slander him with charges of sexual misconduct.
If the Buddha had known this beforehand, he should have informed the bhikṣus that such a thing would occur in the future.
Furthermore, there was a brahmin who, out of jealousy toward the Buddha, killed a brahmin woman—Sundarī—in another location and buried her in the moat of the Jeta Grove.
The Buddha did not know this matter; had he known it, he should have saved this girl’s life when she was beneath the rock pushed down by Devadatta.
Since he did not mention the matter of the Brāhmaṇa woman or the daughter of the Brahmin at that place, it is because he did not know it.
One should know, therefore, that the Buddha does not know everything regarding future lives, and for this reason, he is not an omniscient person.
Furthermore, when the Buddha entered a Brahmin village to beg for food and emerged with an empty bowl— unable to foresee the timing of Māra’s interference and the turning of people's hearts,
such that he did not obtain even a single meal— if the Buddha had known this, he should not have entered the Brahmin village.
Therefore, it is known that "the Buddha does not know all future events.
Furthermore, because King Ajātaśatru wished to harm the Buddha, he released the intoxicated elephant Dhanapāla.
Because the Buddha did not know [of this], he entered the city of Rājagṛha to beg for food; had he known it in advance, he would not have entered the city.
Therefore, he does not know future events, and because he does not know future events, he is not an omniscient person.
Furthermore, the Buddha did not know the circumstances of Akṣamālā’s invitation; he accepted the invitation immediately and, taking the bhikṣus with him, proceeded to the kingdom of Verañjā.
Because this brahmin forgot his prior invitation, he caused the Buddha to eat horse fodder.
Had the Buddha known beforehand, he would not have accepted the invitation and eaten horse fodder for three months.
Therefore, it is known that the Buddha does not know future events; because he does not know future events, he is not an omniscient person.
Furthermore, because the Buddha accepted Sunakṣatra as his disciple, he did not know future events.
This person’s evil mind is firm and difficult to transform; he does not believe the Buddha’s words.
If the Buddha were aware of this, why would he accept him as a disciple?
Because he accepts him as a disciple, he does not know future events; because he does not know future events, he is not an omniscient one.
Furthermore, if the Buddha were an omniscient person, he should have protected those who had not yet committed offenses by establishing the precepts beforehand.

Since he established the precepts only after first being unaware of the causes and conditions for their establishment and only after someone had already committed an offense, it follows that he did not know future events.
Because they do not know future events, they are not omniscient persons.
Furthermore, in the Buddha-dharma, one is placed among the senior monks (upādhyāya) and receives respectful salutations based solely on the number of years since one’s renunciation and ordination.

One does not consider seniority, noble lineage, prominent families, merit, wisdom, extensive learning, meditative concentration, fruits of the path, abandonments, or supernormal powers to be greatness.

If one is an omniscient one, they should be honored and revered as great on account of their seniority, noble lineage, various families, meritorious virtues, wisdom, extensive learning, meditative concentration, fruits of realization, abandonments, and supernormal powers.
If it is thus, it is called "properly regulated.
Regarding "years," this refers to the number of years since receiving the precepts; for example, a practitioner of five years' standing pays homage to one of six years' standing.
Regarding the noble ones: there are four classes of beings in the world—Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras.
A Śūdra should show respect to Vaiśyas, Kṣatriyas, and Brahmins; a Vaiśya should show respect to Kṣatriyas and Brahmins; and a Kṣatriya should show respect to Brahmins.
Regarding "families," these include families of artisans, merchants, householders, elders, ministers, and royal families.
Among these families, a smaller family should show respect to a larger family;
likewise, one who has gone forth from a poor and lowly family should show respect to one who has gone forth from a wealthy and noble family.

Regarding merit: those who have violated the precepts should respectfully bow to and pay homage to those who uphold the precepts, but those who uphold the precepts should not pay homage to those who have violated them;
those who do not practice the twelve *dhūta* ascetic virtues should pay homage to those who do practice them;
and those who do not fully practice the *dhūta* virtues should pay homage to those who do fully practice them.
The wise: those lacking wisdom should pay homage to those possessing wisdom.
The learned: those who have heard little should pay homage to those who have heard much.
Those who do not recite much should pay homage to those who recite much.
Regarding the fruits: a *srotāpanna* should pay homage to a *sakṛdāgāmin*; in this manner, they should successively pay homage to an *arhat*.
All ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) should pay homage to those who have attained the fruits.
Regarding those who have severed [defilements]: one who has severed few fetters and afflictions, or has not yet severed them, should pay homage to one who has severed many.
Regarding those with supernormal powers (*abhijñā*): if one has not yet perfected the supernormal powers, one should pay homage to one who has perfected them.
If the Buddha had thus excellently taught the methods for making offerings and showing reverence in such a sequence, it would constitute a supreme teaching; yet, in reality, he did not do so.
Therefore, one knows that he is not an omniscient person.
Furthermore, even the Buddha cannot know all present matters.
If you ask me, "How do you know that the Buddha does not know present matters? I shall now explain:

there are sentient beings whose fetters (*saṃyojana*) are thin, who have no karmic obstructions, who are free from the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*), who are capable of practicing the profound Dharma, and who are able to accomplish the True Dharma—yet the Buddha does not know them.
After the Buddha had attained enlightenment, when he first intended to preach the Dharma, such a doubt arose within him:

"The Dharma I have realized is profoundly deep, mysterious and remote, subtle and wondrous, quiescent, difficult to know and difficult to understand; it can be known only by the wise within themselves.
Worldly beings are attached to mundane affairs, yet herein all afflictions are severed, craving is extinguished, and weary detachment is achieved—this is foremost among things difficult to perceive."
"If I were to preach the Dharma and sentient beings did not understand it, I would merely exhaust myself in vain.

Giving rise to such doubts, he failed to realize that although there are indeed sentient beings with meager fetters (*saṃyojana*), those without karmic obstructions, those who have escaped the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*), those capable of practicing the profound Dharma, and those able to accomplish the True Dharma—the Buddha was unable to recognize such beings.
Therefore, one should know that he did not know what was occurring in the present.
Furthermore, he thought to himself:
"In the past, when I practiced austerities, the five bhikṣus attended and served me; they should be benefited first."
"Where is he now?
Having had this thought, a deva then announced:
"He is now at Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park."
Therefore, one should know:
the Buddha does not know present matters.
Because he does not know present matters, he is not an omniscient person.
Furthermore, after the Buddha had attained the Way and accepted an invitation to preach the Dharma, he thought:
"Now that I am about to preach the Dharma, who should hear it first?
He then reflected further:
“Udraka Rāmaputra was a man of sharp intelligence and could easily have been awakened.
At that time, however, this person had already passed away when the Buddha went in search of him.
Then a deva announced:
"He passed away last night.
The Buddha again reflected and turned his mind toward seeking out Ārāḍa to deliver him.
The deva spoke again, saying:
"This man has been dead for seven days.
If the Buddha were the Omniscient One, he should have known beforehand that these people had passed away; yet in reality, he did not know.
Because one does not know the affairs of the past, one is not called an omniscient person (*sarvajña*).
An omniscient person, according to the nature of things, should deliver those who can be delivered; those who cannot be delivered, he simply sets aside.
Furthermore, the Buddha has spoken with intentional ambiguity on various occasions; for example, regarding the city of Pāṭaliputra, he said: "This place shall be destroyed by three causes:
either by water, or by fire, or by internal people conspiring with outsiders."
If the Buddha were an omniscient person, he should not have speech characterized by doubt; therefore, it is known that he is not omniscient.
Furthermore, the Buddha asked the bhikṣus:
"What matters were you discussing when you gathered together?"
Regarding such questions as these:
if one were an omniscient person, they would not need to ask about such matters;
because they ask others, they are not omniscient.
Furthermore, the Buddha praises his own body and disparages others, as it is said in a sutra:
"The Buddha told Ānanda:
'I alone am the foremost and peerless; there is no one equal to me.'"
He addressed the bhikṣus:
"The Nirgranthas and their like are wicked and evil men who have accomplished five false dharmas.
These Nirgranthas lack faith, lack shame, lack remorse, are of little learning and indolent, and possess scant mindfulness and meager wisdom."

Furthermore, it is said that when Brahmins, Nirgranthas, and other disciples of external paths engage in various improper acts—such as praising themselves and disparaging others—even worldly people would feel ashamed; how much more so, then, for one who possesses all-knowledge!
Because of these matters, he is not an omniscient person.
Furthermore, the Buddha’s sūtras contradict one another from beginning to end; as it is said in a sūtra:
"O bhikṣus!..."
"I have newly attained the Way," he said.
He further said,
"I have attained the Way that all Buddhas of antiquity attained."

"In this world, even those possessed of worldly wisdom avoid contradictions between the end and the beginning; how much more so for one who has left the household life, a person of all-knowledge (sarvajña), that there should be such contradiction?
Because of this contradiction between the end and the beginning, one should know that he is not a person of all-knowledge."
Therefore, your statement that "the Vajrasamādhi is attained only by those who possess all-knowledge" is incorrect;
because there is no one who possesses all-knowledge, the Samādhi of All-Knowledge is likewise not established.
He replied:
"Do not say such a thing; the Buddha is indeed the Omniscient One. Why is this?"

All phenomena consist of five categories of dharmas: namely, past dharmas, future dharmas, present dharmas, dharmas transcending the three periods of time, and ineffable dharmas. Only the Buddha knows these dharmas as they truly are, in their entirety.
Regarding your previous objection that "because the dharmas to be known are immeasurable and boundless, there can be no person who possesses omniscience," I shall now respond:
If the dharmas to be known are immeasurable and boundless, then wisdom too is immeasurable and boundless.
To know "immeasurable and boundless dharmas" by means of "immeasurable and boundless wisdom" is without fault.
If it is argued that "this knowing must also be known by another wisdom, which would lead to an infinite regress," we shall now reply:
Dharmas should indeed be known by wisdom; as for this wisdom, it is as people in the world say:
“I am wise; I am ignorant; I am one of coarse wisdom; I am one of subtle wisdom.
Because of these conditions, by knowing wisdom through wisdom, there is no fault of infinite regress.
Just as one uses present knowledge to know past knowledge, so too does one come to know all phenomena exhaustively, without exception.
Furthermore, it is like a person counting another's fingers as ten; their knowledge is likewise.
If one knows oneself and also knows others, then there is no fault, just as a lamp illuminates itself and also illuminates others.
As for what you said— that even a combination of hundreds,
thousands, ten-thousands, millions, and billions of wise people cannot fully know all phenomena, let alone a single person— this is not so!
Why is this? Because all those possessed of wisdom are able to know manifold matters;
whereas even if many people are gathered together, if they lack wisdom, they are unable to know anything at all.
Just as a hundred thousand blind people are incapable of serving as guides,
whereas a single person with eyes is capable of being a guide;
so too, because you find fault with even one person, though you possess much knowledge, you possess no knowledge regarding the Buddha.
This is not the case!
As for your claim that "the Buddha is not omniscient because he did not teach external scriptures such as the Vedas," I shall now respond:
within the Vedas there is no dharma of sublime tranquility and cessation; they contain only various kinds of frivolous conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*).
All that the Buddhas have taught is for the sake of excellent quiescence.
Although the Buddha knows such scriptures as the Vedas, they cannot enable people to attain excellent quiescence; therefore, he did not teach them.
Question:

"In the *Vedas* there is also the teaching of wholesome quiescence and liberation: that the world was originally all dark and nothing existed, until a Great Being appeared like the sun; those who see him attain deliverance from the perils of death, and there are further other guides."
Furthermore, it is said:
when the human body is small, the spirit is small; when the person is large, the spirit is large.
The body is the dwelling of the spirit, which constantly resides within it.
If one uses wisdom to unravel and untie the fetters of the spirit, then one attains liberation.
Therefore, you should know that within the Vedas there is tranquil extinction and liberation.
He replied:
"There is no such thing! Why is this?"
In the *Veda* scriptures, there are "four inversions":
the world is impermanent, yet one perceives a separate, permanent world.

For example, it is said that if one constructs a celestial shrine once, it falls; if a second time, it also falls; but if constructed for a third time, it does not fall. This is the "inversion of permanence" within impermanence.
To speak of there being a place of permanence and bliss within a world that is suffering is the "perverted view of pleasure" (*sukha-viparyāsa*) amidst suffering.
Furthermore, to say that one's spirit transmigrates into a child and pray for a lifespan of a hundred years [is likewise a delusion].
The son is another's body; how can he be "I"?
This is the "perverted notion of self" within what is non-self.
It is said that the purity of the body is supreme and peerless.
Gold, silver, and precious jewels do not belong to the self; this is called the "perverted view of purity within impurity.
Since such perversions lack reality, and that which lacks reality cannot possess cessation, how could there be any extinction?
Therefore, within the *Vedas*, there is no dharma of wholesome quiescence (*śānti*).
Question: The *Vedas* state that "one who can know the *Vedas* is pure and secure"; why then do you say there is no dharma of wholesome quiescence?
Answer: Those who know the Vedas, although they speak of peace and security, do not possess ultimate liberation.
Within their distinct bodies, they give rise to the notion of liberation; thus, because of their long-lived celestial realms, they describe those states as liberation.
Therefore, within the Vedas, there is truly no liberation.
Furthermore, within the Vedas, there are briefly three meanings:
first, incantations and prayers; second, eulogies; and third, ritual precepts.
"Prayer for blessings" (*adhiṣṭhāna*) means: "May I obtain a wife and children, cattle and horses, gold, silver, and precious treasures.
"Praise" (*stuti*) means: "O Fire God, you have a black head, a red neck, and a yellow body; you are ever-present within the five elements (*pañca-mahābhūta*) of sentient beings."
“Rules” (vidhi) refer to what should be done and what should not be done.
For example, one may initially receive the fire-ritual from the constellation Kṛttikā; yet in reality, such incantations, blessings, and praises possess no tranquility or liberation.

Why is this? Because one is greedily attached to worldly pleasures, offering clarified butter as a sacrificial oblation while reciting incantations, yet lacks true wisdom and does not sever the afflictions; how, then, can there be liberation?
It is asked:
The Dharma of the Vedas has existed since antiquity and is the most trustworthy;
as for your claim that "it cannot be trusted because it lacks wholesome tranquility and extinction," this is not so!
Why is this? The Buddha-dharma appeared in the world only recently, whereas the *Vedas* are from ancient times and have long been present in the world.
Therefore, the ancient teachings are trustworthy, while the recent teachings are not.
As for your statement that "the Vedas do not contain the Dharma of wholesome quiescence," this is not so.
The answer is:
one cannot rely on time—ignorance arose first, and right knowledge arose later.

Wrong view arises first, and right view arises later; one cannot claim that because ignorance and wrong view arise first they are "trustworthy," while right knowledge and right view, arising later, are "untrustworthy."
Just as there must first be mud before there can be a lotus,
and first illness before there can be medicine,

one cannot claim that what appears earlier is necessarily superior. Therefore, the assertion that the *Vedas* appeared first and the Buddha-dharma appeared later, and thus the latter is not to be trusted, is incorrect.
Furthermore, the various Buddhas of the past, such as Dīpaṃkara and others, all appeared in the world first; their teachings were ancient, whereas the Vedas appeared later.
If you consider that which is ancient and long-standing to be venerable, then these Buddhas and their Dharma should likewise be venerable.
Question:
The Vedas cannot bring about wholesome quiescence; therefore, they are not taught within the Buddha-Dharma.
If the Buddha knows that one cannot achieve nirvana, what is the use of such knowledge?
If he does not know it, then he is not an omniscient person;
both cases involve faults.
The answer is:
Your statement is incorrect. The Buddha already knew beforehand that the Vedas could not lead to true quiescence; therefore, he neither taught them nor practiced them.
Question:
If the Buddha knew that the Vedas offer no benefit and thus taught that they should not be practiced, what was the purpose of his knowing them?
Answer:
A person of great wisdom should fully discern what is the right path and what is the wrong path;
desiring to enable immeasurable multitudes of people to cross over perilous and evil paths, they proceed upon the right path.

For example, just as a guide skillfully distinguishes between wrong paths and the right path, so too is the Buddha: having himself emerged from the perilous road of birth, old age, and death, he likewise desires to cause all beings to emerge from it. Therefore, he thoroughly knows the Eightfold Noble Path, as well as the false and perilous evil paths such as the *Vedas*;
yet, for the sake of causing others to leave the evil paths and proceed upon the right path, he knows them alone without speaking of them.
It is just as when a farmer plants grain; when he harvests in autumn, he also obtains weeds and chaff.

The Buddha is likewise: because he practices with diligent vigor for the sake of the Unsurpassed Way, he attains the path of Bodhi and also understands the *Vedas* and other heterodox paths; therefore, there is no fault.
Regarding what you previously stated—that "no person can possess full knowledge of the four Vedas"—this objection is not valid.
People in the world each possess their own power of memory; some can recite five verses in a single day, some a hundred verses, and some two hundred verses.
If a person does not recite ten verses for a single day, they might say:
"There is no one capable of reciting a hundred verses or producing a hundred verses; this is not true speech.

Because you cannot know everything, you then say, "There is no wise person at all. It is like seeing one person who cannot cross a river and saying, "There is no one capable of crossing it. Such a person is not speaking correctly. Why is this?
Just as there are others of great power who can deliver [beings], so it is with this case as well.
Even if other people cannot know everything, what fault is there in the All-Knowing One knowing it?
Furthermore, the seer Viśvāmitra studied all the Vedas and should likewise have attained omniscience;
if he read the Vedas completely, why do you say that "he lacked omniscience"?
If you say, "There are scriptures that can give rise to greed and anger," I shall now respond:
If a person desires long life, they should avoid the causes and conditions of death;
likewise, the Buddha, desiring to sever the greed and anger of all sentient beings, must know the causes and conditions of greed and anger.
Furthermore, as for your statement that "if one can know the scriptures that give rise to greed and anger, then one possesses greed and anger," this is impossible.
Although the Buddha knows this, he does not employ it nor practice it; therefore, there is no fault.
It is like a person who, knowing the causes and conditions of death, does not die, whereas if one practices the causes and conditions of death, one dies—the same applies to this matter.
If you say, "Because one does not know future events, one is not called 'Omniscient' (sarvajña)," I shall now reply:
this is not a valid objection.
We also acknowledge that there are those who challenge the claim of omniscience, as it is said in the Sūtra:
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Ordinary worldlings lack wisdom and possess three characteristics:
they think what should not be thought, speak what should not be spoken, and do what should not be done."
Therefore, this has already been explained in its entirety.
You ordinary persons of future ages are all included therein.
Since it would be of no benefit, what use is there in separately stating their names and so forth?
If it is argued that "the Buddha knew there would be difficulties and did not answer in advance," this too is unnecessary!

Even now, among the fourfold assembly, there are those capable of skillfully resolving doubts and difficulties, and there are also those able to refute various challenging questions; why was it necessary for him to have answered beforehand?
As you can see today among the bhikṣus, there are those capable of refuting the brāhmaṇas; therefore, it is unnecessary to provide a preliminary answer.

Furthermore, answers have been given previously as well, scattered throughout various sūtras; because people cannot fully comprehend the Buddha-dharma, they do not know where these answers are located.
If it is said that "he accepted Devadatta’s ordination," I shall now respond:
To say that "one who accepts Devadatta’s ordination is not an omniscient one" is incorrect;
Devadatta’s ordination was not conferred by the Buddha.
Question:
If others were to ordain them, why did the Buddha permit it? Answer:
Good and evil each have their own time; it is not necessarily the case that leaving the household life constitutes evil.
After Devadatta left the household life, he possessed various merits such as upholding the precepts; therefore, there is no fault in leaving the household life.
Furthermore, for twelve years Devadatta maintained pure precepts and recited sixty thousand Dharma-piṭakas;
as for this karmic retribution, it will not be in vain in the future, but will certainly bring benefit.
Regarding your statement that "Devadatta’s mechanical device hurled a stone," I shall now explain:
because all Buddhas have perfected the dharma of non-killing, no one in any world is able to take their life.
Question:
If one has accomplished the practice of non-killing, why do flying stones come toward them? Answer:
In previous lives, the Buddha planted karmic seeds through actions that destroy the body; as these are determinate retributions, they must be experienced.
To show sentient beings that the retribution of karma cannot be avoided, he manifested this experience and therefore came of his own accord.
Regarding your statement that the Buddha did not previously speak of the woman Ciñcā, I shall now respond:
although the woman Ciñcā reviled the Buddha, she was unable to destroy the causal conditions of the Omniscient One.
If the Buddha had previously said, "The woman Ciñcā will come to slander me," then Ciñcā would not have come.
Furthermore, due to the karmic causes and conditions of the offenses committed by the Buddha in previous lives, he must now necessarily undergo the retribution.
Regarding your question as to why the Buddha did not prevent Sundarī from entering the Jeta Grove, I shall now answer:
this matter cannot obstruct the causal conditions of an Omniscient One;
for the Buddha does not possess the power to cause all sentient beings to become performers of music.
Furthermore, all Buddhas are free from all disputes; they do not exalt themselves nor are they attached to their observance of the precepts.
For this reason, they do not prevent it.
Moreover, because the karma of the Buddha’s previous lives has ripened, he must necessarily undergo seven days of slander.
Furthermore, because sentient beings see that the Buddha feels no sorrow when hearing slander and no joy when hearing praise, they resolve their minds upon the unsurpassed path, making this vow:
"We, too, shall attain such a pure mind!"
Therefore, there is no fault.
As for what you previously stated—that "the Buddha entered a brahmin village and left with an empty bowl, thus he is not an omniscient one"—this shall now be answered:
It was not that the Buddha first observed the minds of people regarding food and drink; rather, after he had already entered the village, Māra turned their minds [against him].
Question: The Buddha should have known this beforehand: "When I enter the village, Māra will turn the minds of people. Answer:
The Buddha also foresaw this matter; for the great benefit of sentient beings, the Buddhas do not merely provide benefit by receiving the food of others, but rather liberate sentient beings.
There are those who welcome [the Buddha] with a pure mind, pay him homage, and look upon him with a serene countenance—these are all great benefits; why need one necessarily provide food and drink?
One benefits sentient beings through various means; it is not for the sake of emptily entering a village.
Regarding your statement that "the Buddha went against the current to approach a drunken elephant," I shall now respond:
Although the Buddha was aware of this matter, he went there for a specific cause and condition;
namely, that this drunken elephant was certain to attain liberation.
Furthermore, it can also obstruct the karmic retribution for the sin of harming the Buddha.
Moreover, this elephant’s body is like a black mountain; when the multitude sees him bowing his head to pay homage to the Buddha, they all give rise to reverence.
For these reasons, the Buddha intentionally proceeded toward him.
Furthermore, there is no fault in the Buddha approaching this elephant;
if there were an evil matter, such an objection could be raised.
As for your objection regarding "going to the forest hermitage," it is because he undergoes the retribution of the karmic fruits from previous lives.
Regarding your statement that "he kept Sunakṣatra as a disciple," this shall now be explained:
Because the Buddha’s body, speech, mind, and life require no protection and he is free from fear, he permitted him to be his disciple.

Furthermore, because this person constantly stays near the Buddha, they witness various great supernormal powers; they see the kings of the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, and others coming to make offerings to the Buddha and inquire about various profound and essential teachings, whereby their minds attain purity.
Because their minds are pure, they obtain the conditions for benefit; therefore, even though they are evil, they are permitted to become disciples.
Question:
This person has frequently given rise to evil thoughts toward the Buddha; therefore, he should not be permitted to become a disciple. Answer:
If one were not permitted to become a disciple, there would likewise be ill-will; for this reason, permitting one to become a disciple entails no fault.
As for your statement, "Why were the precepts not established before one had committed a transgression? I shall now answer:
The Buddha first established the precepts by teaching the Eightfold Noble Path.
Right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
Because these are said to be the path leading to Nirvana, all precepts have already been explained.

Furthermore, the Buddha taught the three trainings—the training in virtue, the training in mind, and the training in wisdom—and it should be understood that by this he has already explained all precepts.
Furthermore, the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"All evil must certainly not be committed."
Is this not what is called "the precepts being established beforehand"?
Furthermore, when the Buddha taught the ten paths of wholesome action—

abstaining from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, double-tongued speech, harsh speech, false speech, frivolous speech, covetousness, ill will, and wrong views— is this not what is called "the precepts being established beforehand"?
In the first twelve years of his teaching, the Buddha spoke a single verse as the method for the *poṣadha*;
it is said:
"Commit no evil whatsoever; practice all that is good; purify your own mind—this is the teaching of the Buddhas."
Therefore, one should know that the precepts had already been established beforehand.
Furthermore, the Buddha said:
"One should abandon all minor causes and conditions of evil."
As it is said:
"Abandoning all evil conduct of body, And abandoning all evils of speech,
Abandoning all evil conduct of mind, May one distance oneself from all other evils."
Regarding this statement, one should know that the precepts had already been established beforehand.
Furthermore, the Buddha had previously taught:
"The various dharmas for guarding [the mind]."
As it is said:
"To guard the body is good; to guard speech is also good;
to guard the mind is good; to guard all [the sense faculties] is good."
"A bhikṣu who guards all [the sense-faculties] Attains freedom from all evils.
One should know that by speaking thus, the Buddha had already established the precepts.
Furthermore, the Buddha first explained the characteristics of virtue, as it is said:
"Do not recklessly harm hands or feet; be moderate in speech and cautious in conduct.
One should delight in maintaining a concentrated mind; such a person is called a true bhikṣu.
By speaking thus, one should know that the precepts have already been established.
Furthermore, because the qualities of a śramaṇa are being explained, one should know that the precepts were already established beforehand;

a śramaṇa has four dharmas: first, not retaliating against anger; second, remaining silent when reviled; third, being able to endure blows from a staff; and fourth, enduring those who would cause harm.

Furthermore, the Buddha taught the four foundations of mindfulness—contemplation of the body, contemplation of feelings, contemplation of the mind, and contemplation of phenomena—because these are the dwelling places on the path to nirvana; therefore, one should know that the precepts had already been established beforehand.
If even minor evils are not permitted, how much more so the evil karma of body and speech?
For such reasons as these, one should know that the precepts were established beforehand.
It is like a king who establishes a law:
"One should not commit evil!
Should anyone later transgress, according to the gravity of the matter and the nature of the offense committed, they shall be dealt with accordingly.
The Buddha is likewise thus.
First, the precepts are proclaimed in general; subsequently, for those who have committed offenses, the characteristics of their transgressions are explained.
If there are those who commit evil deeds, they are instructed to perform repentance:

"For having committed such a transgression, one should repent in this manner"—this includes such measures as *adarśanārhā-bhikṣu-pravāsanīya* (expulsion for not acknowledging an offense), *pratyāśraya-pravāsanīya* (expulsion for refusing to leave), and *asaṃvāsa* (exclusion from communal living).
Because such matters had occurred, the precepts were subsequently established.
*Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, Scroll Ten;
*Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, Scroll Eleven.
Composed by the Holy Nāgārjuna;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty.

This is the continuation of the "Chapter on Refuting Those Who Claim Omniscience" within the Forty Unique Qualities. Regarding your statement that "the elderly and those from noble families should be designated as *sthavira* (elders)," we shall now provide the answer:
Within the Dharma, seniority, noble lineage, and family background are of no benefit to the Path. Why is this?
One who is born within the Buddha-Dharma is said to be born into a noble lineage and a virtuous family.
One is called "venerable" (sthavira) by counting the number of years since receiving the full precepts.
As for your claim that "the venerable should be venerated," is it not the case that those who first left home and received the precepts are the most senior?
Furthermore, from the time one receives the precepts onward, there are no distinctions such as various castes or lineages.
When the bhikṣus receive the full ordination, they are said to be born into the family of the Buddha; thus, they lose their former great or small families, and all are called a single family.

Regarding what you say concerning "upholding the precepts": one who has gone forth first, has long observed the precepts, has guarded them through the long night, and has lived for many years, should be designated as a senior elder (sthavira).
As it is stated in the section on the formulation of precepts:
regarding your claim that "one who upholds the precepts should not pay homage to one who has broken them," we shall now respond:
if one should not even dwell together with a person who has broken the precepts, how much less should one pay them homage or offer them support?
Because they themselves claim to be bhikṣus, one pays them homage according to their seniority, just as one pays homage to images of gods made of clay or wood out of mindfulness of the "True God."
The Buddha commanded that juniors should pay homage to seniors; by following the Buddha’s teaching, one thereby gains merit.
As for your statement that "one should pay respectful homage because of [the practice of] dhūta," I shall now respond:
if there are five types of persons who practice dhūta, it is difficult to distinguish [who is superior].

First, because they are ignorant and lack knowledge, they greedily accept difficult practices; second, because they have dull faculties, they hope to gain profit; third, because they harbor evil intentions, they deceive others; fourth, because they are deranged; and fifth, because they think:
"The dhūta practices are praised by all Buddhas and noble sages, for they accord with the path to nirvāṇa."
"These five types of people practice the dhūta-dharmas, and it is difficult to distinguish between the genuine and the false.
As for the 'learned,' even those who are learned are like those who practice the dhūtas; they are likewise difficult to distinguish."
Why is this? Because some pursue extensive learning for the sake of delighting in the Path, while others do so for the sake of gain and offerings;
such cases are likewise difficult to distinguish.
Furthermore, in the Buddha-dharma, what is valued is practicing according to the teaching, rather than valuing much reading or much recitation.
Moreover, as the Buddha said: "To practice even a single verse of Dharma that can benefit oneself is called 'much learning' (bahuśruta)."
"Wisdom" is also like this: if one cannot practice according to what has been taught, what is the use of wisdom?
Therefore, one is not designated as an Elder on account of wisdom.
For example, in worldly affairs, even if a younger brother is widely learned and possesses great wisdom, his elder brother does not prostrate before him.
Therefore, one does not first receive offerings or prostrations on account of wisdom alone.
Thus, although one may possess great learning and wisdom, one should pay homage to those who received the precepts first;
if one instead makes offerings to those with greater learning and wisdom, it constitutes a cause for strife and discord.
The remaining matters—“attaining the fruits of śrāmaṇya,” “severing the fetters,” and “attaining supernormal powers”—are most difficult to discern.
Is this person attaining the fruits or not attaining them?
Has this person severed many fetters or few?
Is it that one has attained supernormal powers (abhijñā) while another has not?
One cannot be designated as the senior elder (sthavira) on this basis alone.
If they are equal in having attained the "fruit of the path," severed the fetters (saṃyojana), and mastered supernormal powers, who then shall be the senior elder?
Therefore, practicing in accordance with the Buddha’s teachings is the most supreme.
As for your statement that “the Buddha gave rise to doubt regarding the teaching of the Dharma,” I shall now respond:
If the Buddha harbored no doubt even regarding the profound Dharma, how much less could he have had any doubt concerning what should or should not be taught?
The Buddha did not say,
"I do not teach the Dharma at all.
He only said:
"Only when the mind delights in seclusion and tranquility, and no longer strives to initiate worldly affairs, will there be no fault in preaching the Dharma.
Furthermore, the various non-Buddhists say:
"The Buddha is a Great Sage who remains in silent stillness, free from conceptual proliferation; why does he maintain a following and engage in teaching?"
Even if one were to provide instruction and transformation, it could never be exhausted.
If it is like this, what is the use of preaching the Dharma?
To nurture disciples is a mark of greedy attachment.
For this reason, the Buddha reflected to himself:
"My Dharma is profound, and my wisdom and skillful means are immeasurable and boundless, yet those who can be delivered are few. Therefore, he said to himself:
"It would be better to remain silent."
Furthermore, in order to prevent the censure and reproach of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), he caused the Brahmā King to entreat him to preach the Dharma.
Thereupon, the Brahmā King and others addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Sentient beings are to be pitied; among them there are those with sharp faculties and thin fetters (*saṃyojana*) who are easily transformed and delivered."
For this reason, he accepted the invitations of the Brahma Kings and others.
Just as one who has discovered a great treasure trove should show it to others, so too should those noble ones who have themselves attained the benefit of the Dharma likewise bring benefit to others.
Regarding what you have said—that the Buddha did not know that Ārāḍa Kālāma and others had already passed away when he wished to preach the Dharma for them—I shall now respond:

The Buddha does not dwell upon their death or lack of death; rather, he dwells upon the fact that this person’s fetters are thin and subtle and that they are capable of being transformed and delivered. Wisdom arises precisely according to the object upon which his mind is focused.
Therefore, it is logical that the Buddha first spoke himself and was subsequently informed by the devas.

Furthermore, since the Buddha had previously gone forth as a renunciant and stayed overnight with these two individuals, the devas and people might have suspected that he received their sublime Dharma or attained the Way elsewhere.
Desiring to sever their doubts, the Buddha immediately proclaimed:
"That person has suffered such long-term decline; how could they not have heard the sublime Dharma?
By inferring this principle, the matter of the five bhikṣus can likewise be understood: one merely considers the causal conditions for their deliverance, rather than where they currently reside.
Later, when he reached his dwelling place, he immediately came to know [the truth].
Therefore, one should not disparage an omniscient person.
As for your statement that "he spoke with doubt regarding the destruction of Pāṭaliputra," this shall now be answered:
The causes and conditions for the destruction of this city are not fixed; to speak of them as fixed when they are not fixed constitutes an error.

Furthermore, among the forty unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) previously mentioned by me, the Buddhas possess "skillful knowledge of the indeterminate"; one who answers [in accordance with this] will not be subject to such an objection.
Regarding what you said—
that the Buddha asked the bhikṣus, "For what purpose have you gathered?"—
I shall now provide the answer to that which was spoken.
Because the Buddha was about to expound a Dharma-gate, he asked such a question;
or because he wished to establish the precepts, he commanded him to speak of them himself;
since it was for various purposes such as these in expounding the Dharma, there is no fault in his questioning.
In the world, there are also instances where one asks despite already knowing— such as seeing someone eating and asking,
"Are you eating? or,
when it is cold, asking:
“Is it cold?
The Buddha likewise knows this yet asks again; there is no fault in following worldly convention.
As for your statement that “one who praises himself and disparages others is not an omniscient one,” I shall now respond:
The Buddha does not crave his own body, nor does he crave offerings;
he harbors no anger toward others,
and he is free from overweening pride.

The reason why he himself declares, "I am the foremost in the world," is that there are sentient beings with faith whose faculties are sharp and keen; they abandon evil associates and take me as their teacher. Such persons shall attain peace and security throughout the long night [of saṃsāra].
For this reason, the Buddha praises his own person.
Furthermore, there are those who seek the path of supreme bliss yet are indolent and unable to exert diligence; for this reason, the Buddha said:
"One should not be indolent in the pursuit of the unsurpassed benefit."
"I am the foremost teacher in the world; I have skillfully expounded the True Dharma. You should apply yourselves with diligent vigor, for you can attain the fruits of the Path.
For such reasons as these, he praises himself, not out of self-exaltation or contempt for others.
Regarding "rebuking evil persons": this is intended to cause them to eliminate unwholesome dharmas, not out of hatred or malice toward sentient beings.

There may be those who seek benefit in accordance with the Dharma, whose minds are pure and upright, yet who associate with evil friends; it is for the purpose of causing them to distance themselves from such people that one rebukes and censures them.
Even before attaining Buddhahood, he gave his marrow and brain to others; how much more so now that he has attained Buddhahood—how could he possibly revile or scold?
You claim that "the Buddha’s Dharma is contradictory from beginning to end," but now I shall answer:

within the Buddha’s Dharma, there is no such thing as a contradiction between the beginning and the end. It is because you do not understand the meaning of the Buddha’s Dharma that you perceive it as contradictory.
As for this path to nirvāṇa, since the parinirvāṇa of Kāśyapa Buddha, no one has again preached it, nor has anyone attained it; therefore, he says, "I have newly attained the path.
Elsewhere, it is further stated that "I have attained the ancient path."

This path is that which was attained by all Buddhas, such as Dīpaṃkara; it is the so-called "Noble Eightfold Path that leads to Nirvāṇa. Because it is a single path and a single causal condition, it is called the "Ancient Path."
Therefore, one should know that the Buddha has attained all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*).
Question: Regarding what is called "all-knowledge," why is it named all-knowledge?
Is one called "omniscient" (sarvajña) because of knowing all things?
The answer is:
an omniscient one is one who knows that which is knowable.
That which can be known consists of five dharma-treasuries:
the past, the future, the present, that which transcends the three periods of time, and the ineffable.
To employ knowledge of these five treasuries is called "knowing."
Therefore, it is known that both cognition and the object of cognition are called "all. Question:
To claim that cognition and the cognizable constitute "all" is not correct.
Why is this? Because these phenomena are but a single unity; that which is knowable is itself knowable.
As it is said in the world:
"This person knows what is sharp; this person knows what is dull.
He replied:
"If all things were one, then even opposing states such as cold and heat would have to be one."
Light and darkness, suffering and pleasure, and other such contradictory phenomena would likewise have to be one;
however, this is not the case. Therefore, one cannot say that "all things are one."
Question:
Your own position is subject to the same fault. If "that which is knowable" were one, then suffering, pleasure, and so forth would also have to be one; yet in reality, they are not one.
The answer is:
I do not say that "all that can be known is one";
it is because you maintain the position that "all things are one" that my fault is not the same as yours.
Furthermore, because you state that there is the fault of "identity," you yourself incur a fault within your own position.
If a person admits the fault inherent in their own tenet, they fall into a position of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
Since you recognize that your own position is flawed, you should not further attribute faults to others;
therefore, your claim that "the same fault applies" is incorrect.
Furthermore, if one were to claim that "the two dharmas of cognition and the cognizable are one," then one should employ the "cognizable dharma" to know objects such as jars and garments;
yet in reality, it is cognition that knows all things.

If you claim that "the jar, the garment, and so forth are no different from cognition," then since jars, garments, and the like cannot themselves cognize objects, they must indeed be different; yet in actual practice, it is cognition that cognizes all objects.
Because there are faults in each of these cases, one cannot say that "all are one.
Furthermore, the knower and the known are two; these together are called "all.
Because he knows all dharmas, he is named the Tathāgata and the Omniscient One.
This is the Omniscient One; because of the vajra-samādhi, the vajra-samādhi is thus accomplished.
As for your previous statement that "the vajra-samādhi is not accomplished and omniscience is not accomplished," this is not the case!

23. Chapter Twenty-three on Skillfully Knowing the Indeterminate among the Forty Unique Qualities. Regarding skillfully knowing indeterminate phenomena: when all phenomena have not yet arisen, have not yet emerged, have not yet been formed, have not yet been determined, and have not yet been differentiated, it is therein that the Tathāgata’s wisdom attains its power.
As the Buddha said in the *Vibhaṅga-karmasūtra*:
“The Buddha told Ānanda:
‘There are those who perform wholesome deeds of body, wholesome deeds of speech, and wholesome deeds of mind, yet at the end of their lives they fall into hell;’”
"There is a person who performs evil deeds with the body, evil deeds with speech, and evil deeds with the mind, yet at the end of life, this person is reborn in the heavens.
Ānanda said to the Buddha,
"For what reason is this so?"
The Buddha said:

"This person may have the karmic conditions for their offenses and blessings from previous lives already matured, while those for the present life have not yet matured; or, at the moment of death, they may give rise to right view or wrong view, a wholesome or unwholesome mind. This is because the power of the mind at the point of death is exceedingly great."
Furthermore, the *Śuka-sūtra* states:
"The brahmin youth Śuka addressed the Buddha, saying:
'Gautama!'"
"Among the brahmins who remain householders in white robes, there are those capable of cultivating merit and roots of goodness who surpass those who have left the home life;
how is this so? The Buddha said, "In this matter, I do not give a definitive answer."
"If one who has left the household life does not cultivate goodness, then they are not as good as one remaining at home.
If one at home can cultivate goodness, then they are superior to one who has left the household life.
Furthermore, it is said in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*:
“The city of Pāṭaliputra shall be destroyed by three things: either by water, or by fire, or by internal people conspiring with outsiders.
Furthermore, because of the words of the brahmin Pārilava:
“It is impossible that this naked ascetic Pārilava, if he does not abandon these words, this mindset, or this wrong view, should come before my eyes.”
"If the leather strap breaks, or if the body breaks, it will never reach the presence of the Buddha.
Furthermore, the *Raft Simile Sūtra* states:
"This Dharma of mine is extremely profound; I have taught it through skillful means to make it shallow and easy to understand."
If there is one with a straightforward mind who practices according to the teaching, they will obtain two kinds of benefit:
either the exhaustion of outflows in this very life;
or, if the outflows are not exhausted, they shall attain the path of the Non-returner.
Furthermore, in the *Śākālī-sūtra* of the *Ekottarika Āgama*, it says:
“The Buddha told Ānanda:

‘If a person intentionally creates karma, there is no case where they attain the Path without experiencing its retribution—whether that retribution is experienced in the present life, in the next life, or in subsequent lives.’”
Furthermore, the *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
“The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
‘When evil persons die, they are reborn as animals or fall into the hells;’”
"The birthplace of a virtuous person is either among the devas or among humans.
Furthermore, it is said in the *Vīraputra-sūtra*:
"Vīra addressed the Buddha, saying:"
"Can that which the Buddha has taught cause others to become angry?
The Buddha said,
"Prince!..."
This matter is not fixed.
Sometimes, out of a heart of compassion, the Buddha causes others to feel anger so that they may plant the seeds of wholesome causes and conditions.
It is like a nurse who uses a curved finger to hook out a harmful object from a small child’s mouth; although it causes injury, there is no harm.
Furthermore, it is said in the *Abhidharma*:
"There are three categories of sentient beings:

from the indeterminate group (*aniyata-rāśi*), some fall into the group of the fixed in error (*mithyātva-niyata-rāśi*), while others fall into the group of the fixed in correctness (*samyaktva-niyata-rāśi*)."
Within these four Dharma-treasuries, there are countless determinate matters numbering in the millions.

Question: If a person’s wisdom is not fixed and lacks a decisive mind, such that regarding matters they sometimes say "it is so" and sometimes "it is not so," then they cannot be called an omniscient one.
The Omniscient One speaks with non-duality, speaks with certainty, and speaks with clarity; therefore, skillfully knowing what is indeterminate cannot be called a unique quality of a Buddha.
The answer is:
Indeterminate matters—whether it be "thus" or "not thus"—depend upon various causes and conditions; therefore, one should not provide a definitive statement regarding them.
Furthermore, if one were to give a definitive answer concerning an indeterminate matter, one would not be called an omniscient person.
Therefore, regarding matters that are indeterminate, one must necessarily employ indeterminate cognition; for this reason, there exists the unique quality (āveṇika-dharma) of indeterminate cognition.
Furthermore, if a person possesses fixed knowledge regarding all phenomena, that person falls into the category of those who hold fixed false doctrines.
If all phenomena were fixed and determined, then all actions would not require human effort or skillful means to achieve.
As it is said:
"If beauty and ugliness were already fixed, then human effort would likewise be fixed."
It does not require various causes and conditions, but is practiced through skillful means.
Furthermore, it is seen that if one does not protect one's own body, there will be manifold sufferings;
if one protects one's own body, there will be benefit and peace.
Furthermore, just as in various types of labor one undergoes many forms of exhaustion and suffering, yet later obtains various fruits of wealth and joy;
or again, there may be someone who in this life remains silent and does nothing at all, yet still obtains a karmic fruit.
Therefore, there exists this matter of indeterminacy; because one knows this matter of indeterminacy, one possesses the knowledge of indeterminacy.
[The opponent] asks:

Regarding your statement that "whether there is guarding or non-guarding, whether effort is applied or not, there is still the occurrence of indeterminate matters"—there are those who, though they diligently protect themselves, encounter suffering and distress, while others who do not protect themselves do not encounter such suffering.
Furthermore, it is not fixed that one who exerts effort and undergoes personal toil and suffering fails to obtain the fruit of their merit,
while one who does not exert effort yet obtains the fruit of merit.
The answer is as follows:
What you have stated establishes my position that there is no fixed definition: "If there is an indeterminate matter, there must be an indeterminate cognition thereof. I do not say:
"If a person does not guard themselves, they will all experience suffering."
Nor does it say:
"Apart from karmic effort, there is retribution.
There are those who, despite having exerted effort, do not obtain happiness due to the hindrances of their past-life sins.
Since it is not stated that "all things are thus," your objection is invalid.
This is called the Buddhas' unique possession of the complete knowledge of the indeterminate regarding indeterminate matters.
Regarding the knowledge of the formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*): Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas know the sentient beings born in the formless realms and a small portion of phenomena therein;
the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, fully and completely know both the sentient beings in the formless realms and all phenomena.
In this formless realm, some beings are born here, some are born there, some are born in the first station of the formless attainments, and some are born in the second station.
A certain number of beings are born in the third station; a certain number of beings are born in the fourth station.

A certain number of beings have been born for such a length of time; a certain number of beings shall pass away after such a length of time; a certain number of beings have a maximum lifespan of such a length of time.
Some sentient beings have a fixed lifespan, while some sentient beings do not have a fixed lifespan.
Some sentient beings, having passed away from the desire realm, are reborn here.
Some sentient beings pass away from the realm of form and are reborn here;
some sentient beings pass away from the formless realm and are likewise reborn here.
Some sentient beings, having passed away from among humans, are immediately reborn here;
some sentient beings, having passed away from among the devas, are immediately reborn here.
These sentient beings, having passed away from this place, are reborn either in the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm.

These sentient beings, having passed away from here, are reborn either in the heavenly realm, the human realm, or the asura realm; or they are reborn within the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts.

These sentient beings enter nirvana in that place; some of these sentient beings are all ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), some are the noble disciples (*ārya-śrāvaka*) of the Buddha, and some are the disciples of ordinary worldlings.
Some sentient beings attain the vehicle of the śrāvaka; some sentient beings attain the vehicle of the pratyekabuddha; some sentient beings all attain the Great Vehicle.
Some sentient beings do not attain the vehicle of the śrāvaka; some sentient beings do not attain the vehicle of the pratyekabuddha, nor do they attain the Great Vehicle.
Some sentient beings practice cessation; some sentient beings do not practice cessation.
Some sentient beings practice the higher [vehicle]; some sentient beings are disciples of a certain Buddha.
The Buddhas further know:
this is definitely experienced as a flavor, while that is not definitely experienced as a flavor;
this is wholesome, and this is indeterminate.
This concentration severs various fetters;
this concentration is superior, middling, or inferior.

To speak briefly of the formless concentrations, only the Buddhas, by means of their knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), are able to fully distinguish them: whether they are great or small, deep or shallow, associated with the mind or dissociated from the mind, and whether they are karmic results or not results, and so forth.
This is called the Buddhas' complete and thorough knowledge of the states of formless concentration.

Regarding those who have attained mastery over the cessation of phenomena—namely, the Pratyekabuddhas, the Arhats, and those who have entered parinirvāṇa in the past and present—the Buddhas have fully realized them.
As it is said in the Sūtra: "O Bhikṣus!
Ninety-one kalpas prior to this Bhadrakalpa, Vipaśyin Buddha appeared; continuing down to the thirty-first kalpa, two Buddhas appeared."
First was named Śikhin, and second was named Viśvabhū.
Within this Bhadrakalpa, Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, and Kāśyapa Buddhas appeared.
Thus, regarding the great knowledge and vision of the Buddhas of the past,

it should be stated here: "And their śrāvaka disciples who have entered parinirvāṇa into the nirvana without remainder, as well as the pratyekabuddhas named Siṃha, Puṣpākṣa, Dṛṣṭadharma, Dharmakośa, Priyadarśana, Vimala, and Anupalabdha."
The Buddha fully comprehends all such Pratyekabuddhas who have entered nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*).

Furthermore, he comprehends those who have not yet passed away but abide in nirvana with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*), for whom the conditions for rebirth are entirely exhausted; this comprehension is also called "thoroughly understanding the knowledge of cessation."
As it is said in the Sūtra:
“The Buddha told Ānanda:

‘Regarding this person, I know fully that there is not even the slightest darkness within him; this person will certainly exhaust all internal dharmas, and at the end of his life, he shall enter nirvāṇa.’”
It is also called "knowledge of cessation.
Furthermore, regarding other persons who have realized the Four Noble Truths, being able to know their situation is also called "knowledge of cessation.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"Why do I not simply cause this person to attain the exhaustion of outflows and liberation right here?
As the Buddha told Ānanda:
"You delight in meditative concentration; you delight in severing the fetters and latent tendencies."
It is also called "thoroughly penetrating knowledge of cessation.
As the Buddha told Śāriputra:
"I know nirvāṇa; I know the path leading to nirvāṇa; and I know those sentient beings who have reached nirvāṇa."
Such sūtras as these should be explained here; this is called the Buddhas’ thorough penetration and knowledge of cessation (*nirodha*).

Regarding those factors dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta*) and non-material (*arūpa*), such as the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the roots of wholesome morality, wholesome discipline (*saṃvara*), unwholesome discipline, and so forth—all these factors dissociated from mind and non-material—Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas cannot thoroughly penetrate, whereas the Buddhas are fully able to penetrate them as if they were before their very eyes.
Among the dharmas dissociated from the mind, this is because one has attained the foremost power of wisdom.
Question: Since the wholesome restraint of morality and the unwholesome restraint are material dharmas (*rūpadharma*), why do you say they are not material dharmas?
Answer: Regarding the wholesome restraint of the precepts and the unwholesome restraint, there are two kinds:
manifest action (*vijñapti*) and non-manifest action (*avijñapti*). Manifest action is material form (*rūpa*); non-manifest action is not material form.

Non-manifestation (*avijñapti*) is not form; because of the Buddha’s unique power (*āveṇika-bala*), he can know it directly, whereas other persons know it through inferential knowledge (*anumāna-jñāna*).
Question:
Do the Buddhas only skillfully know non-associated and non-material dharmas, but not skillfully know associated dharmas?
Answer: If one has attained penetration regarding dissociated phenomena (*viprayukta-dharma*), there is no further need to discuss associated phenomena (*saṃprayukta-dharma*).
It is like a person who can shoot a hair; coarse objects are then no longer discussed.
Furthermore, among the seven hundred dissociated phenomena (*viprayukta-dharma*), śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, by means of the sixth consciousness, are able to know seven things:
first, name; second, appearance; third, meaning; fourth, impermanence; fifth, arising; sixth, non-arising; and seventh, transcendence.
The Buddha, by means of the sixth consciousness, is able to know all things.

The Buddha knows the characteristics of the Four Noble Truths as well as conventional phenomena; therefore, it is said that the Buddhas skillfully know mind-non-associated factors and formless dharmas.

The perfection of power (*balapāramitā*) refers to the attainment of the power of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) regarding all knowable phenomena without exception, because it is supported and accomplished by the ten powers (*daśabala*), the four fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*), and the four bases of spiritual power (*catasraḥ pratisaraṇāḥ*).
Furthermore, because he has skillfully attained the ten powers (*daśabala*), the Buddha is thus able to accomplish the perfection of power (*balapāramitā*).
This power is further enhanced upon reaching the sixteenth moment of mind; omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) is ever-present within the Buddha’s body, even until his entry into *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
Because of this matter, one attains unimpeded wisdom regarding all phenomena.

As for the perfection of unimpeded wisdom, it consists of the fourfold dharmas—phenomena (*dharma*), meaning (*artha*), phrasing (*nirukti*), and eloquence (*pratibhāna*)—in which its power is immeasurable and its penetration is unimpeded.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
'The Tathāgata has four disciples who have accomplished the foremost power of mindfulness, the power of wisdom, and the power of endurance.'"
Just as a skilled archer can shoot through a leaf with ease, so too have these disciples come with questions and challenges regarding the four foundations of mindfulness.

For a hundred years, except for the times of eating, relieving myself, and sleeping, the Tathāgata has constantly answered them, delighting in the exposition of wisdom without ever reaching exhaustion.
"In this regard, the Buddha speaks of his own wisdom by means of the characteristic of few desires.

Suppose there were as many three-thousandfold world systems as there are atoms of dust filling all the four continents within a single three-thousandfold world system; and suppose that in each of those world systems, there were as many sentient beings as there are atoms of dust, each being like Śāriputra or a pratyekabuddha, fully accomplished in wisdom and eloquence, with lifespans lasting for as many great kalpas as the number of those atoms. If all these people were to spend their entire lives questioning the Tathāgata based on the four foundations of mindfulness, the Tathāgata would answer their questions using the meaning of the four foundations of mindfulness; his words and meanings would not be repetitive, and his eloquence would be inexhaustible."
The unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*) is the ability to skillfully differentiate the names and designations of all phenomena, penetrating them without obstruction.
The unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*) is the penetration of the meanings of all phenomena without obstruction.

Unimpeded eloquence (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*) means that according to the various types of sentient beings, one causes them to understand the meaning through all manner of speech and words, penetrating them without obstruction.
Unimpeded skill in exposition (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*) means that when answering questions, one skillfully teaches the Dharma without ever reaching exhaustion.
Other noble ones cannot exhaustively fathom it; only the Buddhas can reach its ultimate limit. Therefore, it is called the Perfection of Unimpeded Wisdom (*anāvaraṇajñānapāramitā*).
Regarding the Perfection of Complete Answering: among all difficult questions and challenges, the Buddha is skillfully able to provide complete answers.

Why is this? Because among the four types of questions and answers, they are free from confusion and well-versed in their meaning; because they are fully endowed with the perfection of indestructible meaning; and because they desire to deeply understand the natures, conducts, and inclinations of all sentient beings.
As Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha teaches the wholesome Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, and within it, many sentient beings attain realization;”
Having realized this, the mind is free from craving.
Because it is free from craving, there is nothing in the world that is grasped.
Having nothing grasped, the mind is extinguished within.
"In the realm of wholesome dharmas, the Buddha’s unsurpassed matters he knows exhaustively without remainder; there is no one superior to him.
[The interlocutor] asked:
"You speak of four kinds of questions and answers; what are these four?"
The answer is: first, the categorical response; second, the analytical response; third, the response by counter-question; and fourth, the response by setting aside.
Regarding the categorical response: for example, a certain bhikṣu asked the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
Is there perhaps any form that is permanent and unchanging?
World-Honored One!”
“Are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness permanent, unchanging, and immutable?
The Buddha replied, “Monks!”
"There is no form that is permanent and unchanging; there is no feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness that is permanent and unchanging.
Such statements as these are called definitive answers.

Regarding the answer by way of analysis: it is like when the brahmin Puttaliputra asked Sāmaṭa, "If a person intentionally performs actions of body, speech, and mind, what kind of retribution do they receive?"
Samādhī answered definitively:
"There are those who, by means of body, speech, and mind, perform actions and consequently receive the retribution of suffering.
This question should have been answered with an analytical distinction; when this brahmin later asked the Buddha about this matter, the Buddha replied:
“Potaliputra!
If a person performs an action through body, speech, or mind, that action will result in either a painful retribution, a pleasant retribution, or a retribution that is neither painful nor pleasant.”

"Karmas that are painful result in the retribution of suffering; karmas that are pleasant result in the retribution of pleasure; and karmas that are neither painful nor pleasant result in the retribution of being neither painful nor pleasant.
Such sūtras as these all provide analytical answers.
Regarding the method of answering through counter-questions: it is as when the brahmin Śreṇika questioned the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I shall question you in return; answer according to your own understanding. Śreṇika!"
"What do you think? Is form the Tathāgata?
Are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness the Tathāgata?
He replied:
“No, World-Honored One. “Is it apart from form,
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness that the Tathāgata exists?”
He replied, "No, World-Honored One."
Such sūtras as these should be explained in detail; this is called the "answering by counter-question.
As for the "answering by setting aside," it refers to the fourteen types of false views, namely:
the world is eternal, the world is non-eternal, the world is both eternal and non-eternal, and the world is neither eternal nor non-eternal.
The world is finite; the world is infinite; the world is both finite and infinite; the world is neither finite nor infinite.

After the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, he exists; after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, he does not exist; after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, he both exists and does not exist; after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, he neither exists nor does not exist.
"The body is identical to the self" and "the body is distinct from the self.

Just as all sentient beings above [in the world] do, and just as a great pratyekabuddha would joyfully explain with wisdom, they questioned the Buddha using these four types of inquiries; the Buddha answered each question in accordance with them, neither more nor less. Therefore, it is said that the Buddha is fully endowed with the perfection of answering (*prativacanapāramitā*).

No one is able to harm the Buddha, because he has attained the dharma of being incapable of being killed; no one can sever the Buddha’s body parts or limbs, for he possesses mastery over life and death.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"If anyone should attempt to harm the Buddha through skillful means, such a thing is impossible."
Question: Is the lifespan of the Buddha fixed or unfixed? Answer:
Some say: "It is not fixed.
If the Buddha’s lifespan were fixed, what difference would there be between him and others whose lifespans are fixed?
In reality, the Buddha’s lifespan is indefinite; that no one is able to harm him is truly rare. Some say:
"The Buddha’s lifespan is fixed."
"Although the lifespans of other beings are fixed, their hands, feet, ears, and noses may be severed; for the Buddha, such a thing does not occur.
Question: In what sense is the Buddha incapable of being harmed? This is an uncommon quality (*āveṇika-dharma*).
Answer: The Buddhas are inconceivable, yet they can be understood through metaphors.

Suppose all sentient beings in the worlds of the ten directions possessed power, and there were a single Māra with as much power as all of them; furthermore, suppose every single sentient being in the ten directions were made as powerful as that evil Māra, and they all desired to harm the Buddha together—they would still be unable to move even a single hair of the Buddha’s body, let alone cause him any injury.
Question:
If that is so, how was it that Devadatta was able to harm the Buddha? Answer:
This matter has already been answered previously.

The Buddha wished to demonstrate to sentient beings the characteristics of the three poisons: although Devadatta maintained the precepts and cultivated goodness, he was greedily attached to gain and offerings, thereby committing great evil.
Furthermore, let it be known:
toward all humans and devas, the Buddha’s mind is without distinction; moreover, he regards Devadatta and Rāhula with compassionate pity as if they were his own left and right eyes.
The Buddha constantly teaches an impartial mind, and at this time he manifests that very equanimity.
When devas and humans see this, they give rise to a sense of wonder and their faith and joy increase all the more.

Furthermore, when those in the Heaven of Long Life (Āyuṣmat-deva) see that the Buddha had committed unwholesome deeds in previous lives, they might think—if he does not undergo the consequences now—then evil actions bear no retribution. To sever such false views, the Buddha manifests the experience of these karmic results.
Furthermore, regarding suffering and pleasure, the Buddha’s mind remains unchanged; he is free from the notion of a self because all things are ultimately empty.
His faculties are harmoniously disciplined and cannot be altered;
thus, he does not need to employ expedient means to abandon suffering or experience pleasure.
As it is said in the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka*:
"The Buddha, by means of skillful means, manifests the acceptance of these matters; this should be understood extensively.
This is called the unique quality (āveṇika-dharma) of the Buddha's invulnerability to being killed.

Regarding the statement that the teaching of the Dharma is not in vain: all the words spoken by the Buddhas possess karmic fruition; therefore, the Buddhas’ teaching of the Dharma is not in vain. Why is this?

When the Buddhas have not yet preached the Dharma, they first observe the beginning and end of sentient beings—where their minds reside, the thickness or thinness of their fetters (saṃyojana), the merits they have accumulated in previous lives, the degree of their faculties and capacities, and the locations, times, and circumstances of their obstacles.
Some should be delivered through gentle dharmas; some through difficult practices; or again, some should be delivered through both gentle and difficult practices.
Some must be delivered by a slight arousal [of the mind], while others are delivered through extensive analysis.
There are those who attain liberation through the aggregates, the sense bases, the elements, and the twelve links of dependent origination;
or there are those who enter [the path] through the gate of faith or the gate of wisdom.
This person should be delivered by the Buddha; this person should be delivered by a śrāvaka; this person should attain deliverance through other conditions.
This person should accomplish the Śrāvaka-yāna; this person should accomplish the Pratyekabuddha-yāna; this person should accomplish the Mahāyāna.
This person has long practiced desire, practiced hatred, and practiced delusion;
this person has practiced desire and hatred;
this person has practiced desire and delusion—thus they are distinguished one from another.

This person falls into the view of annihilationism; this person falls into the view of eternalism; this person is greatly attached to the view of a self-identity; this person is habituated to the view of extremes; this person is habituated to the grasping of precepts and rituals and the grasping of views.
This person has frequently practiced arrogance; this person has frequently practiced self-deprecation and flattery. This person’s mind is full of doubt and regret.
This person delights in verbal expression; some value the principles of meaning, some delight in profound meanings, and some delight in superficial matters.
This person accumulated the factors conducive to enlightenment in past lives; this person accumulates the factors conducive to enlightenment in the present life.
This person merely accumulates roots of goodness that result in merit; this person merely accumulates roots of goodness that lead to penetration.
"This person shall quickly attain the Way; this person shall attain the Way only after a long time.
Having first observed and deliberated upon them, the Buddha preaches the Dharma according to their capacity for deliverance and thereby brings them across to liberation.
Therefore, all teachings of the Dharma are entirely non-empty.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"The World-Honored One teaches the Dharma having first known and seen; he does not teach the Dharma without knowing and seeing."
"Without error and without fault" means that the Buddhas' teaching of the Dharma is without error and without fault.
"Without error" means that the words and their meanings do not contradict one another.
"Without fault" means that they do not fail to convey the true meaning.
