there are eight types of contrary dharmas; one should not practice the eight dharmas such as cessation and so forth.
If a bodhisattva thoroughly understands these dharmas, they will not fail to attain the Buddha-way and shall never regress.
*Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle Ten;
*Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle Thirteen.
Composed by the Venerable Nāgārjuna.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty.
From the remainder of the "Chapter on Similes": Question:
Regarding the Bodhisattva who thoroughly understands all these dharmas and never regresses until attaining the Buddha-way—what is the analogy for this?
The answer is:
Like a powerful guide who well knows the characteristics of the excellent path—
where it leads from here and where it goes, and what is appropriate for turning the course.
Providing all provisions and requisites for the journey,
they ensure that within those perilous paths the multitude attains peace and security;
reaching the great city, they enable the multitude to be free from affliction.
Because this Great Guide is well able to know the path,
he thoroughly understands the progression through the stages and is fully endowed with the factors conducive to enlightenment.
The Bodhisattva, being skilled in knowing the path, discerns what is favorable and unfavorable, as well as the various locations.
Having crossed over the perilous straits of birth and death myself,
I shall also guide many sentient beings to reach the place of peace and security— the city of unconditioned nirvana.
May they all, within the evil realms, never encounter manifold sufferings and afflictions.
Because the Bodhisattva possesses the power of skillful means and is well able to know the path, the characteristics of a favorable path are as follows: it abounds in firewood, grass, and water;
it is free from bandits, lions, wolves, tigers, and various other evil beasts and venomous insects.
It is neither cold nor hot; there are no treacherous mountains, ditches, pits, ravines, narrow passes, deep thickets, dense forests, or obstructing thickets.
There are no elevations or depressions; it is level, straight, even, and accessible. It has few forked paths, is broad and spacious, and is a place frequented by many people.
One travels without weariness; it abounds in flowers, fruits, and edible things.
Such matters as these are called the characteristics of a good path;
that which is contrary to these is called the characteristic of an evil path.
"This place" refers to a location where groups of people stay, eat, and rest.
"Another place" (*anyatra*) refers to going from this location to a different location;
even the space between two dwellings is called "another place.
"Changing the path" (*mārga-vivartana*) means seeing a diverging road that leads to a great city, such that one thinks, "This is the path I should travel, and the others should be abandoned."
"Provisions" refers to parched grain, honey, cakes, and so forth, which are eaten while on the road.
"Great power" refers to great influence, possessing abundant wealth and being well-versed in the methods of governance.
"Fully provided with" means having an abundance of food and drink, lacking nothing.
"Peaceful" means being free from the terrors of bandits and robbers.
"Secluded" means being free from illness, suffering, and misfortune.
The "great city" is so named because it can accommodate a vast multitude of people, enabling many multitudes to reach that great city.
The "guide" is well-versed in the characteristics of the path; he is himself free from affliction and hardship, and likewise ensures that the multitude of people is free from affliction and hardship.

Because they are well-versed in the Way, they are free from such afflictions as cold and heat, hunger and thirst, hostile bandits, fierce beasts, venomous insects, treacherous mountains, treacherous waters, and deep pits and ravines.
Why is this? Because they well know the characteristics of good and bad paths.

By means of this analogy, the ten stages such as the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā*) are illustrated: just as a person traveling on a road who proceeds without rest can reach a great city, so too does a bodhisattva traverse these ten stages and attain the Buddha-dharma, entering the great city of *nirvāṇa*.
Just as that excellent road has an abundance of firewood, grass, water, and so forth, the practitioner lacks for nothing.
"Grass" refers to how, when a person rides a horse on a path with much good grass, the horse’s strength becomes vigorous;
the merits of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) are likewise—because the four superior bases (*abhibhvāyatana*) of truth, relinquishment, cessation, and wisdom assist all merits, they are called "grass."

Why is this? If a person values actual reality, delights in following truthful speech, and constantly associates with those who speak truthfully; if they see that truth brings benefit and joy, deeply detests false speech, stays far away from it, perceives the faults of falsehood, and has no desire to hear it—through such causes and conditions, one attains the "Victorious Abode of Truth" (*satya-āyatana*).
One should understand that the other three abodes, beginning with "Equanimity" (*upekṣā*), are to be known in the same way.
Just as that good road requires elephants, horses, oxen, donkeys, and so forth to reach the great city, with grass assisting to provide their strength;
so too, the bases of truth (*satya*), relinquishment (*tyāga*), cessation (*nirodha*), and wisdom (*prajñā*) can cause one to reach the Buddha-dharma and enter the great city of *nirvāṇa*.
“Fuel” refers to the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, which are capable of leading to the activity of great wisdom.
Just as fuel can cause fire to ignite and also cause it to blaze intensely.
In this way, the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation can give rise to great wisdom and cause it to increase.
Just as fire can burn, cook, and illuminate, so too is the fire of wisdom:
it burns away all afflictions, brings all roots of goodness to maturity, and illuminates the Four Noble Truths.
Fire is wisdom; firewood represents the various dharmas that can produce wisdom and so forth.
"Abundant water" means having many rivers, streams, and canals from which one may take as much as desired to satisfy the great multitude—something that springs, wells, and ponds cannot achieve.
Furthermore, "abundant water" is like a person traveling by boat along a river to a great city; in that case, the water from wells, springs, ponds, and pools cannot compare to it.
As the *Sūtra* says:
"Faith is like a great river, with merit as its banks.
Just as a river removes heat, quenches thirst, and cleanses impurities, it can generate power;..."

Within wholesome dharmas, faith is likewise able to extinguish the heat of the three poisons, remove the defilements of the three evil conducts, and eliminate the thirst for the three realms of existence;
for the sake of nirvana, it gains power within wholesome dharmas.
"Just as that excellent path, abounding in various roots and medicinal herbs, leaves the practitioner without want, so too is the path of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
'Roots' refers to what is cherished by the profound mind (*gambhīracitta*); because these roots exist, sprouts, stalks, branches, leaves, and all manner of fruits are produced."
With a profound mind that loves the Way, one gives rise to various merits such as right mindfulness and great vows.
"Medicinal herbs" refers to the various *pāramitās*;
just as medicinal herbs can eliminate all poisons, [so too do these virtues].
The medicinal herbs of the various pāramitās likewise extinguish the poisons of greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as the diseases of all afflictions.
Just as that excellent path does not lose its way-markers (vaidya), one travels the path with peace and security.
*Veda*—in the language of Qin, it means "that which has no counterpart"—is like a tally-token or a writ.
Just as a practitioner who does not lose his tally-token can reach wherever he desires without obstruction, so too is the path of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*):

if one does not lose the *veda*, then regarding all the stages traversed and the roots of goodness accumulated therein, one is able to assist their fulfillment and increase present roots of goodness according to one's will.

Furthermore, he is able to teach and transform sentient beings in the paths of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and the various heavens of the desire realm and form realm, causing them to abide in the Buddha-way.
If neither Māras nor non-Buddhists can disturb or confuse it, this is called not losing the *vaipulya*.
Just as that excellent path is free from mosquitoes, gadflies, and venomous insects;
so too is the path of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), where there is no sound of sorrow or weeping.
Just as that excellent road is free from the peril of bandits;
so too is the path of the ten stages, which is devoid of the five hindrances and the various evil bandits.
As the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“Village bandits refer to the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*). Just as bandits first seize a person’s property and subsequently take their life, so too do the bandits of the five hindrances:
they first rob one of the roots of goodness (*kuśala-mūla*) and subsequently sever the life-force of wisdom; thus one falls into negligence and dies.”
Just as on a road there are no lions, tigers, wolves, or various other evil beasts;
so too is the path of the ten stages (daśabhūmi), wherein there is no anger or contention.
Just as ferocious beasts such as lions delight in harming others,
so too do anger and the like arise for the purpose of harming others.
Just as these beasts devour flesh and drink blood, [so it is with these afflictions].
It is likewise with those who consume the flesh of wisdom from extensive learning and drink the blood of wisdom from cultivation;
they are also like that excellent path, which is free from the defects of cold and heat.
The path of the ten stages is also like this: because one does not fall into the寒冰 (Cold Ice) Hell, there is no defect of cold.
Because one does not fall into the Hot Hells, there is no fault of heat.
Just as that excellent path has no difficulties such as deep pits;
so too is the path of the ten stages (daśabhūmi), which is free from the difficulties of the ascetic practices of non-Buddhists (tīrthika), namely:

Smearing the body with ashes, entering ice, plucking out one's hair, washing three times daily, standing on one leg, eating once a day, eating every other day... up to eating once a month, remaining silent until death, constantly holding one arm aloft, always practicing patience, scorching the body with the five fires, lying upon thorns, entering fire, entering water, throwing oneself from high cliffs, standing amidst deep furnaces, burning the body with cow dung, proceeding directly toward a single direction without avoiding any hardships, constantly wearing wet clothes, sleeping in water, and so forth—such bodily and mental sufferings do not lead to right knowledge.
Because [this practice] lacks such [extremes], it is called "without hardship."
Just as a path has no byways;
so too is the path of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), for because it is free from evil karma of body, speech, and mind, it is called having no byways.
Just as a path has no thorns; [so too is the path of the ten stages].
The ten stages of the path (*daśabhūmi*) are also like this; because they are free from the thorns of karmic obstructions (*karmāvaraṇa*), they are called "thornless.
Just as a thorn piercing the foot prevents one from traveling, so too do the thorns of karmic obstructions obstruct the practice of the Buddha-dharma and entry into *nirvāṇa*.
Just as the path is straight;
so too are the ten stages of the path (bhūmi), for because they are devoid of all guile, crookedness, and deception, they are called "straight.
Just as the path has few diverging roads;
The ten stages of the path are also like this, with fewer alternative paths. Why is this?
Because those who set out in the Mahāyāna practice the paths of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas only rarely; therefore, there are few alternative paths.

There may be bodhisattvas who practice the paths of the two vehicles; it should be known that they have not yet reached the bodhisattva stages nor entered the state of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*), because they are practicing peripheral conduct.
Just as that excellent road is free from the obstructions of thickets and forests;
so too is the path of the ten dwellings (*daśavihāra*), for it is devoid of the thickets of the five desires and all evils.
Question: Why does it not say "the forest of the five desires is entirely non-existent," but rather only say "there is no forest of evil"? Answer:

For those who have set out in the Mahāyāna, there are the causal conditions for merit and virtue that include the foremost five desires; therefore, one cannot say they do not exist, though they are merely devoid of evil.
Furthermore, just as a dense thicket is difficult to enter and traverse because it contains many obstacles, the five desires of a bodhisattva are not like this;
unlike ordinary people, they do not give rise to various faults and evils regarding the five desires.
For this reason, it is said that there are no thickets.
Just as a road is broad and vast, providing ample space so that things do not obstruct one another;

so too is the path of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). It has great capacity for inclusion, such that immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings may together resolve their minds toward the unsurpassed path (*anuttara-mārga*) without mutual obstruction. Whether these hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings, or all sentient beings together, resolve their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and practice this path together, they do not obstruct one another.
Just as a road is traveled by many people, so too is the path of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*);
when the Buddhas of the past and present, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, practiced the bodhisattva path, they all traversed this very path.
Just as one who follows a good path does not grow weary in their journey, so too is the path of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*); it abounds in various joys of cause and effect, namely:

being frequently reborn among humans and devas to receive karmic rewards; experiencing the joy of detachment from desire, the joy of rapture (*prīti*), the joy of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), the joy of non-rapture (*aprīti*), and present-time bliss.
Because one attains these various joys, there is no weariness or fatigue.
Just as a path may abound with flowers, fruits, and roots;
so too is the path of the ten stages (daśabhūmi), abounding in roots, flowers, and fruits.
The "roots" are the three wholesome roots.
The "flowers" are the flowers of the seven factors of enlightenment.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"The seven flowers" refers to the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*).
"Fruit" refers to the four fruits of the ascetic life (*catur-śrāmaṇyaphala*).
Because there is no such fault as contradicting these excellent qualities of the Path, it is called "leaving evil behind."
Just as a guide knows the road, understanding where one should eat and where one should rest, and likewise where one should stay overnight;
so too does a bodhisattva practicing the ten stages know where it is appropriate to rest and where it is appropriate to take sustenance.
"Can be lodged in" means there are various places where present Buddhas reside.
"Can be eaten" means it is a place where one can cultivate wholesome dharmas.
Just as food can benefit the sense faculties and also sustain life; [so too is this place].
All wholesome dharmas are likewise; they can benefit the faculties such as "faith" and assist in establishing the life of wisdom.
"Staying overnight in another place" means going from the presence of that Buddha to the presence of another Buddha.
Furthermore, the space between this buddha-land and that buddha-land is also called "a different place.
One who skillfully knows how to turn the path is like a guide who turns away when he knows the road is not secure;
the bodhisattva is likewise, skillfully knowing which path leads to the stage of a śrāvaka, which path leads to the stage of a pratyekabuddha, and which path leads to Buddhahood.
Having understood this, one abandons the path of the śrāvaka and the path of the pratyekabuddha and proceeds solely toward the path of the Buddha.
Just as that excellent road abounds in food and drink, so too is the path of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*):
it is rich in the practice of giving, the observance of precepts, and the cultivation of meditative concentration.
Just as that guide possesses abundant wealth, is skilled in the methods of governance, and has great power;
so too is the bodhisattva, for by possessing wealth and being skilled in the methods of governance, he likewise has great power.
Wealth refers to the seven riches, namely: faith, ethical discipline, shame, dread of blame, relinquishment, learning, and wisdom.
As for the method of subduing, it is the ability to completely crush and overcome all Māras, various śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and non-Buddhist teachers; this constitutes its majestic power.
Just as that great city is called "secure" because it is free from enemies and bandits, epidemics, untimely deaths, and various forms of decay and affliction,

so too is the great city of Nirvana called "secure" because it is free from all Māras, the various streams of external paths, greed, hatred, negligence, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and weeping.
Just as that great city is called "abundant" because it possesses much food and drink,
so too is the city of Nirvana called "abundant" because it contains many profound meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), and samādhis.
Just as that great city is called "great" because it accommodates many,
so too is the city of Nirvana called "great" because it receives many sentient beings.
Even if all sentient beings were to enter *nirvāṇa* without remainder because they no longer grasp at any phenomena, the nature of *nirvāṇa* would neither increase nor decrease.
Just as a guide is called a "guide" because he can safely lead a great multitude and show them the good path, so too is the Bodhisattva:

skillfully leading sentient beings to show them the Buddha-dharma and to show them *nirvāṇa*, enabling them to travel from the perilous path of birth and death to reach *nirvāṇa*, he is therefore called a "Great Guide."
Just as that guide, because he knows the characteristics of the path well, has no evil in himself nor in those he leads;
so too is the Bodhisattva: he does not personally engage in the hindrances such as greed and hatred, nor in various evils, ascetic practices, or the deep pits of old age and death;
nor does he fall into the cold and hot hells or the realm of hungry ghosts. Therefore, it is said that he himself does not incur evil, and those who follow him likewise do not incur evil.
Therefore, it is said in the *Gāthā*:
"Because they well know the characteristics of the path, they themselves do not incur evil, nor do others incur evil.
Thus concludes this brief exposition of the Bodhisattva’s Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
When Bodhisattvas dwell within this state, they often become kings of Jambudvīpa;
Always free from the defilement of stinginess and greed, they do not lose their mindfulness of the Triple Gem.
Their minds constantly aspire to become Buddhas, in order to rescue and protect all sentient beings.
The first stage is named "Joyful"; this has already been explained in brief.
The dharmas of all Buddhas are immeasurable and boundless, and this stage is their foundation.
If they were explained in detail, they would likewise be immeasurable and boundless; therefore, it is said to be "explained briefly."
When a Bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they frequently become a powerful universal monarch (cakravartin) over Jambudvīpa.
Because of the causes and conditions cultivated in previous lives for this stage, they have faith and delight in giving, free from the defilement of stinginess and greed;
and because they constantly bestow gifts upon the Triple Gem, they do not lose mindfulness of the Triple Gem.
Constantly mindful of attaining Buddhahood to save all sentient beings— such wholesome thoughts as these shall always abide within the mind.
If one desires to leave the household life, by practicing with a diligent and energetic mind,
one can attain several hundred concentrations and behold several hundred Buddhas.
He can shake a hundred worlds, and his flight through the air is likewise;
if he wishes to emit radiance, he can illuminate a hundred worlds;
he can manifest hundreds of kinds of beings and abide for a lifespan of a hundred kalpas.
They can discern hundreds of dharmas, And can manifest as a hundred bodies.
They can transform into a hundred bodhisattvas, Appearing as their retinue;
Their sharp faculties exceed these numbers, By virtue of the Buddha’s spiritual power.
Having already explained the characteristics of the first stage (*bhūmi*), as well as the dharmas for purification through the power of its fruition,
I shall now further explain the second, the Stainless Stage (*vimalā-bhūmi*).
"Fruition" refers to attaining several hundred meditative concentrations, seeing several hundred Buddhas, and so forth.
"Power" refers to the ability to transform hundreds of sentient beings.
The meaning of the remaining verses has already been explained; I shall not further interpret them here. Now, I will explain the second stage, the Stainless Ground (vimalā-bhūmi).
Question:

You wish to explain in detail the dharmas practiced by bodhisattvas; yet the meaning of even the first stage (*bhūmi*) is already vast. Scholars may fear that as it becomes further expanded, their minds will grow indolent, and they will be unable to read or recite it.
Therefore, you should now provide a brief explanation of the dharmas practiced by bodhisattvas for those who are unable to recite and study extensively.
He replied:
"All the dharmas possessed by a bodhisattva—these dharmas should all be put into practice."
All evils should be abandoned; this is what is called the brief exposition.
As for the dharmas that can produce and increase the various stages (*bhūmi*), they have been explained in the preceding chapters;
as for those explained in other places, they should all be brought forth.
A bodhisattva should distance themselves from all faults and evils.
This is called a brief explanation of what a bodhisattva should practice.
As it is said in the *Dharmapada*:
“Commit no evil, practice all that is good, and purify your own mind; this is the teaching of all Buddhas.
There is one dharma that encompasses the Buddha-way, which a bodhisattva should practice.
What is this one thing?
It is as follows:
"To be single-mindedly heedful regarding wholesome dharmas."
As the Buddha told Ānanda:
"Because I was not negligent, I attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
As it is said:
Through heedfulness one attains Buddhahood; there is none in the world equal to such a one.
If one can be heedful, what task will not be accomplished?
Furthermore, there are two further dharmas that can encompass the path of the Buddha:
First, heedfulness; second, wisdom.
As it is said:
"Heedfulness and wisdom—the Buddha calls these the gateway to benefit."
One does not see anyone who fails to achieve their goal through heedfulness.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas that can encompass the Buddha-way:
first, training in the superior precepts; second, training in the superior mind; and third, training in the superior wisdom.
As it is said:
"Precepts give rise to supreme samādhi; Samādhi gives rise to wisdom;
Wisdom disperses all afflictions, Just as the wind blows away floating clouds."
Furthermore, there are four dharmas that can encompass the Buddha-way:
first, the station of truth; second, the station of equanimity; third, the station of cessation; and fourth, the station of wisdom.
As it is said:
Fully endowed with the foundations of mindfulness and equanimity, Attaining sharp and pure wisdom,
And seeking the Buddha-way with diligence— One should gather these four dharmas.
Furthermore, there are five dharmas that can encompass the Buddha-way:
First, the faculty of faith; second, the faculty of diligence; third, the faculty of mindfulness; fourth, the faculty of concentration; fifth, the faculty of wisdom. As it is said:
"The faculties of faith and diligence, And the steadfastness of mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom."
This Dharma is conjoined with great compassion; One shall never retreat from the Buddha-way.
Just as a person who obtains the five faculties Is able to penetrate the five sense objects, So by obtaining the faculties such as faith, One is able to penetrate the characteristics of all dharmas.
Furthermore, there are six dharmas that can encompass the Buddha-way:
namely, the pāramitās of giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
As it is said:
"By practicing the six perfections as described, subduing all afflictions,
and constantly increasing roots of goodness, one shall before long attain Buddhahood."
Furthermore, there are seven dharmas that can encompass the Buddha-way.
These are the so-called seven right dharmas:
faith, shame, remorse, learning, diligence, mindfulness, and wisdom.
As it is said:
If one wishes to attain the seven right dharmas, One should delight in concentration and diligence;
By eliminating the seven wrong dharmas, One will be able to know all meritorious qualities.
Such a person can swiftly attain the unsurpassed *bodhi* of the Buddha;
they uproot those submerged in birth and death, causing them to dwell in a place of peace and security.
Furthermore, there are eight dharmas that can encompass the path of the Buddha, namely, the eight awakenings of the great person (*aṣṭau mahāpuruṣavitarkāḥ*):
Having few desires, contentment, seclusion, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, and delighting in the absence of frivolous proliferation.
As it is said:
"If a person possesses a resolute mind and abides in the eight awakenings of the great men,"
For the sake of seeking the Buddha-way, eliminate all evil thoughts and reflections.
In this way, before long, you will swiftly attain the unsurpassed path;
just as one who practices goodness will surely obtain wondrous fruits.
Furthermore, there are nine dharmas that can encompass the Buddha-way, namely:
great patience, great loving-kindness, great compassion, wisdom, mindfulness, firm resolve, non-greed, non-anger, and non-delusion.
As it is said:
"Endowed with great patience, Great loving-kindness and great compassion,
And further abiding in wisdom, Mindfulness, and a steadfast mind."
With a profound mind one enters into non-attachment, non-hatred, and non-delusion—the roots of goodness.
If one can act in this way, the path of the Buddha is then held in the palm of one's hand.
Furthermore, there are ten dharmas that can encompass the path of the Buddha, namely, the ten paths of wholesome action:

One refrains from killing oneself, does not instruct others to kill, does not approve of killing when seeing it, and does not take pleasure in killing when seeing it; this applies likewise even to wrong views.
Dedicate this merit toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
As it is said:
"Do not harm or afflict sentient beings, Nor practice robbery or theft."
Not committing sexual misconduct with another’s wife— these three constitute bodily karma;
Not speaking falsely, not using double-tongued speech, Not using harsh words or frivolous chatter,
And being free from covetousness, malice, and wrong views— These seven are the actions of speech and mind.
In this way, one can open the gate to the unsurpassed path of the Buddha;
those who wish to attain Buddhahood should practice this primary gate.
Such dharmas as these are what a bodhisattva should bring forth.
Once it has arisen, one should protect it; once protected, one should cause it to increase.
Regarding even a single wholesome deed, one should cause it to grow from one instance to the next.
Furthermore, one should know that those who seek the Buddha-way must swiftly abandon even a single unwholesome dharma.
This refers to being far removed from heedlessness.
As it is said:
"If a person cannot cross over the perilous and evil path of birth and death,"
This is to be censured; it is the most sinful of deeds:
though one may delight in wealth and pleasure, yet be born into a poor and lowly family, unable to plant roots of goodness, and become a servant to others.
All arise from heedlessness, brought about by causes and conditions;
therefore, the wise should distance themselves from them as quickly as they would from a virulent poison.
If one has not yet perfected great compassion or attained the non-arising patience that is irreversible, [one must remain vigilant].
To act with negligence is what is called death.
Furthermore, there are two faults that one should swiftly abandon:
first, craving for the stage of a śrāvaka; second, craving for the stage of a pratyekabuddha.
As it is said:
"If one falls to the stage of a śrāvaka, or to the stage of a pratyekabuddha,
this is called the death of a bodhisattva, and it is also called total loss."
Though one may fall into hell, one should not give rise to fear;
if one falls into the two vehicles, a bodhisattva should feel great dread.
Though one may fall into hell, it does not permanently obstruct the path to Buddhahood; [but falling into the two vehicles does.]
If one falls into the two vehicles, one ultimately obstructs the path to Buddhahood.
The Buddha said that those who cherish their lives feel great terror at the severing of their heads;
likewise, those who wish to become Buddhas should feel great terror toward the two vehicles.
Furthermore, there are three faults that one should quickly abandon:
first, hatred toward bodhisattvas; second, hatred toward the conduct of bodhisattvas; and third, hatred toward the profound Mahāyāna sūtras.
As it is said:
"Those of small wisdom, with their limited objects of perception, harbor hatred toward all bodhisattvas,
as well as toward the bodhisattva path, and likewise toward the Mahāyāna sūtras."
Because they do not understand, they lack faith;
falling into the great hells, they cry out in terror and alarm—this matter should be avoided.
Furthermore, there are four other faults that should be swiftly abandoned:
First, flattery; second, crookedness; third, a quick temper; fourth, a lack of compassion.
As it is said:
Claiming for oneself to be a bodhisattva, While one's mind is full of flattery and crookedness.
Being acutely intolerant and failing to practice a heart of compassion—
this is to be near the Avīci Hell and far removed from the Buddha-way.
Furthermore, there are five faults that one should swiftly abandon:
First, sensual desire; second, ill will; third, sloth and torpor; fourth, restlessness and remorse; fifth, doubt.
These are called the five hindrances that shroud the mind.
As it is said:
"If a person is negligent, the various hindrances will shroud their mind;
even attaining rebirth in heaven is difficult for them, let alone realizing the fruits [of the path]."
If one practices with diligent vigor, one can then rend asunder all hindrances;
if one can rend asunder all hindrances, one will obtain everything according to one's vows.
Furthermore, there are six faults that are contrary to the six pāramitās, which one should swiftly abandon:
First, stinginess and greed; second, violation of precepts; third, anger and hatred; fourth, laziness; fifth, restlessness and frivolity; sixth, ignorance.
As it is said:
"With a mind defiled by the stain of stinginess and greed, Violating the precepts and indolent,
Ignorant as cattle or sheep, And prone to anger like a venomous snake."
The mind is as distracted as a monkey; if one does not distance oneself from the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), it is extremely difficult to be born in heaven, let alone attain the path of the Buddha.
Furthermore, there are seven faults that should be swiftly abandoned:
First, delighting in many affairs;
second, delighting in much recitation and chanting;
third, delighting in sleep.
4. Speaking with pleasant words;
5. Craving for gain and offerings;
6. Constantly desiring to make others happy.
Seventh, being deluded and distressed regarding the Path, the mind follows the course of craving.
As it is said:
"The base person delights in worldly affairs, And delights in reciting many external scriptures."
Foolish people delight in sleep and take pleasure in gathering together for idle chatter.
Though they aspire to become Buddhas, they remain deeply attached to gain and offerings;
as slaves to craving and affection, they are bewildered and distressed regarding the path of the Buddha.
Such evil persons claim for themselves to be bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, there are eight things that one should swiftly abandon:
first, wrong view; second, wrong thought; third, wrong speech; fourth, wrong action; fifth, wrong livelihood; sixth, wrong effort; seventh, wrong mindfulness; and eighth, wrong concentration.
As it is said:
If there is a person who is deluded, practicing the eightfold wrong path,
studying the various teachings of false scriptures, and delighting in following after false teachers.
Far removed from the Eightfold Noble Path and the profound, wondrous virtues,
Firmly and deeply attached to afflictions, yet perhaps aspiring for Bodhi—
Such a foolish person wishes to cross the great ocean.
Having abandoned a fine and sturdy ship, one embraces a stone in an attempt to cross over.
Furthermore, there are nine things that should be swiftly abandoned:
first, not hearing of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
2. Having heard it, one does not believe;
3. If one believes, one does not accept;
4. If one accepts, one does not recite or uphold it.
Fifth, if one recites and maintains [the teachings] but does not understand their meaning and intent;
sixth, if one understands them but does not explain them.
7. If one speaks but does not act according to what was spoken;
8. If one acts according to what was spoken;
They cannot practice constantly;
ninth, even if they can practice constantly, they cannot practice skillfully.
As it is said:
The deluded person does not wish to hear the unsurpassed, true, and correct path;
having heard it, they cannot believe it, nor can they recite and uphold it;
they do not understand its meaning and do not speak of it, and they do not act according to what has been taught.
Unable to practice virtue constantly, and lacking mindfulness and settled wisdom—
such foolish people are incapable of attaining the fruits of the Path,
just as a person of evil deeds cannot be reborn in the heavens.
Furthermore, there are ten faults that one should quickly abandon, namely the ten unwholesome paths of action.
As it is said:
"The deluded person, for a short time, is defiled by craving for the five sensual desires."
Abandoning the ten paths of wholesome action, they practice the ten paths of unwholesome action.
With the pleasures of the devas already in their hands, they cast them aside of their own accord— like one who,
out of greed for the profit of a few small coins, discards a great treasure trove.
Question:

When you spoke of the characteristics of the unsurpassed path, you used various causes and conditions to rebuke and revile the bodhisattvas who merely make vows, the self-proclaimed bodhisattvas, and the bodhisattvas in name only.
If these three types are not called bodhisattvas, then by accomplishing what dharma is one called a true bodhisattva?
The answer is:
It is not merely by making empty vows and declaring oneself a bodhisattva that one is called a bodhisattva by name;
[one must practice accordingly].
Briefly stated, one who can accomplish the thirty-two dharmas is called a bodhisattva.

If a person resolves their mind to seek the Buddha-way and claims for themselves the title of "bodhisattva" yet merely receives this name in vain—failing to practice merit, compassion, the various pāramitās, and so forth—they are not truly called a bodhisattva.
It is like calling an earthen city a "Jewel City"; it merely deceives oneself, deceives the Buddhas, and deceives the sentient beings of the world.
If a person possesses the thirty-two sublime dharmas and is also able to make vows, they are called a true Bodhisattva.
What are the thirty-two?
First, with a profound mind, to seek all forms of peace and happiness for the sake of all sentient beings.
Second, to be able to enter into the wisdom of all Buddhas.
3. Self-examination to know whether one is capable of becoming a Buddha or not.
4. Not harboring hatred toward others.
Fifth, the resolve for the Path is firm and steadfast.
Sixth, one does not resort to hypocrisy or form alliances based on worldly affection.
Seventh, until one enters parinirvāṇa, one constantly acts as a kinsman and friend to all sentient beings.
8. To have a single heart with both kin and non-kin;
9. To have a mind that does not regress once a virtuous deed has been pledged;
10. To never cease great compassion toward all sentient beings.
11. To never cease great compassion for all sentient beings.
12. To constantly seek the true Dharma with a mind free from weariness or indolence.
13. To diligently exert vigor with a mind that knows no satiety.
14. Being learned and understanding the meaning;
15. Constantly examining one's own faults;
16. Not deriding the deficiencies of others.
17. To constantly cultivate the bodhicitta amidst all matters of seeing and hearing.
18. To practice giving without seeking reward.
19. To maintain the precepts without seeking rebirth in any realm of existence.
Twenty: Toward all sentient beings, one practices patience and remains free from anger and resentment.
Twenty-one: One is able to cultivate all roots of goodness with diligent vigor.
22. Not being born in accordance with the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*).
23. Wisdom embraced by skillful means (*upāya*).
24. Skillful means embraced by the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).
Twenty-five: Regarding those who uphold the precepts and those who violate them, he regards them with compassion and equanimity, making no distinction between them.
Twenty-six: He listens to the Dharma with a single-minded focus.
Twenty-seven: He dwells in forest hermitages with a single-minded focus.
28. Not delighting in the various worldly affairs.
29. Not being greedily attached to the Hīnayāna.
30. Perceiving the benefits of the Mahāyāna as great.
31. To distance oneself from evil associates.
32. To draw near to virtuous associates.
When a bodhisattva abides in these thirty-two dharmas, they are able to accomplish seven dharmas.
That is to say:
the four immeasurable minds,
and the ability to sport with the five supernormal powers.
They always rely on wisdom;
they never abandon sentient beings, whether good or evil;
and their speech is resolute.
Their speech is invariably truthful.
They gather all wholesome dharmas with a mind that never knows satiety.
These are the thirty-two dharmas, which comprise seven groups. A bodhisattva who accomplishes these is called a true bodhisattva.
All Bodhisattvas who have already attained and fully perfected the first stage, desiring to attain the second stage, should give rise to ten kinds of mind.

All Bodhisattvas, having already attained the Joyful First Stage, give rise to ten kinds of mind for the sake of attaining the Second Stage; by means of these ten minds, they are able to attain the Second Stage.
Just as a person who wishes to ascend a multi-storied tower must rely on a ladder to do so.
It is asked:
What are these ten mental states that serve as the skillful means for attaining the second stage?
The answer is: The mind of straightforwardness, the capable and steadfast mind, the gentle, submissive, and tranquil mind,
the true and wondrous mind unmixed with greed, and the swift, great mind— these constitute the ten.
When bodhisattvas have fully perfected the first stage and desire to attain the second stage, they give rise to these ten minds of skillful means:

first, the straightforward mind; second, the resilient mind; third, the supple mind; fourth, the subduing mind; fifth, the tranquil mind; sixth, the truly wondrous mind; seventh, the unadulterated mind; eighth, the non-greedy mind; ninth, the vast and joyful mind; and tenth, the great mind.
A straightforward mind is one that is free from flattery and crookedness.
Because it is free from flattery and crookedness, the mind becomes supple and pliant.
"Supple" means not being rigid or coarse.

When a bodhisattva attains this supple mind, they give rise to various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), cultivate all wholesome dharmas, and contemplate the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena; thus, the mind becomes fit for use.
Because the mind is serviceable, one gives rise to the subduing of the mind.
As for "subduing the mind":
it means being well able to subdue the various faculties, such as the eye and so forth.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"What is the wholesome path?
It refers to a bhikṣu who subdues the faculty of the eye, up to and including the faculty of the mind."
Because the six sense faculties have been subdued, it is called "subduing the mind.
Once the mind has been subdued, it is easy to give rise to a mind of quiescence.
As for this "mind of quiescence":
It is able to extinguish all afflictions such as greed, hatred, and delusion.
Having already been suppressed by "subduing the mind," it is further caused to attain quiescent extinction.
Furthermore, some say:
"Attaining the various dhyānas and samādhis is called the mind of quiescence;
as the Sūtra says:
'If a person skillfully knows the characteristics of dhyāna and does not crave its flavor, this is called the mind of quiescence.'"
"Once one has attained the mind of quiescence, one will necessarily give rise to the truly wondrous mind.

This 'truly wondrous mind' means that regarding all matters of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and aspirations, one attains their application according to one's wish, just as pure gold may be used for any purpose at will."
Once the practitioner has attained the straightforward mind up to the truly sublime mind, in order to protect these minds, they delight in giving rise to an unadulterated mind.
An unadulterated mind is one that does not engage in worldly affairs with either householders or those who have left the home life.
This person thinks:
"I have attained such states of mind as these entirely through the power of meditative concentration;
by means of these various minds, I shall attain immeasurable benefits, such as the second bhūmi and others."
If one mingles with the multitude, then one loses this benefit.
Why is this? If a person practices in association with the multitude, then at times the six sense faculties, such as the eye and so forth, will give rise to various unwholesome dharmas.
Why is this? Because by associating with things that can provoke attachment, aversion, or delusion, the sense faculties are stirred and the fire of afflictions blazes;
because the fire of afflictions blazes, one then loses these benefits.
"Because one perceives these faults, one gives rise to a mind free from mingling; one should not associate with those who are householders or those who have left the home life.
Once this person has attained this mind free from mingling, they next give rise to a mind free from greed."
Regarding "one who is free from greed":
among householders and renunciants—such as parents, brothers, preceptors, teachers, and elders—one does not give rise to greedy attachment. One reflects thus:
"If I were to give rise to greedy attachment toward householders or renunciants, I would inevitably have to visit them and exchange greetings; how then could my mind remain unadulterated?"

"Therefore, for those who wish to abide in the benefits of various meditative concentrations with an undistracted mind, they should abandon the mind of attachment toward both householders and renunciants.
[The interlocutor] asked:
"According to the Dharma of a Bodhisattva, one should not abandon sentient beings, nor should one give rise to a mind of abandonment."
As it is said in the *Bodhyāpattideśanā*:
"When a bodhisattva first exerts diligence, By all the power of their skillful means,
They should cause all sentient beings To abide within the Mahāyāna."
If one were to instruct as many sentient beings as there are grains of sand in the Ganges to abide in the stage of an Arhat,
it would not be as excellent as instructing a single person to abide in the Mahāyāna.
If a person has little power and is unable to resolve upon the Mahāyāna, [one should instead encourage them in other ways].
Next, one should instruct them to abide in the vehicles of the Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas;
if people are unable to abide in the vehicles of the Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas,
one should instruct these sentient beings to practice the causes and conditions of merit.
Unable to abide in the three vehicles, and finding no satisfaction in the pleasures of humans and devas,
I shall employ the affairs of this world to benefit beings accordingly.
If there are sentient beings who do not receive the benefit of the Bodhisattva, [I shall act for them].
One should not abandon this, but should instead give rise to great compassion.
How can you say:
"The Bodhisattva attains an unmixed mind and gives rise to a mind free from greed"?
If a bodhisattva does not covet sentient beings, they would then abandon them; how then could they deliver them?
The answer is:
one should accord with the bodhisattva path and practice the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Why is this? Because by means of the mind of relinquishment, this person gives rise to a mind of vast joy and thinks:
"If I relinquish these crowds and clamor, I shall attain meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); through meditative concentration, I shall give rise to the sublime, vast, and joyful Dharma."
"Once you have attained this Dharma, you will thereafter be able to benefit sentient beings many millions of times more than you do now.

For this reason, in order to bring great benefit to sentient beings, one should temporarily relinquish the mind [of worldly attachment], provisionally abandon the clamor of the crowd, and thereby attain the benefits of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and so forth, to benefit sentient beings.
For what reason does a bodhisattva employ such skillful means?
It is because the bodhisattva seeks to attain the Great Mind and thus reflects:
"Since great beings delight in great benefit, they do not dwell upon minor gains."
"Therefore, I shall now seek the Dharma of the Great Man and train accordingly;
I should apply myself with such diligent effort for the sake of great benefit—namely, the various meditative concentrations, supernormal powers, the cessation of suffering, liberation, and so forth."
Therefore, what you say is incorrect. Question:
Since the factors such as "direct mind" already exist within the first stage (bhūmi), why is it stated again:
"If a bodhisattva wishes to attain the second bhūmi, they must give rise to ten mental states?
He replied:
"Although these dharmas exist in the first bhūmi, one has not yet attained profound joy, nor is it yet firm and stable."
In this stage, one constantly delights in it, and this delight becomes increasingly deep and firm, rendering one capable of its application; therefore, your objection is incorrect.
Question:
If one deeply delights in and firmly adheres to this Dharma, what extraordinary result is attained?
The answer is:
If one attains it at once, with a mind of profound joy and firm resolve,
no further effort is required, as if it were constantly following after one.
Just as if something were to arise at one time and constantly follow a person;
so too, once a Bodhisattva has attained this profound joy and firm mind at one time, it constantly follows them thereafter.
It no longer requires effort to arise, and may arise even through slight causes and conditions.
Why is this? Because the roots have grown deep, the stems and nodes continue in succession.
Question:
If a bodhisattva attains these ten kinds of mind, what fruit is obtained?
The answer is:
if one attains these various minds, one dwells correctly in the second stage.
Possessing the three kinds of freedom from defilement— namely, evil karma and afflictions—
if a bodhisattva attains these ten states of mind, such as "straightness" and so forth, they are said to dwell in the second bodhisattva stage.
First, "Vimalā" (Stainless) is the name of the stage;
second, "Vimalā" refers to being free from the stains of the karmic offenses of the ten unwholesome paths within this stage;
third, "Vimalā" refers to being free from the stains of various afflictions such as greed and hatred; therefore, it is named Vimalā.
Furthermore, regarding the meaning of "freedom from defilement" (*vimala*):
*Daśabhūmivibhāṣā-śāstra*, Scroll 10; *Daśabhūmivibhāṣā-śāstra*, Scroll 14.
Composed by the Holy Nāgārjuna;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty:
When a Bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they naturally refrain from committing evil.
Because they deeply delight in wholesome dharmas, they naturally practice the path of goodness.
Question:
Why do they naturally refrain from the ten unwholesome paths and naturally practice the ten wholesome paths?
Of these two kinds of paths, how many are bodily formations (*kāyasaṃskāra*),
how many are verbal formations (*vāksaṃskāra*),
and how many are mental formations (*manaḥsaṃskāra*)?
The answer is:
There are two or three types of bodily and mental [actions], and the four types of verbal wholesome actions are likewise;
this is the brief explanation, which should now be analyzed in detail.
There are three types of unwholesome bodily conduct:
namely, taking the life of another, stealing, and sexual misconduct.
There are four types of unwholesome verbal conduct:
False speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous speech.
There are three types of unwholesome mental actions:
covetousness, ill will, and wrong view.
Wholesome bodily conduct also has three types:
abstaining from taking life, stealing, and sexual misconduct.
Wholesome verbal conduct also has four types:
One abstains from false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and idle chatter.
There are three types of virtuous mental conduct:
non-covetousness, non-ill will, and right view.
Regarding the paths of action of body, speech, and mind—whether they are wholesome or unwholesome—they must be discussed so that people may attain understanding.
First, as for the unwholesome path of taking life:
it refers to there being another sentient being whom one recognizes as such, and intentionally inflicting harm upon them; because of this harm, that being loses its life.
To initiate this bodily action is called the first unwholesome path of taking life.
To abstain from such an act is called the wholesome practice of refraining from taking life.
As for robbery:

Regarding what belongs to another: knowing that an object belongs to another, one conceives the intent to steal, takes hold of this object with the hand, and moves it from its place; whether by robbery or theft, calculating it as "this is my property" and giving rise to the sense of possession—this is called the practice of stealing.
To abstain from these matters is called the virtuous practice of refraining from theft.
As for sexual misconduct:
it refers to any woman who is protected by her parents, protected by her relatives, protected by her clan, protected by worldly law, or protected by the precepts.
If one has sexual desire for another’s wife, knowing that there are obstacles such as the threat of flogging, beating, or other forms of harm, and gives rise to physical action based on this desire;
or if one acts toward one’s own wife or concubine when she is observing precepts, pregnant, nursing, or not via the proper path—this is called sexual misconduct.
To remain far removed from these matters is called wholesome bodily conduct.
As for false speech:
it consists of concealing one's signs, concealing one's mind, concealing one's views, concealing one's patience, and concealing one's desires.
To know such characteristics and yet speak otherwise is called false speech.
To distance oneself from this is called the virtuous practice of abstaining from false speech.
As for double-tongued speech:
Desiring to cause division among others, one speaks of this matter to that person and of that matter to this person;

for the sake of causing division, one causes those who are united to become separated, and regarding those already separated, one complies with their desire for separation, delights in separation, and takes pleasure in separation—this is called double-tongued speech (*paiśunya*).
To abstain from such matters is called the virtuous practice of refraining from divisive speech.
As for harsh speech:
all evil words, harmful words, painful words, coarse words, and vile words existing in the world that cause others to feel anger and distress—this is called harsh speech.
To distance oneself from these matters is called the virtuous practice of abstaining from harsh speech.
Regarding frivolous speech:

speaking at improper times, speech that is unbeneficial, speech that is contrary to the Dharma, speech lacking coherence between beginning and end, and speech devoid of causal basis—these are termed frivolous speech.
To remain far removed from these matters is called the virtuous practice of abandoning distraction.
As for "covetousness":
it is the state of mind that covets, desires, and wishes to obtain what belongs to another, what is desired by another, another's fields and groves, or another's property.
In this regard, not being greedy, not being envious, and not desiring to obtain [something] is called the wholesome practice of non-greed.
As for malice:
it is the state of mind characterized by resentment and obstruction toward other sentient beings, giving rise to anger and forming such a thought:
"To beat, bind, or kill!"—
this is called malice (*vyāpāda*).
To be free from such things is called the virtuous practice of non-malice (*avyāpāda-kuśala-caryā*).
Wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) is as follows:

to say that there is no giving, no offering of gratitude, and no retribution for good and evil deeds; that there is no present world and no future world; that there are no parents; and that there are no śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who, through clear and thorough penetration, can personally realize and witness this world and the world beyond—this is called wrong view.

Right view is as follows: there is a giver; there is the requital of kindness; there is the retribution for good and evil deeds; there are this world and future worlds; and there are śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, through their knowledge of this world and future worlds, have clearly attained penetration and personally realized them for themselves. This is called right view and wholesome conduct; it is in this way that the bodhisattva enters the path of right view.
Regarding the wholesome and unwholesome paths, there are twenty types of differentiation each;
knowing from where they arise and so forth constitutes twelve types of differentiation.
Thus, the Bodhisattva knows twenty types of differentiation concerning the various distinct characteristics of the ten unwholesome paths and the ten wholesome paths.
Furthermore, regarding these twenty kinds of discrimination, one should skillfully understand the twelve kinds of discrimination, such as "from where they arise.
Within these ten unwholesome paths of action, there are twenty kinds of discrimination;
namely, not being separated from the transgression of taking another's life:
1. It is unwholesome (akuśala).
2. It is bound to the desire realm (kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta).
3. It is with outflows (sāsrava).
4. Non-mental factors (acaitasika-dharma).
5. Dissociated from mind (citta-viprayukta).
6. Not following the movement of the mind (na citta-anuvartin).
7. It may arise simultaneously with the mind, or it may not arise simultaneously with the mind.
What is meant by "arising simultaneously with the mind"?
When there is a sentient being who perceives that being as such, and intentionally takes its life through bodily action—this is called arising simultaneously with the mind.
What is meant by "arising of non-common thought"?
If a person wishes to kill a sentient being, they seize, drag, and throw them to the ground, and only then does death occur; this is called the arising of non-common thought.

Furthermore, if one neither moves the body nor speaks with the mouth, but merely gives rise to the thought, "From this day forth, I shall kill sentient beings," the sin of taking another's life is incurred; this is called a non-commonly-arisen [sin].
Furthermore, this non-abandonment of taking another's life, whether in sleep or wakefulness, is constantly accumulated and increased; it is also called "arising with a non-associated mind.
Eighth, it is either form or non-form:
The first killing offense, which arises simultaneously with the mind, is form (*rūpa*); the second, third, and fourth killing offenses are not form.
Ninth, regarding what is manifest action (*vijñapti*) or non-manifest action (*avijñapti*):
that which is form is manifest action; the remainder is non-manifest action.
Tenth, there are those with objects and those without objects:
form has an object, while the others have no object.
Question:
Is this mind with an object (sālambana) or without an object (anālambana)?
Answer: It is not with an object.
Question:

If the mind is not "with an object" (sālambana), such that when the body does not move and the mouth does not speak, one merely gives rise in the mind to the thought, "From this day forth, I shall kill sentient beings," how can such a karmic offense be called "without an object"?
Answer: If the sin of killing were the mind itself, it would necessarily have an object;
however, the actual sin of killing is not the mind.
If the mind were itself the offense of killing, it would be a bodily action (*kāyakarman*);
however, the mind is in fact not a bodily action. Therefore, the offense of taking life is not said to have an object (*sālambana*).
Rather, the offense of taking life arises within the body together with the mind; because it is an unmanifest action (*avijñapti*), it is said to be non-objective.
11. This is karma; 12. it is not associated with karma;
13. it does not follow the course of karma.
14. There are those born of common karma and those born of uncommon karma:
they are no different from those born of a common mind, except that the distinction lies in their arising together with volition (*cetanā*).
Fifteen, it is not the karmic retribution of previous lives.
Sixteen, it cannot be cultivated.
Seventeen, it should be thoroughly understood.
18. It should be realized through wisdom, not realized through the body.
19. It is capable of being abandoned.
20. It is capable of being known and seen.
Not being separated from the offenses of stealing, not being separated from the offense of sexual misconduct, and not being separated from the offense of false speech:
these exist in two ways—first, arising together with the mind; second, not arising together with the mind.
First, with form; second, without form.
First, active; second, non-active.
First, with an object; second, without an object.
The rest is as explained in the section on killing.
It is the same for not abstaining from double-tongued speech and not abstaining from harsh speech.
Regarding not abstaining from frivolous speech:
It is either unwholesome or indeterminate:
that which arises from an unwholesome mind is unwholesome, and that which arises from an indeterminate mind is indeterminate.
It is either bound to the desire realm or bound to the form realm.
That which is bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) refers to speech that is distracted by the body and mind of the desire realm; this is what is bound to the desire realm.
The same applies to that which is bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).
The remainder is as explained in the section on false speech.
Greed and grasping:
bound to the realm of desire;
these are with outflows (sāsrava).
Mental factors (caitta-dharma) are not associated with the mind,
nor do they follow the mind.
It arises simultaneously with the mind;
it is formless and non-manifesting.
It has an object-condition,
but it is not associated with karma,
nor does it follow after karma.
It is not produced by collective karma;
it is not the retribution of past karma, except for that which arises from causes and retribution;
it is not something to be cultivated.
One should know this well;
one should realize it with wisdom and realize it with the body;
it can be abandoned.
It can be seen and known that hatred and affliction are either associated with the mind or dissociated from the mind.

Those comprised within the *paryavasthānas* (active outbursts) are called associated with the mind (*cittasaṃprayukta*); those comprised within the *anuśayas* (latent tendencies) are called dissociated from the mind (*cittaviprayukta*).
The same applies to those that follow the mind (*anuvartaka*) and those that do not follow the mind (*ananuvartaka*).
Co-arising with the mind and not co-arising with the mind:
sentient beings possessing consciousness arise together with the mind;
sentient beings lacking consciousness do not arise together with the mind.

Just as it is with that which is associated with the mind, follows the mind, and arises together with the mind, so too it is with that which is associated with karma, follows karma, and arises together with karma.

Just as it is with that which is dissociated from the mind, does not follow the mind, and does not arise together with the mind, so too it is with that which is dissociated from karma, does not follow karma, and does not arise together with karma.
The remaining conceptualizations are as explained in the section on covetous grasping.
As it is with malice and affliction, so it is with false views.
Within the ten paths of wholesome action, [the first is] abstaining from taking the lives of others:
This is of a wholesome nature.
It is either bound to the desire realm or not bound to the three realms:
that which is bound to the desire realm consists of taking the life of another with a body belonging to the desire realm; this is what is meant by being bound to the desire realm.

That which is not bound to the three realms refers to the right action of abstaining from killing, which is subsumed within the Eightfold Noble Path of those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
This is either with outflows (sāsrava) or without outflows (anāsrava):
that which is bound to the desire realm is with outflows, while that which is not bound to the three realms is without outflows.
It is not a mental factor;
it is not associated with the mind;
it does not follow the mind.
They may arise simultaneously with the mind, or they may not arise simultaneously with the mind.
What is meant by "arising simultaneously with the mind"?

For example, when a practitioner sees an insect and forms this thought: "I shall, through my bodily action, remain far removed from harming it"—this is called the wholesome practice of abstaining from taking life arising simultaneously with the mind.
What is the arising of the wholesome, uncommon mind that is free from taking life?

There may be a person whose body does not move and whose mouth does not speak, yet who in their mind thinks, "From this day forth, I shall not take life. This is called the arising of the uncommon mind.

Furthermore, there are those who have previously abstained from taking life; whether sleeping or awake, with their minds directed toward other matters, they do not kill in every moment of thought. Thus, their merit constantly increases, and it does not arise simultaneously with the mind.
Either material or non-material:
first, material; second, non-material.
First, conditioned; second, unconditioned.
First, with an object; second, without an object.
This is karma, not associated with karma.
They do not follow the course of karma;
they may arise from common karma or arise from uncommon karma—
just as there are mental states that arise from common minds or uncommon minds, with the exception that "mind" and "volition" differ.
It is not a result of prior karma, except for that which arises from causes;
it can be cultivated and can be rightly understood.
They can be realized through bodily witness or realized through wisdom.
They may be abandoned or not abandoned:
those that are with outflows (sāsrava) can be abandoned, while those that are without outflows (anāsrava) cannot be abandoned.
It should be understood that seeing is also like this.
It is the same for abstaining from stealing, abstaining from sexual misconduct, abstaining from false speech, abstaining from divisive speech, and abstaining from harsh speech.
Abstaining from frivolous speech:
it may be associated with the desire realm, associated with the form realm, or unassociated with the three realms.
That which is associated with the desire realm means that one’s body and mind within the desire realm are free from frivolous speech.
The same applies to those bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
As for those not bound to the three realms, it is as explained in the section on non-killing.
They are either with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*).
That which is with outflows (sāsrava) is bound; that which is without outflows (anāsrava) is unbound.
The rest is as explained in the section on abstaining from false speech.
Regarding "not greedily grasping":
This is of a wholesome nature.
It is either bound to the desire realm or not bound to the three realms.

That which is bound to the desire realm refers to the non-attachment and non-grasping of ordinary beings in the desire realm, as well as the wholesome conduct of non-attachment of noble ones; this is what is bound to the desire realm.
Regarding that which is not bound to the three realms: the noble ones do not greedily grasp at untainted wholesome conduct.
This [conduct] is either tainted or untainted:
that which is bound to the desire realm is tainted; that which is not bound to the three realms is untainted.
These are mental factors (caitta-dharma);
they are associated with the mind and follow the movement of the mind.
It arises simultaneously with the mind,
is formless,
and is non-manifesting.
It has an object-condition; it is not karma;
it is associated with karma.
They follow the course of karma and arise together with it;
they are not the fruition of prior karma, except for that which arises from causes.
It can be cultivated;
it can be well understood;
it can be realized by the body and realized through wisdom.
Some may be abandoned, while others cannot be abandoned:
those with outflows (*sāsrava*) can be abandoned, whereas those without outflows (*anāsrava*) cannot be abandoned.
The same applies to knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*).
Freedom from ill will is wholesome by nature;
it is either bound to the desire realm, or bound to the form realm, or bound to the formless realm, or unbound to the three realms.
Those bound to the desire realm are the wholesome roots of non-hatred and non-affliction belonging to the desire realm;
the same applies to the other two realms.
Those that are unbound are the remaining unbound [wholesome roots].
These are either with outflows (sāsrava) or without outflows (anāsrava):
those bound to the three realms are with outflows; the remainder are without outflows.
They are mental factors (caitasika-dharma).
It is either associated with the mind or dissociated from the mind:

the wholesome root of non-hatred that is contrary to the *paryavasthānas* (active outbursts) is associated with the mind; the wholesome root of non-hatred that is contrary to the *anuśayas* (latent tendencies) is dissociated from the mind.
The same applies to those that follow the mind and those that arise together with the mind.
They are formless and non-manifesting.
There are those with objects and those without objects:
that which is associated with mind has an object; that which is dissociated from mind has no object.
It is not karma.
Some are associated with karma and some are not; some follow the course of karma and some do not; some arise from common karma and some arise from uncommon karma:
this is also as explained regarding the mind.
It is not a karmic retribution, except for that which arises from causes.
It can be realized through the body and realized through wisdom. It may be severed, or it may not be severed.
That which is with outflows (sāsrava) can be abandoned; that which is without outflows (anāsrava) cannot be abandoned.
It should be known that the same applies to seeing (darśana).
Right view (samyagdṛṣṭi):
This is of a wholesome nature.
It is either bound to the desire realm, the form realm, the formless realm, or not bound to any of the three realms:
that which is bound to the desire realm refers to the right view associated with the mindfulness of those who are ordinary persons or noble ones within the desire realm.
The same applies to the realms of form and formlessness.
That which is not bound to the three realms is the untainted right view of the noble ones (ārya);
it is either tainted (sāsrava) or untainted (anāsrava).
That which is bound to the three realms is with outflows (sāsrava); that which is not bound is without outflows (anāsrava).
These are mental factors (caitasika) and are associated with the mind (citta-saṃprayukta).
It follows the mind,
arises simultaneously with the mind,
and is formless.
It is non-active,
conditioned,
and not karma.
Associated with karma,
following the course of karma,
and arising together with karma.
It is not a result of prior karma, except for that which arises from causes and retribution;
it can be realized through the body and realized through wisdom.
It may be severed, or it may be inseverable.
That which is with outflows (*sāsrava*) can be abandoned; that which is without outflows (*anāsrava*) cannot be abandoned.
That which is visible and cognizable is also like this.
These are called the twenty kinds of discrimination, beginning with "wholesome" (*kuśala*).
The twelve inquiries concerning "from what it arises" and so forth are:

first, from what does it arise; second, by whom does it arise; third, from what cause does it arise; fourth, for whom does it act as a cause; fifth, what is its condition; sixth, for whom does it act as a condition; seventh, what is its object-condition; eighth, for whom does it act as an object-condition; ninth, what is its predominant influence; tenth, for whom does it act as a predominant influence; eleventh, what is its fault; and twelfth, what is its fruit.
Regarding from what the sin of killing arises:
it arises from the three unwholesome roots;
furthermore, it arises from wrong mindfulness.
Furthermore, by whichever mind one takes the life of a living being, it arises from that mind.
As for "from whom it arises":
it arises from all phenomena associated with the transgression of killing—those already arisen, those currently arising, and those yet to arise.
The cause is thus, and the condition is likewise.
As for what is the object of focus:
it is sentient beings.
Furthermore, by what mind does one take the life of a sentient being? It is also conditioned by this very mind.
As for with what it acts as a condition:
all phenomena associated with the offense of killing—whether already arisen, presently arising, or yet to arise—these phenomena are conditioned by the offense of taking life.
What are the faults?
They include ill repute in this life, being distrusted by others, and so forth.
What are the fruits?
They fall into the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, the asuras, and other evil states, where they receive the retribution of suffering and affliction.
Regarding the "predominance" (adhipati) and with whom it is predominant:
this is as explained in the section on "from what [cause] does it arise."

It is the same for stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, divisive speech, harsh speech, idle chatter, covetousness, malice, and wrong view; they differ only in their objects: the object of the offense of stealing is the thing used;

the object of sexual misconduct is a sentient being; the objects of lying, divisive speech, harsh speech, and idle chatter are names; the object of covetousness is the thing used; the object of malice is a sentient being; and the object of wrong view is names.
The remaining points are also as above.
Abstaining from killing arises from the three roots of goodness;
it also arises from right mindfulness.
Furthermore, whichever mind one follows to abstain from taking life, it arises from that mind.
As for "from what does it arise":
it arises from all phenomena belonging to this dharma—whether they have already arisen, are currently arising, or will arise; the causes and conditions are likewise so.
As for the object of focus:
it takes sentient beings as its object.
With whom does it take as its object?
Because of this, all dharmas pertaining to the side of non-killing—whether already arisen, currently arising, or yet to arise—are conditioned by non-killing.
As for their predominance:
it is the predominance of all wholesome roots.
Right mindfulness also becomes predominant;
whatever mind one uses to refrain from taking life, that mind also becomes predominant.
With respect to whom does it become predominant?
Regarding all phenomena associated with the side of non-killing— whether they have already arisen, are currently arising, or will arise hereafter—
as for what constitutes their benefit:
that which is contrary to the transgression of killing is called "benefit."
As for "what is the fruit":
that which is contrary to killing is called the fruit.

It is the same for non-stealing, non-incestuous conduct, non-false speech, non-divisive speech, non-harsh speech, non-frivolous speech, non-covetousness, non-ill-will, and right view; they differ only in their respective objects of focus.
One does not steal objects used for their purposes;
one does not engage in sexual misconduct toward sentient beings;
and one does not speak falsely, nor use double-tongued speech, nor harsh words, nor frivolous chatter regarding names.
One does not greedily grasp at objects as conditions;
one does not harbor anger or affliction toward sentient beings as conditions;
and with right view, one takes either names or meanings as conditions.
The outflowing [consciousness] takes names as its object, while the outflow-free [consciousness] takes meanings as its object.

Regarding these twelve treatises, beginning with the *Śāstra on Goodness* and the *Śāstra on Arising*, this bodhisattva should practice the ten paths of wholesome action and understand them through such distinctions.
Furthermore,
know that the seven kinds of unwholesome states arise from greed, hatred, and delusion;
they are further analyzed by way of four gates, with two types each for karma and sentient beings.
This bodhisattva knows that the seven unwholesome paths of action arise from greed, hatred, and delusion, and thus discriminates them within the world.
Furthermore, he knows that among these seven unwholesome paths of action, there are four ways of classification.
This crime of killing arises either from greed, from hatred, or from delusion. That which arises from greed is as follows:

if a person, upon seeing a living being, gives rise to a mind of greedy attachment, and by reason of this cause and condition, seeks to enjoy fine forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles—or requires their teeth, horns, fur, skin, flesh, sinews, marrow, or bones—and because this person has given rise to such a greedy mind, they take the life of that being; this is called the crime of killing arising from greed.
If a person, with a mind of anger and displeasure, kills sentient beings, this is called killing born from hatred.
If a person holds wrong views and, not knowing the good and evil karma of future lives, kills sentient beings, this is called the offense of killing born from delusion.
Some kill for the sake of merit, or with the desire to cause others to transcend suffering, as in the case of the Western kingdom of Anxi and others;

furthermore, there are those who kill for the sake of the causal conditions of acquiring merit, desiring thereby to be reborn in heaven, such as the people of Eastern India who kill within temples dedicated to the gods, seeking to be born in the heavens through this act—this is said to arise from delusion.
Furthermore, there are those who, out of a greedy mind, take the property of others, thinking:
"By this I shall obtain at will desirable forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles. This is called arising from greed.

Furthermore, there are those who, out of a mind of hatred and because they take no pleasure in another person, plunder their wealth with the intent to cause them distress; this is said to arise from hatred.
Furthermore, there are those with wrong views who, being ignorant of the law of karmic retribution, plunder the property of others; this is said to arise from delusion.

As the various brahmins say, "All the worldly wealth and treasures are my property; because my power is weak, these petty people have taken and used them through unrighteous means. If I were to take them back, I would merely be taking my own property and there would be no fault. To plunder the property of others with such a mind is likewise born of delusion.

This is called sexual misconduct arising from hatred.
If a person holds wrong views and intentionally commits it without understanding the karmic retribution, this is called [sexual misconduct] arising from delusion.
For example, as someone might say:
“Among human beings, there is no such thing as sexual misconduct. Why is this?
Women are born for the sake of men, just like any other object of utility; if one engages with her as required, there is no offense of sexual misconduct.”
To engage in sexual desire with such a mind is said to arise from delusion (*moha*).
As it is with the offense of theft, so it is with false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*):
to speak falsely for the sake of coveting wealth is said to arise from greed (*lobha*).
Speaking falsely with the desire to deceive others and cause them suffering is called arising from hatred.
Speaking falsely because of wrong views and ignorance regarding the karmic retribution of actions is called arising from delusion.
The same applies to divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous speech.
These three unwholesome paths are the roots; from them arise the seven kinds of karmic fruits of body and speech through further differentiation.
Question:
Is everything that does not abstain from killing the offense of killing?
Or, is everything that is the offense of killing necessarily not abstaining from killing?
Answer:
