There are cases where not abstaining from taking life constitutes the offense of killing, and there are cases where not abstaining from taking life does not constitute the offense of killing.
What is it that, when one does not abstain from taking life, constitutes the offense of killing?

If there are sentient beings who, knowing them to be sentient beings, intentionally kill and take their lives, thereby initiating bodily action (kāyakarman), this is called not being free from killing and constitutes the offense of killing.
What is it that constitutes not being separated from the taking of life, yet not incurring the offense of killing?
It is when a person has previously created the causes and conditions for killing, yet sentient beings do not die.
Furthermore:

If one does not move the body nor speak with the mouth, but merely thinks in the mind, "From this day forth, I shall kill sentient beings," this is called not being separated from killing; it is not, however, the actual offense of killing.
This twofold classification is further divided into four types of discrimination, namely, two each for the wholesome and the unwholesome.
Not only regarding the wholesome and the unwholesome, one should also know that there are two types of karma—
bodily and mental— and furthermore, there are other classifications as well.

Excluding bodily acts of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct, the remaining acts—such as beating, binding, confining, tethering, whipping, flogging, dragging, and pulling—which do not result in death, are likewise unwholesome bodily karma, though they are not subsumed under the category of taking life and so forth.

Wholesome bodily actions such as welcoming and seeing off, joining the palms, prostrating, showing respect, inquiring after one's well-being, bathing, massaging, and giving alms are not subsumed under [the precept of] abstaining from killing and so forth.

Within mental karma, excluding covetousness, malice, and wrong views, there are all other unwholesome factors such as the failure to restrain and collect the mind, as well as the various fetters and latent tendencies.
Furthermore!

Within mental karma, excluding non-covetousness, non-ill will, and right view, there are the remaining wholesome factors that guard and collect the mind: faith, ethical discipline, learning, concentration, equanimity, wisdom, and other such wholesome dharmas.
Seven courses of action are also actions; three courses of action are not actions.
Killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and idle chatter—these seven are both actions and courses of action.
Greed, malice, and wrong view are paths of action, not action itself.
The volition associated with these three factors is action.
Question:
Why are the first seven matters both karma and paths of karma? Answer:
Because the practice of these seven matters increases further and further, leading to rebirth in the hells, as animals, or as hungry ghosts, they are called "paths of karma" (*karmapatha*);
because these seven are capable of performing [actions], they are called "karma" (*karman*).
The third category consists of those that are paths of action (*karmapatha*) but not actions (*karman*):
these are the roots of unwholesome karma, and for this reason they are called the three paths of action rather than actions themselves.
It is the same regarding the wholesome: namely, abstaining from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and idle chatter.
It is both karma and a path of action (*karmapatha*).
As for the remaining three— non-covetousness, non-ill will, and right view—
they are paths of action, but not karma.
These three associated volitions (cetanā) are karma.
Question:
Why are the preceding seven matters both karma and paths of action (karmapatha)?
Answer: Because one constantly cultivates these matters and is thereby able to reach the excellent realms of humans and devas, it is called the Path (*mārga*).
Because these seven are capable of producing results, they are called karma (*karman*).
Question:
Why are the other three only paths of action (*karmapatha*), and not actions (*karman*) themselves? Answer:
Third, it is the root of all wholesome karmas; because all wholesome karmas proceed from within it, it is called a "path of karma" (*karmapatha*), yet it is not itself karma.
Furthermore: The dharma of precepts is itself karma; Karma may be precepts, or it may not be precepts.
Regarding karma and the paths of action, there are fourfold distinctions.
Bodily and verbal karma constitute ethical discipline (śīla).
Mental action (*manas-karman*): this is action, but not discipline (*śīla*).
Regarding the fourfold classification of both action and the paths of action (*karmapatha*):
There is karma that is not a path of action; there is a path of action that is not karma; there is karma that is also a path of action; and there is that which is neither karma nor a path of action.
Regarding karma that is not a path of action:
it refers to the three types of unwholesome bodily karma not subsumed under the paths of action, namely those involving the hand, the fist, the whip, the staff, and so forth.

Furthermore, there are three types of wholesome bodily karma not subsumed under the courses of action (*karmapatha*), namely: going out to meet, paying respects, and so forth. These two—wholesome and unwholesome karma—are not included within the courses of action.
Some may say: "These are also courses of action (karmapatha). Why?
Because these two types of karma sometimes lead to good or evil destinations; therefore, they are called courses of action."
"Because they are indeterminate, they are not called courses of action (karmapatha).
Courses of action that are not actions are:
the last three unwholesome [courses] and the three wholesome [courses]."
Because these are of the nature of afflictions, they are not karma;
because they can give rise to karma, they are called "paths of action" (karmapatha).
The three wholesome [roots] are of the nature of wholesome roots, and thus are not karma.
Because they are capable of giving rise to wholesome karma, they are called "paths of action" (*karmapatha*).
Those that are both karma and paths of action are the seven matters, namely: killing and non-killing, and so forth.
That which is neither karma nor a path of karma refers to other dharmas.
At the threshold of the Bodhisattva’s first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), by means of the threefold purity, [one attains it].
Abiding securely in the ten paths of wholesome action, one then gives rise to a mind of certainty.
Thus, within the second stage, this bodhisattva clearly discerns and knows these ten wholesome and ten unwholesome paths.
Having understood this, one dwells in the ten paths of wholesome action through three kinds of purity:
namely, not killing oneself, not commanding others to kill, and having no joy in the offense of killing;
and so it continues up to right view, which is likewise.
Question:
Since the bodhisattva has already abided in the ten paths of wholesome action within the first stage (*bhūmi*), why are they stated again here? Answer:

In the first stage (*bhūmi*), it is not that one does not abide in the ten paths of wholesome action; rather, it is here that they are further enhanced and increased by means of the three kinds of purity.

Although one may have acted as a king of Jambudvīpa while in the initial dwelling, one was unable to practice these three kinds of purity; therefore, it is said here that the Bodhisattva abides in this second stage by means of the three kinds of purity.
Knowing that such various karmas are thus differentiated, one gives rise to a resolute mind:
"All evil realms in the world arise from the ten unwholesome actions;
all wholesome realms in the world arise because of the ten wholesome actions."
All the evil realms in the world are as follows:
namely, the three types of hell realms—the hot hells, the cold hells, and the black hells;
and the three types of animal realms—animals that move in water, animals that move on land, and animals that move through the air.

Among the various paths of the hungry ghosts, there are those who are hungry ghosts, those who eat impurities, those with mouths of fire, as well as asuras, yakṣas, and others—all of whom arise from practicing the ten unwholesome paths due to superior, middling, and inferior causes and conditions.
All the wholesome paths of the supramundane—whether those of devas or humans—are born from practicing the ten wholesome paths and are subsumed within the three realms.
As for the devas, there are twenty-eight;
as for humans, they are the people of the four continents.
Having thus gained certain knowledge, one forms this thought:
"I desire to be born myself in a good destination, and I shall also cause other beings to be born in good destinations.
For this reason, I ought personally to abide in the ten paths of wholesome action.
I shall also cause other sentient beings to abide immediately in this path of goodness.
Whether born in a favorable realm or an unfavorable realm, all belong to either the ten paths of wholesome action or the ten paths of unwholesome action;

I know that these worldly phenomena exist through the causes and conditions of karma, and there is no fixed master over them. Therefore, I should first practice the ten paths of wholesome action myself, and only then cause all sentient beings to likewise abide in the ten paths of wholesome action.
Question:
For what reason must one first establish oneself in the ten paths of wholesome action before causing others to do so?
Answer:
One who practices evil deeds makes it difficult for others to practice what is good;
because they do not practice goodness themselves, others will not believe or accept them.
If an evil person does not practice goodness themselves yet wishes to cause others to practice goodness, that is exceedingly difficult.
Why is this? Because such a person does not practice virtue themselves, others do not trust or accept their words.
As a verse says:
If a person is not themselves virtuous, they cannot cause others to be virtuous;
if they are not themselves at peace, they cannot cause others to be at peace.
For this reason, you should first practice virtue and tranquility yourself.
Thereafter, one teaches others, causing them to practice wholesome quiescence.
This bodhisattva should thus practice wholesome dharmas,
from the Avīci Hell up to the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra).
One should discern the ten types of karmic fruits and the places where their retribution is experienced.

One should understand correctly in this way: from the Avīci Hell below up to the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception above, all are places where the various fruits of wholesome and unwholesome karma are received.
Because one habitually practices the ten unwholesome paths therein, one is born in the Avīci Hell; if [the practice] is slightly diminished, one is born in the Mahāraurava Hell;

if slightly diminished further, one is born in the Raurava Hell; if slightly diminished further, one is born in the Mahārauta Hell; if slightly diminished further, one is born in the Kālasūtra Hell; if slightly diminished further, one is born in the Saṃghāta Hell; if slightly diminished further, one is born in the Mahāpatha Hell; if slightly diminished further, one is born in the Kālasūtra Hell; if slightly diminished further, one is born in the Sañjīva Hell; and if slightly diminished further, one is born in the minor subsidiary hells such as the Sword Forest (Asipatravana). One should likewise apply this same principle of differentiation to the lesser degrees of diminution.
Practicing the ten unwholesome paths of action leads to birth among animals;
even among animals, there should be a slight degree of discrimination.
Practicing the lower unwholesome paths leads to birth among hungry ghosts.
Thus has it been stated in general terms; herein, the distinctions should be analyzed in detail:
there are certain asuras, yakṣas, and those born in the realm of pretas who, while others such as nāga kings are born among animals, experience pleasures equal to those of the devas.
These sentient beings are born due to unwholesome causes and conditions, yet once born, they receive the retribution of wholesome karma.

Practicing the ten paths of wholesome action to the lowest degree, one is born among humans in Jambudvīpa, but in a poor and lowly household—such as those of the Caṇḍālas, border-dwellers, artisans, or commoners.

He is reborn into an increasingly superior householder family, an increasingly superior brahmin family, an increasingly superior kṣatriya family, an increasingly superior minister’s family, and an increasingly superior royal family.

Those who are increasingly superior in the ten paths of wholesome action are reborn in Godānīya; those who are further superior are reborn in Pūrvavideha; those who are further superior are reborn in Uttarakuru.

Those who are further superior are reborn among the Four Great Kings; those who are further superior are reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, and the Nirmāṇarati Heaven.
By practicing the ten paths of wholesome action to a superior degree, one is born in the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations.
Within this, there should also be various distinctions of small and great differences, such as among humans:
minor kings, great kings, kings of Jambudvīpa, and wheel-turning sage-kings (cakravartin).

In the realm of the Four Great Kings dwell the Four Great Kings; among the Trāyastriṃśa gods is Śakra Devānām Indra; above the Yāma heaven is the Yāma Heavenly King; above the Tuṣita heaven is the Saṃtuṣita Heavenly King; above the Nirmāṇarati heaven is the Sunirmita Heavenly King; and above the Paranirmita-vaśavartin heaven is the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heavenly King.
Beyond this, one must practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and contemplation (*cintā*) in order to be born in the higher realms.
Question:

If it is by means of meditative concentration and contemplation that one is born in the higher realms, why is it said that "even up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), birth therein is attained through the ten paths of wholesome action (*daśakuśalakarmapatha*)"?
Answer:

Although one may cultivate meditative concentration (dhyāna) to be reborn in the form realm or the formless realm, one must first firmly abide in the ten paths of wholesome action before being able to cultivate meditative concentration.
For this reason, in those realms, the ten paths of wholesome action constitute a great benefit.
Therefore it is said:
"Up to and including the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, all are born there by means of the causes and conditions of the ten paths of wholesome action."

Why is this? First, one practices the ten paths of wholesome action with purity and detachment from desire. By cultivating the lower degree of thought in the first dhyāna, one attains birth in the Heaven of the Brahma-multitude; by cultivating the middle degree of thought in the first dhyāna, one is born in the Heaven of the Brahma-purohitas;

and by cultivating the superior degree of thought in the first dhyāna, one attains birth in the Great Brahma Heaven. By cultivating the lower degree of thought in the second dhyāna, one is born in the Heaven of Limited Light; by cultivating the middle degree of thought in the second dhyāna, one attains birth in the Heaven of Infinite Light; and by cultivating the superior degree of thought in the second dhyāna, one attains birth in the Heaven of Splendid Light.

By cultivating the lower degree of thought within the third dhyāna, one is reborn in the Heaven of Limited Purity; by cultivating the middle degree of thought within the third dhyāna, one is reborn in the Heaven of Immeasurable Purity; and by cultivating the upper degree of thought within the third dhyāna, one is reborn in the Heaven of Universal Purity.

By cultivating the lower degree of thought within the fourth dhyāna, one is reborn in the Ānabhraka Heaven; by cultivating the middle degree of thought within the fourth dhyāna, one is reborn in the Puṇyaprasava Heaven; and by cultivating the upper degree of thought within the fourth dhyāna, one is reborn in the Bṛhatphala Heaven. By cultivating the thought of the state of non-perception, one is reborn in the Heaven of Non-perception.

By cultivating the four dhyānas with untainted (anāsrava) inferior reflection, one is born in the Apramāṇaśubha Heaven; by cultivating the four dhyānas with untainted superior reflection, one is born in the Apramāṇābha Heaven; by cultivating the four dhyānas with untainted superior reflection, one is born in the Parīttaśubha Heaven; by cultivating the four dhyānas with untainted superior reflection, one is born in the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven; and by cultivating the four dhyānas with untainted supreme reflection, one is born in the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.

Cultivating volition associated with the meditative concentration of the sphere of infinite space leads to rebirth in the heaven of the sphere of infinite space; cultivating volition associated with the meditative concentration of the sphere of infinite consciousness leads to rebirth in the heaven of the sphere of infinite consciousness; cultivating volition associated with the meditative concentration of the sphere of nothingness leads to rebirth in the heaven of the sphere of nothingness; and cultivating volition associated with the meditative concentration of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception leads to rebirth in the heaven of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. These are called the world of birth and death, the place where sentient beings come and go.
Chapter 29: Distinguishing the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas. Question:
These ten paths of wholesome action are merely the causes and conditions for birth as humans or devas; are there further benefits besides these?
Answer: There are.
All those belonging to the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the Mahāyāna.
All derive great benefit from the ten paths of wholesome action.
Regarding the causes and conditions for escaping birth and death, there are only three vehicles:
the Śrāvaka, the Pratyekabuddha, and the Mahāyāna.
These three vehicles all take the ten paths of wholesome action as their great benefit. Why is this?

These ten paths of wholesome action can cause a practitioner to reach the stage of a śrāvaka, can also cause them to reach the stage of a pratyekabuddha, and can also cause them to reach the stage of a Buddha.
Question: By means of these ten paths of wholesome action, what kind of sentient beings can be led to the stage of a śrāvaka? Answer:
Lacking great compassion for others, they fear the three realms;
delighting in a mere fraction of merit, their resolve is exceedingly weak.
Their hearts take pleasure in renunciation, constantly contemplating the impermanence of the world.
And knowing that all phenomena are likewise devoid of self,
even for the duration of a single thought-moment, they take no delight in rebirth;
they constantly lack faith in any worldly dharma that offers true peace and security.
One views the great [elements] as venomous snakes, the aggregates as thieves with drawn swords, and the six sense bases as an empty village; thus one finds no delight in worldly riches.
It is more noble to firmly uphold the precepts for the sake of meditative concentration.
Always delighting in peaceful meditation, practicing all wholesome dharmas,
contemplating only nirvana as the supreme refuge,
constantly seeking the wisdom that exhausts suffering, and joyfully accumulating the practices for liberation.
Valuing only self-benefit, they come from various superior states;
yet these wholesome paths can only lead such persons to the stage of a śrāvaka.
Those who follow the voices of others hear what is spoken by another and act in accordance with it, unable to generate wisdom on their own.
Question:
Do the ten paths of wholesome action cause all those who hear them from others to become śrāvakas?
Answer: No.
Not so! If one lacks the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), the ten paths of wholesome action can cause that person to reach the stage of a *śrāvaka*;

however, if there is a bodhisattva who has heard the Dharma from the Buddhas, because they possess the mind of great compassion, the ten paths of wholesome action cannot cause them to reach the stage of a *śrāvaka*.
Question:
For all those who lack the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), can the ten paths of wholesome action (*daśakuśalakarmapatha*) lead them to the stage of a śrāvaka?
Answer:
Not so! For those who fear the three realms, the ten paths of wholesome action can lead such persons to the path of the śrāvakas.
As for others who do not fear them, because they delight in the three realms, these practices cause them to be born in the good destinations of humans and devas.
Question: It is said that for all who fear the three realms, the ten paths of wholesome action can lead them to the stage of a śrāvaka.

If this is so, then bodhisattvas also fear the three realms; yet, for the sake of their own bodies and for the sake of sentient beings, they practice with diligent effort and seek nirvāṇa. In such a case, these ten paths of wholesome action should likewise lead them to the stage of a śrāvaka.
Answer: It is not necessarily the case that all who fear the three realms fall into the stage of the śrāvaka.
What constitutes "falling"?

Regarding those who delight in practicing even a small portion of the meritorious qualities: among the six *pāramitās* taught by the Buddha, they practice only a small portion; such persons fall into the stage of the *śrāvaka*.
If a person can grasp the merits of all Buddhas and universally study their wisdom, the ten paths of wholesome action will surely cause this person to proceed directly to the path of Buddhahood.
There are two types of persons who, having heard the voice of another, become terrified of the three realms and grasp only a small portion of merit:
those who, by means of the ten paths of wholesome action, reach the stage of a śrāvaka, and those who reach the stage of a pratyekabuddha.
Question:

How is it that these people, having heard from others in both cases, fear the three realms and grasp a small portion of merit, yet through the ten paths of wholesome action are able to reach the stage of a śrāvaka or the stage of a pratyekabuddha?
The answer is:
those of inferior and weak resolve become arhats;
those of slight firmness become pratyekabuddhas.
Question:
Do the ten paths of wholesome action cause all those of inferior and weak resolve to reach the stage of a śrāvaka?
Answer: [They do.]
Not so! Why is this? It is because their resolve is weak, and they delight in wearying themselves of and seeking escape from birth and death.
It is not only those of inferior resolve who lack the mind of weary detachment (*nirveda*). Question:
By observing what thing can one know that the mind delights in weary detachment?
Answer:
One who contemplates that "conditioned phenomena are impermanent" and "all phenomena are without self" should be known as one who necessarily delights in wearying detachment.
Question:

Having already known joy and developed weary detachment, the Bodhisattva likewise contemplates that "conditioned phenomena are impermanent and all dharmas are without self. Why, then, would these ten paths of wholesome action not cause such a person to fall into the stage of a Śrāvaka?
The answer is:

Because this person is profoundly weary and detached, and lacks great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), they do not delight in taking birth even for a single thought-moment, nor do they believe that there is any state of peace and security within the world.
As the Buddha told the bhikṣus in a sutra:
"For example, even a small amount of excrement is foul-smelling and impure, how much more so a large amount?
In this same way, birth within a single thought-moment is already suffering, how much more so many such births?"
"O Bhikṣus! You should train yourselves to sever rebirth, so that you shall not undergo it again.
Because the śrāvakas accepted these words with faith, they did not take pleasure in undergoing rebirth for even a single thought-moment.
This person further reflects:
"The world is impermanent; in all that one does and in the life one receives, there is no sign of security at all.
Death constantly pursues one; who can know the timing of death?"
One does not know at the time of death what karmic retribution will be received,
nor what state of mind will arise;
because such matters are unstable and unreliable, one should swiftly seek the exhaustion of suffering.

The Bodhisattva, however, is not like that; for the sake of attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and delivering all sentient beings, they undergo birth throughout immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Therefore, it is said in the verse:
"Even for the duration of a single thought-moment, one does not delight in rebirth"—this wholesome path enables such a person to reach the stage of a Śrāvaka.
Question:
For what reason does this person delight in cultivating and accumulating [merit], yet not delight in taking birth? Answer:

This person contemplates the four great elements—earth, water, fire, and wind—and because they give rise to joy, anger, and resentment; because they are impure, foul-smelling, and filthy; and because they do not know gratitude, one conceives of them as being like venomous snakes.

Regarding the five aggregates—form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—one should conceive of them as hostile robbers, for they are capable of robbing one of the life-force of wisdom.

Regarding the six sense bases—eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—one should conceive of them as an empty village, for they are devoid of permanence, and lack a self, a mine of self, being immovable, unchanging, and indestructible.

If a person, regarding all births in the world and the enjoyments that sustain life, does not give rise to a mind of delight because they are impermanent, deceptive, and do not abide for even a moment;
Such a person, in all places of birth, conceives no sense of security; only the single dharma of nirvāṇa can provide protection.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"O Bhikṣus!..."
The entire world is ablaze. That is to say:
the eye is ablaze, forms are ablaze, eye-consciousness is ablaze, eye-contact is ablaze, and the feeling born of the condition of eye-contact is likewise ablaze.
For what reason is this so?

It is because they are ablaze with the fire of greed, the fire of hatred, and the fire of delusion; they are set aflame by the fires of birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair.
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
One should contemplate that all conditioned phenomena are ablaze, and that only the dharma of the quiescent extinction of nirvana can provide protection and refuge.
"Because they value the single dharma of nirvāṇa, they abandon all worldly affairs and diligently practice seated meditation.

Question: If it is said that "one contemplates all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) as being ablaze, and that only the tranquility of nirvāṇa can provide protection," then do the ten paths of wholesome action lead only to the stage of a śrāvaka?
Answer: It is not so!
The precepts established by the Buddha are for the sake of meditative concentration; therefore, these precepts are held in high esteem.
Possessing a resolute mind, they do not transgress their precepts; they renounce all worldly affairs and take sole delight in sitting meditation.
Seeking the wisdom that exhausts suffering, they constantly and diligently cultivate the causes and conditions for liberation.
In previous lives, those who have come from one superior state or two superior states can, through the ten paths of wholesome action, reach the stage of a śrāvaka.
Why is this? Because when one's observance of the precepts is pure, the mind has no regret;
because the mind has no regret, one attains joy.
Because one attains joy, the body becomes light and supple;
because the body is light and supple, the mind experiences happiness;
because the mind experiences happiness, one gathers the mind and attains concentration.
Because the mind is gathered and concentration is attained, there arises wisdom that accords with reality;
because wisdom that accords with reality arises, there arises disenchantment;
from disenchantment arises detachment, and from detachment one attains liberation.
Whether one or two have come from a state of excellence (*abhibhvāyatana*): such as the Venerable Rāhula, who has come from the state of excellence of the Truths (*satya*);
the Venerable Śivaka, who has come from the state of excellence of Equanimity (*upekṣā*);
and the Venerable Revata, who has come from the state of excellence of Cessation (*nirvāṇa*).
Just as the Venerable Śāriputra has come from a superior state of wisdom,
or from the two superior states of truth and relinquishment,
or from the two superior states of truth and cessation;
Either from the two superior stations of truth and wisdom;
or from the two superior stations of equanimity and cessation;
or from the two superior stations of equanimity and wisdom.
Or they may come from the two superior stations of tranquility and wisdom.
These ten paths of wholesome action can lead one to the stage of a śrāvaka.
*Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle 14.
*Daśabhūmivibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle Fifteen.
Composed by the Venerable Nāgārjuna;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty.
The remainder of the Chapter on the Distinction between Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas. Question:
By what kind of person are the ten paths of wholesome action brought to the stage of a pratyekabuddha? Answer:
Regarding the conduct of the śrāvakas, they excel in the ten paths of wholesome action;
deep in dhyāna, they do not follow others, and always delight in seclusion.
They constantly enjoy the diligent cultivation of the profound law of dependent origination.
Far removed from the power of skillful means and the mind of great compassion;
possessing few desires and few concerns, they loathe and despise clamorous speech;
always delighting in secluded places, they are persons of profound and heavy majestic virtue.
Delighting in the ground of the field of merit, constantly contemplating the nature of emergence,
accomplishing matters that accord with principle, and showing reverence to all masters;
having already achieved the binding of the mind, knowing the mind as it abides upon its objects.
Always delighting in meditative concentration, possessing the strength of a person of middle capacity,
and rejoicing in the way of renunciation, their virtuous mind does not shrink or sink away.
Those who have attained the light of wisdom do so either from one of two superior states.
Or, coming from the three superior stations, the ten paths of wholesome action can cause such a person to reach the stage of a pratyekabuddha.

Regarding those who practice the ten wholesome paths more excellently than the conduct of śrāvakas, they surpass the ten wholesome paths practiced by śrāvakas, yet they do not equal those practiced by bodhisattvas.
He formed this thought:
"The śrāvakas should follow what they hear from others to practice the Path, and only thereafter attain self-realized wisdom.
I am not like that; I do not delight in following others."
For this reason, I should cause the ten paths of wholesome action to become even more excellent.
By these causes and conditions, I delight in not following others; it is the ten paths of wholesome action that lead me to the stage of a Pratyekabuddha.
Having reflected thus, he constantly delights in seclusion.
He forms this thought:
"If I were to constantly delight in bustle and clamor, I would be accumulating various evil and unwholesome states, because of being near to things that can provoke lust, anger, and delusion."
"Therefore, amidst this seclusion, one should cultivate the profound law of dependent origination.
He further thought:
"If I do not cultivate the profound law of dependent origination, I shall inevitably fail to follow the wisdom of others."
"Why is it that I do not now constantly cultivate the profound principle of dependent origination, after which I may attain knowledge that does not rely on others?
"Profound" means its bottom is difficult to reach and it cannot be fully penetrated.

All ordinary beings, throughout the beginningless cycle of birth and death, may reach the limits of all secular scriptures and their various arts and crafts; however, they cannot fathom the depths of the profound principle of dependent origination.
Just as small insects such as rabbits cannot reach the bottom of the great ocean,
if a person possesses skillful means, a mind of great compassion, and cultivates and accumulates profound causes and conditions, they will attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
If one is free from these two matters and cultivates the profound wisdom of dependent origination, one becomes a pratyekabuddha.
"Skillful means" refers to not erring in various reflections while accomplishing the teaching and transformation of sentient beings, and likewise not grasping at signs regarding the profound Dharma.
Great compassion means having profound pity for sentient beings; it surpasses that of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, let alone that of ordinary people!
Having few desires and few affairs, and loathing clamorous speech—by such means one attains the stage of a pratyekabuddha.

If one possesses great aspiration, great undertakings, and a fondness for gathering people, and is protected by skillful means and great compassion, then Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi will be easy to attain.
Why is this? Those who seek the state of a pratyekabuddha and possess few desires form this thought:
"I shall deliver myself alone."
Regarding "having few affairs": it means "one merely accomplishes one's own roots of goodness, but does not extend to others.
Because such a person has abandoned the task of teaching and transforming sentient beings, they do not associate with crowds and bustle.
The Bodhisattva possesses great aspiration and a great task, forming this thought:
"I should deliver all sentient beings.
By virtue of these causes and conditions of great aspiration, he performs the great task of teaching and transforming sentient beings.
To transform sentient beings is no small matter; if one loathes clamor and noisy speech, this task will not be accomplished.
Therefore, a bodhisattva enters into the midst of clamor and employs the speech of the clamorous, yet remains entirely without attachment.
Furthermore, to conceal one's true merits is called having few desires;
to have few affairs is termed having few concerns.
To loathe and despise clamor and bustle is called having few desires.
Because they delight in dwelling alone, they are said to have few affairs.
Such persons have few desires and few affairs, and do not delight in the clamor of crowds.
They delight in approaching places that are secluded, formidable, and profound; their minds are deep and vast.
This person thinks:
"If I dwell in a place that is secluded, fearsome, and deep, people will not come.
Because he dwells in such a secluded place, his mind also becomes profound and far-reaching.
If a person is not deeply settled within themselves and delights in playful diversion, it will not be difficult for outsiders to come and go.
Such a person does not form attachments with sentient beings; although they relinquish them, they still desire to cause sentient beings to plant various roots of goodness as a great benefit.
They form this thought:
"How might I not associate with sentient beings and yet still be able to benefit them?
Having reflected thus and understood the truth, [he thought: "I shall act as a field of merit for sentient beings and accept their offerings;
in this way, although I do not associate with sentient beings, I can still bring about great benefit."
This person further reflects:
"How shall I obtain a ground of merit?
He then perceives and knows for himself:

"If I deeply delight in being a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), and constantly contemplate the nature of transcendence (*niḥsaraṇa*), then the qualities of a field of merit will come forth spontaneously;
even the dharmas of the nature of transcendence will likewise come forth spontaneously—namely:
ethical discipline (*śīla*), meditative concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and so forth."
Again, he formed this thought:
"How may I swiftly reach the ground of the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) and the qualities of emergence (*nairyāṇika-dharma*)?

I shall become one who practices right contemplation, fully accomplishing all matters within the realms of manifest principle and phenomena, and making offerings to and honoring the masters—thus, the ground of the field of merit and the qualities of emergence shall be swiftly attained before long."
"Why is this? Because I shall accomplish what is reasonable, correctly contemplate all phenomena, and attain knowledge that does not depend on others.
Furthermore, by making offerings to and honoring the masters, my roots of goodness will increase and thicken."
Because the roots of goodness are thickened, wisdom becomes profound;
because wisdom is profound, one is able to penetrate the reality of things;
because one is able to penetrate the reality of things, one is able to give rise to disenchantment.

From revulsion arises detachment; from detachment one attains liberation. Because of attaining liberation, the roots of goodness accumulated previously and subsequently become fields of merit, and thereafter one realizes the dharma of the nature of transcendence.
"O lords, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones,
are the greatest causes and conditions at the time when one plants these various roots of goodness.
This person then reflects further:
"How can I quickly accomplish the state of one who acts with reason?
This person then knows and sees for themselves:
"If I collect and bind my mind to a single point, knowing its object, I shall always delight in meditative concentration."
If this person can bind the mind to a single point, they will be able to attain samādhi.
Because they have attained samādhi, all matters—both principle and phenomena—can be accomplished.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"One who has attained meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) is able to know things as they truly are and see them as they truly are.
If a person practices by binding the mind, they will swiftly enter into samādhi.
Because they swiftly enter into samādhi, they are called one who possesses meditative concentration and one who is constantly concentrated."
If one can thus cultivate and assemble all dharmas, that constitutes making offerings to and honoring all Buddhas.
If a person offers incense, flowers, or the four requisites to a Buddha, it is not called making an offering to a Buddha.
If one can be single-minded and free from negligence, drawing near to and cultivating the Noble Path, this is called making offerings to and revering all Buddhas.
As it is said in a Sūtra:
"At the time of his Parinirvāṇa, the Buddha told Ānanda:"
Even if the heavens rain down mandārava flowers and sandalwood powder incense, and celestial music is performed, this would not be called making offerings to or revering the Tathāgata, Ānanda!
If bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, with single-mindedness and without negligence, draw near to and cultivate the noble Dharma, this is called truly making offerings to the Buddha.
"Therefore, Ānanda,
you should practice and learn the true供养 (pūjā) of the Buddha.
Such manifold merits as these all belong to those of middling power.
Those who delight in leaving the household life and whose virtuous minds do not shrink or sink possess the supreme power and are able to attain Buddhahood;
those with inferior power become śrāvakas;
for this reason, those with middling power become pratyekabuddhas.
Because one delights in leaving the household life, one is able to accomplish manifold merits. Why is this?
If one remains in the household, one cannot have few desires and few affairs; one cannot achieve physical and mental seclusion, nor can one attain meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

If the mind is contracted and lacks purity, one will be unable to accomplish various tasks, unable to understand the profound law of dependent origination, unable to realize the nature of transcendence, and unable to make true offerings and show reverence to the Buddhas in accordance with the Dharma.
Sentient beings with such middling power form this thought:
"I am a person of middling power; I always delight in leaving the household life, and my mind does not shrink or sink."
"All matters of merit and aspiration will come to me spontaneously.
He further reflected:
"What fruit does this power seek to obtain?"
One should know that the fruit of wisdom will then be attained. Why is this?
Because wisdom is able to provide illumination.
As it is said in the Sūtra: "O Bhikṣus!
Among all lights, the light of wisdom is supreme."
Again, he thought:
"How shall I obtain the light of wisdom that I delight in?
He immediately knew that it would come from either two or three bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
The two bases of mastery have already been explained previously.
As for the three bases of mastery, they are: truth, equanimity, and cessation;
or alternatively, truth, equanimity, and wisdom.
Or [the truths], cessation, and wisdom.
For this reason, I shall cultivate and accumulate such sublime bases.
Having cultivated and accumulated these, I shall attain the radiance of wisdom.
The wisdom one aspires to arrives spontaneously.

For one who thus possesses such characteristics and thus cultivates and accumulates the factors conducive to the path, the ten paths of wholesome action can lead them to the stage of a pratyekabuddha.
Chapter Thirty: The Mahāyāna Chapter. Question:

As you have already stated, the ten paths of wholesome action can cause people to reach the stages of Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha; by what further means do these ten paths of wholesome karma cause sentient beings to reach the stage of a Buddha?
The answer is:
Those who practice the ten paths of wholesome action surpass two kinds of people;
practicing them immeasurably and rarely, they surpass all the world.
They give rise to two firm and wholesome vows, accomplishing great compassion free from obstruction.
Skillfully receiving and practicing expedient means, they endure all forms of suffering and affliction.
Never abandoning any sentient beings, they cherish the wisdom of all Buddhas deeply.
In the sovereign power of the Buddha, those who delight in practicing to the very end;
Who can shatter the mind of false views, cherish and protect the Buddha’s True Dharma,
Are robust and capable of receiving diligence, and with firm resolve transform sentient beings.
Not craving for one's own pleasure, nor for an immeasurable life-span,
supreme among all things, one’s actions are free from fault.
Pure in every respect, one comes from all places of excellence.
The wholesome path leads this person to the World-Honored One of Ten Powers.
Regarding the ten wholesome paths practiced by the Bodhisattva, they are far superior to those of the two types of persons who seek the state of a Śrāvaka or a Pratyekabuddha.

As for "progressively superior," it refers to practicing with a single-minded focus, practicing constantly, practicing for one's own benefit, practicing for the benefit of others, and practicing with purity.
The practitioner of single-mindedness applies their intent to cultivation;
the constant practitioner does not rest midway.
Those who practice for the sake of self-benefit create the causes and conditions for rebirth among devas or humans, as well as the causes and conditions for *nirvāṇa*.
For those who practice for the benefit of others, the Bodhisattva practices the ten paths of wholesome action in order to dedicate [the merit] toward the benefit and peace of all sentient beings.
By reason of these causes and conditions, he is able to deliver more sentient beings than can be calculated by number.
The practitioner of pure conduct practices without corruption, without admixture, without turbidity, with mastery, with fullness, and without attachment—conduct praised by the wise.
"Corrupt" refers to practicing [the precepts] at times and not practicing them at others; the opposite of this is called "unimpaired conduct.
"Mixed" refers to not performing [the practice] oneself but causing others to do so; the opposite of this is called "unmixed conduct."
"Turbid" refers to acting in conjunction with afflictions and sinful karma; that which is contrary to this is called "unturbid conduct.
Regarding "sovereignty": one who violates the precepts is bound by fields, wives, children, and wealth, and thus lacks sovereignty;
one who upholds the precepts has no such concerns, enjoying sovereignty according to their will, free from all attachments.

To be "fully endowed" means to practice all precepts, both great and small, to restrain all afflictions, and to constantly maintain mindfulness and protection; to serve as the causal condition for meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), to dedicate [the merit] toward the Buddha-way, and to be able to cause [the practitioner] to accord with the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). This is called being fully endowed.
"Non-attachment" means not turning toward the world and not grasping at the marks of precepts to exalt oneself and disparage others.
"Praised by the wise" means that within the Dharma of the Śrāvakas, one does not follow saṃsāra but acts solely for the sake of nirvāṇa; thus it is called "praised by the wise.
In this Mahāyāna Dharma, one does not even dedicate [merit] toward the vehicles of the Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha, much less toward saṃsāra!
To direct oneself solely toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is what is called the ten paths of wholesome action praised by the wise.
Question: What characteristics does cultivation possess to be called "well-cultivated"?
Answer:
By practicing the ten paths of wholesome action in an immeasurable and rare manner, one surpasses all the world; this is called "skillful cultivation.
Question:
How does a bodhisattva, by means of this cultivation, surpass all the world?
The answer is:
because bodhisattvas cultivate through five matters, they surpass all the world.
First, aspiration; second, firm resolve; third, profound mind; fourth, excellent purity; fifth, skillful means. Regarding aspiration:
it is the aspiration practiced by Bodhisattvas, which is not possessed by any ordinary persons, nor by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
For this reason, the aspiration practiced by Bodhisattvas surpasses all that of the world.
As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, in the "Questions of the Daughter Vimaladattā," the Buddha spoke on account of Maudgalyāyana:

"From the first generation of the aspiration until reaching the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), a bodhisattva can serve as a field of merit for all the gods and humans of the world, and moreover, surpasses all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas."
Furthermore, as stated in the *Viniścaya-vibhaṅga*, Mahākāśyapa spoke before the Buddha:
“The World-Honored One has excellently spoken of what is rare!
That is to say, the very first aspiration of a bodhisattva surpasses all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.”
Furthermore, as it is said in the verses:
"When a bodhisattva first resolves their mind, it is conjoined with great compassion;
for the sake of the unsurpassed path, this very mind is supreme."
"Therefore, by this vow, one dwells above the world.

As for "firm-minded," it means that regarding all the sufferings and afflictions of the bodhisattva—namely, the various tortures within the Reviving Hell, the Black Rope Hell, the Crushing Hell, the Minor Howling Hell, the Great Howling Hell, the Minor Scorching Hell, the Great Scorching Hell, the Avīci Hell, the Boiling Excrement, the Sword Forest, the Ash River, the Arbuda, Nirarbuda, Aṭaṭa, Hahava, Huhuva, Utpala, Kumuda, Sumana, Puṇḍarīka, and Padma hells, both cold and hot—the [mind] remains steadfast.

Such are their sufferings: animals, hungry ghosts, asuras, humans, and devas all devour one another and live in mutual terror; they endure famine and soaring grain prices, and fall from their celestial realms.

Avarice, envy, anger, affliction, separation from loved ones, union with those one hates, and the sorrows of birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, and distress—regarding all such sufferings within these six realms of existence, whether seen, heard, or personally experienced—if one cultivates the ten paths of wholesome action for the sake of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, the mind will never be broken. For this reason, this bodhisattva, by cultivating the ten paths of wholesome action with a firm mind, surpasses all the world.
As it is said:
"The sufferings of the six realms— the hells and animals, the hungry ghosts and asuras,
and gods and humans— cannot move his mind."
Therefore, by means of this firm mind, the ten paths of wholesome action practiced by all bodhisattvas surpass everything in the world.

Regarding the "profound mind"— the great mind, the applied mind, the affectionate mind, and the mindful mind— when bodhisattvas practice the ten paths of wholesome action with such minds as these, they surpass everything in the world, except for the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and those bodhisattvas who have long practiced.
As it is said:
With a profound mind, a focused mind, And a mind that benefits the world,
By means of these minds, the bodhisattva Surpasses all the world.
Regarding "thoroughly pure," the Bodhisattva cultivates the threefold purity of the ten paths of wholesome action, which others do not possess;
for this reason, they surpass all the world.
As it is said:
"The Bodhisattva is a jewel among men; possessing a profound mind and a pure mind, by the power of these wholesome dharmas, they surpass all that the world can reach."
Regarding skillful means: by the power of skillful means, the bodhisattva cultivates wholesome dharmas that others do not possess;
therefore, he surpasses all those in the world who practice immeasurable [virtues].
A bodhisattva is said to practice "immeasurable cultivation" for five reasons:
first, immeasurable time; second, immeasurable roots of goodness; third, immeasurable objects; fourth, immeasurable culmination; and fifth, immeasurable dedication.

Regarding "immeasurable at that time": this refers to the bodhisattva’s cultivation of the paths of wholesome action exceeding the measure of time; because the measure of time has been exceeded, the paths of wholesome action cultivated are likewise immeasurable, and for this reason, they surpass all the worlds.
As it is said:
"The lion-like Bodhisattvas, having practiced the paths of wholesome action beyond the reach of all calculation, therefore their cultivation of goodness is most supreme."

Regarding "immeasurable roots of goodness": all bodhisattvas cultivate immeasurable and boundless roots of goodness; the wholesome paths of action cultivated from these roots are likewise immeasurable. For this reason, they surpass all worlds.
As stated in the *Viniścaya-viśuddhi-sūtra* within the Mahāyāna teachings, the Buddha told Kāśyapa:

"For example, if there were clarified butter (*ghṛta*) filling the four great oceans, the conditioned roots of goodness and provisions of a bodhisattva would likewise be so vast; yet these merits are dedicated toward unconditioned wisdom."
Thus, they bring great benefit to all sentient beings; for this reason, although Bodhisattvas dwell within the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), they are able to surpass all the world.
As it is said:
"For the sake of all sentient beings, and for the sake of seeking the Buddha-way..."
Roots of goodness are thus immeasurable, and by this they surpass the world.
Regarding "immeasurable conditions," it means that a bodhisattva cultivates and accumulates roots of goodness because they do not take limited sentient beings as their condition.

Regarding the roots of goodness they cultivate, they do not say they are for the benefit of a certain number of sentient beings; rather, the Bodhisattva cultivates and accumulates roots of goodness solely by taking all sentient beings as their object. Therefore, the paths of wholesome action cultivated by the Bodhisattva, having as their object immeasurable sentient beings, are themselves immeasurable and surpass all the worlds.
As stated in the *Viniścaya-viśuddhi-sūtra*:
The Buddha addressed the devaputras, saying,
"If a great bodhisattva possesses even a slight degree of compassion and seeks to benefit others, this mind can bring benefit and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings."

It is the same for a Bodhisattva who has deeply resolved their mind and practices with diligent vigor: they are able to teach and transform immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* sentient beings, causing them to attain the bliss of *nirvāṇa*.
As it is said:
"The Bodhisattva’s immeasurable virtues and merits adorn themselves;
all are for the sake of delivering sentient beings from their immeasurable great suffering."

Regarding "ultimate immeasurability": because ten ultimates were already explained in the context of the first stage (*bhūmi*) for the sake of making vows, and because these ultimates are immeasurable, the paths of wholesome action cultivated by the bodhisattva are likewise immeasurable; therefore, they surpass all worlds.
As it is said:
"The Bodhisattva cultivates the path of goodness, arising from the ten perfections;
therefore, he surpasses all, and none can destroy him."

Regarding dedication to the immeasurable, it is as explained in the context of the first stage (*bhūmi*): the Bodhisattva’s dedication of the fruit of retribution is immeasurable; because this dedication of the fruit of retribution is immeasurable, the wholesome karma thus cultivated is also immeasurable. For this reason, it surpasses all that belongs to the world.
As it is said:
"By means of immeasurable causes and conditions, one cultivates the paths of wholesome action;
because these are dedicated toward the Buddha Vehicle, they are therefore supreme."
Regarding "rare": when bodhisattvas cultivate the path of goodness, it is called rare by virtue of five causes and conditions:

first, because they are capable of receiving [the teaching]; second, because of their diligence; third, because of the firmness of their minds; fourth, because of their wisdom; and fifth, because of the fruit.
As for "being capable of receiving": if one can thus accept the thought, "I shall become the Honored One among gods and humans, the possessor of all-encompassing wisdom," this is truly rare.

If a person were to lift the trichiliocosm with a single finger and cause it to remain suspended in mid-air for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, such a thing could be accomplished; it would not be considered difficult.
If one makes a vow, saying, "I shall become a Buddha," this is rare and extremely difficult.
As it is said:
"For the sake of immeasurable Buddha-dharmas, One establishes the oath: 'I shall become a Buddha.'"
This person has no equal, let alone anyone superior. Regarding diligence:
although many are capable of conceiving the aspiration for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they are unable to practice the six *pāramitās* with diligence.

If a person is capable of receiving [the teaching] and resolves their mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and is able to practice the six *pāramitās* with diligent application, this is called truly being capable of receiving immeasurable merit.
Because diligence is rare, the paths of wholesome action cultivated thereby are also rare, as it is said:
"Extraordinary is great diligence; Ordinary people are terrified by the mere thought of it, Yet the Bodhisattva practices it in reality— How could this not be extraordinary?"

Regarding "firmness of mind": there are those who resolve to cultivate and accumulate the Buddha-way through the mind of diligence; yet if they encounter obstacles and their minds lack firmness, they will not succeed.
Therefore, by resolving to practice diligence and abiding in that which is rare, one accomplishes the task through a firm mind.
To destroy all obstacles is the foremost rarity among the bodhisattvas’ cultivation of the path of wholesome karma. As it is said:
"If a person lacks a firm mind, They cannot even accomplish small matters, How much less can they achieve the Buddha-way, The unsurpassed state in the world?"

Regarding wisdom: receptivity, diligence, and firm resolve all have wisdom as their root. Therefore, for a bodhisattva, wisdom is the foremost rarity, because it can give rise to such receptivity, diligence, and firm resolve; thus, wisdom is considered rare.
Because wisdom is rare, the wholesome deeds cultivated through it are also rare.
As it is said:
Just as there may be a person capable of receiving [the teaching], who desires to attain the Buddha-dharma,
and through diligence attains a firm mind— all of these have wisdom as their foundation.
As for the fruit: because one cultivates wholesome karma, one attains the dharmas of immeasurable and boundless Buddhas; therefore, it is rare and marvelous.
As it is said:
"By practicing this path of goodness, One attains the power of immeasurable merit."
As the teacher of all sentient beings, who would hear this and not put it into practice?
Regarding "firm resolve," a bodhisattva is said to possess firm resolve for five reasons:

first, the mind does not waver from the Śrāvaka vehicle; second, it does not waver from the Pratyekabuddha vehicle; third, it does not waver from the affairs of non-Buddhists; fourth, it does not waver from any demonic activities; and fifth, it does not waver in the absence of causal conditions.
As it is said:
"Having heard of the liberation of the two vehicles, why not follow this path?
If one does not enter this stage, then one loses the bodhisattva path."
Furthermore, they may crave the matters of non-Buddhists, or be corrupted by Māra, or else,
due to a lack of causes and conditions, abandon the bodhisattva path themselves.
Regarding "those with virtuous vows," a bodhisattva is said to have virtuous vows because of five causes and conditions:

First, one who first deliberates upon gain and loss; second, one who knows the Path; third, one who knows the fruit of the Path; fourth, one who does not covet or cherish personal pleasure; fifth, one who desires to extinguish the great suffering of sentient beings.
Making such a vow is called a "virtuous vow," as it is said:
"First seeing the faults and afflictions of the world, And the great benefit of the Buddha-way,
One knows the practice of the unsurpassed path And its immeasurable fruits."
Having renounced their own bliss of quiescence, they desire to eliminate the suffering of sentient beings;
having made this peerless vow, they are praised by all Buddhas.
One who possesses great compassion and is unimpeded is known to have great compassion for five reasons:
First, for the sake of benefiting and bringing peace to immeasurable sentient beings, one does not give rise to greed or stinginess regarding the necessities of life;
second, one does not cherish the body;
third, one does not cherish one's life.
4. Not considering whether the time is long or short;
5. Benefiting enemies, friends, and neutral parties with an impartial mind.
As it is said:
Regarding all cherished things, both internal and external, he feels no greedy attachment;
for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, he even relinquishes his own body and life.
Throughout immeasurable kalpas of birth and death, he regards them as lasting but a single blink of an eye.
To be impartial toward enemies and kin alike is called the great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) of a bodhisattva.
Regarding "unimpeded": there are five causes and conditions by which a bodhisattva’s compassionate mind becomes impeded:

first, because of the suffering of hell-beings; second, because of the suffering of animals; third, because of the suffering of hungry ghosts; fourth, because of the lack of gratitude and reciprocity among wicked people; and fifth, because of the faults and evils of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
If these five matters do not obstruct one's mind, this is called unimpeded great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
As it is said:
"First is the suffering of hell, the suffering of animals and hungry ghosts,"
Wicked people and the cycle of birth and death— Not being obstructed by these is called "great compassion.
When a bodhisattva can act in this way, The Buddha calls it "unobstructed compassion.
Regarding those who skillfully receive and practice the means (*upāya*): because of five causes and conditions, a bodhisattva is said to be one who skillfully receives and practices the means.

First, knowing the directions and times; second, knowing the inclinations of the minds of others; third, knowing how to enter the path; fourth, knowing the sequence of activities; and fifth, knowing how to guide sentient beings.
One who knows the directions and times knows that in this particular place, one should preach the Dharma in such a way;
and that at this particular time, one should preach the Dharma in such a way.
One knows that in this particular place, one should deliver sentient beings through such causes and conditions.
Knowing that at this time one should deliver sentient beings through such causes and conditions,
the bodhisattva first understands these matters and then acts in accordance with them.
As it is said:
If one is to explain the intention of the World-Honored One for the sake of others,
one should first understand two matters and only then speak according to the time and place.
If one does not know the time and place, yet wishes to expound the Buddha’s intention, [it will be in vain].
Failing to achieve the intended benefit, one instead incurs further fault.
To "know what the other's mind delights in" means to know in what matter the other's deep-seated intention resides.
What is it that they delight in?

Having first understood this, the bodhisattva enters into what sentient beings know and delight in, and accordingly gives rise to the skillful means for their deliverance; in this way, [the effort] is not in vain.
As it is said:
"The Bodhisattva knows the sentient beings' profound mind and unfathomable intent;
having first understood their intent, he gradually causes them to abide in the Buddha-mind."
One who thoroughly understands worldly affairs, benefiting both oneself and others—
if one can act in such a manner, they are said to possess skillful means.
One who knows how to enter the Path is able to transform the minds of non-Buddhists and ordinary worldlings, causing them to enter the Buddha-way.
They also transform the evil deeds of sentient beings, causing them to abide in wholesome matters;
they also know how to transform the paths of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, causing them to enter the Mahāyāna;
and for those already within the Buddha-dharma, they do not allow them to enter the paths of externalists.
Having first understood this matter, one practices in accordance with it, as it is said:
"If a person causes sentient beings To distance themselves from the teachings of non-Buddhists And all that is unwholesome,
They shall enter the Buddha’s supreme nirvāṇa."
If one knows the superior, middling, and inferior minds of all sentient beings,
and having known them, is able to guide them, this is called skillful means (*upāya*).
Regarding "knowing the sequence of affairs":

Just as in the Śrāvaka Vehicle, it first teaches generosity, next the observance of precepts, next rebirth in the heavens, next the faults and afflictions of the five desires, next the suffering and distress of the household life, next the benefits and joy of leaving the household life, next the Truth of Suffering, next the Truth of Origination, next the Truth of Cessation, next the Truth of the Path, next the fruit of Srotāpanna, next the fruit of Sakṛdāgāmin, next the fruit of Anāgāmin, next the fruit of Arhat, next the indestructible liberation, and finally, it teaches the various forms of unimpeded knowledge.
Within the Pratyekabuddhayāna it is also taught:
"The self and things belonging to the self possess many faults and afflictions; by abandoning these things fraught with faults, one attains great benefit.
Living as a householder is a fault and evil, while going forth from home is beneficial."
Next, speaking amidst the clamor and confusion of the crowd is a fault; practicing alone is a benefit.
Dwelling in a village is a fault; dwelling in an araṇya (forest hermitage) is a benefit.
To feel weary of and detached from many desires and many affairs, and to delight in few desires and few affairs, is a benefit.

Guarding the sense faculties, knowing moderation in eating, awakening at the proper times during the first and last watches of the night, observing conditions and grasping their characteristics, delighting in dwelling in empty dwellings, and valuing ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom; not manifesting wonders to please others, but benefiting oneself alone and delighting in the profound Dharma without following the wisdom of others.
Regarding the sequence in the Mahāyāna, it first teaches the dānapāramitā, followed by the śīlapāramitā, kṣāntipāramitā, vīryapāramitā, dhyānapāramitā, and prajñāpāramitā.
First, the *satya-viśeṣa-sthāna* (abiding in the excellence of the truths) was taught; next, the *upekṣā-viśeṣa-sthāna*, the *nirodha-viśeṣa-sthāna*, and the *prajñā-viśeṣa-sthāna* were taught.

Furthermore, first there was the praise of generating the bodhicitta; next, the ten kinds of vows; next, the ten perfections (*daśa-niṣṭhā*); next, the praise of remaining far removed from factors that cause the loss of the bodhicitta; next, the cultivation and accumulation of factors for not losing the bodhicitta; next, firm resolve and diligence; next, steadfastness and endurance; and finally, firm vows.

Furthermore, first, the dharmas that enable one to attain the various stages (*bhūmi*) are taught; next, the dharmas that enable one to abide in the various stages; next, the dharmas that enable one to reach the depths of the various stages; next, the dharmas that enable one to distance oneself from the defilements of the various stages; next, the dharmas that enable one to purify the stages; next, the dharmas for the long-term endurance of the stages; next, the dharmas that enable one to reach the limits of the various stages; next, the dharmas that enable one to avoid falling back from the various stages; next, the fruits of the various stages are taught; and finally, the power of the fruits of the various stages is taught.

Furthermore, first the Stage of Joy is taught; next, the Stage of Purity; next, the Radiant Stage; next, the Difficult to Conquer Stage; next, the Manifest Stage; next, the Far-reaching Stage; next, the Immovable Stage; next, the Stage of Good Wisdom; and finally, the Cloud of Dharma Stage.
As it is said:
"First comes generosity, followed by the observance of precepts; as their fruit, one is born in the heavens.
Yet there is the fault of impermanence in the household life; renouncing the world brings great benefit."
Next, regarding the unsurpassed Four Noble Truths:
by severing the fetters and realizing the four fruits, this sequence of skillful means causes people to abide in the initial vehicle.
First, the faults of saṃsāra are taught; next, the benefits of nirvāṇa are taught.
Guarding the sense faculties, maintaining ethical discipline and meditative concentration,
not following the wisdom of others, delighting in merit and dwelling alone,
relying on oneself rather than another, one delights in seeking one's own welfare and happiness.
Nor does he abandon others; he deeply practices the dhūta ascetic virtues.
For those who seek the Middle Vehicle, the teaching and its characteristics are thus.
By means of the forty unique qualities, he proclaims the Buddha’s immeasurable virtues.
It also describes all the practices performed during the stage of a bodhisattva.
For the sake of benefiting sentient beings, these teachings are explained in successive order;
both self-benefit and benefit for others, as well as various merits, are set forth.
It is also said that the sons of the Buddhas delight in the ten stages (*bhūmi*);
those who seek the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*) cross over through them in this sequential order.

The Guide, knowing the gateways according to the inclinations of sentient beings, leads them through these gateways. Following their inclinations and according to their respective capacities, he enables them to attain liberation, as it is said:
There may be sentient beings who can be guided by profound scriptures, difficult tasks, or crafts;
by incantations, kind words, eloquent speech, or material wealth;
and by the giving of generosity, morality, concentration, and wisdom.
Having deliberated in this manner, they lead others into the Mahāyāna.
Sometimes manifesting in female form, they guide all men;
again manifesting in male form, they guide all women.
He shows the assembly the pleasures of the five desires, and then explains the faults of desire,
so that all people may become free from the five desires.
To skillfully practice these five matters is called the Bodhisattva’s skillful means of receptive practice.

Regarding those who can endure suffering and affliction: if there is someone who, throughout kalpas exceeding calculation, can endure all sufferings and afflictions within birth and death, the ten paths of wholesome action can cause this person to abide in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Question:
All people delight in pleasure and loathe suffering; how can such a person endure affliction and distress? Answer:
It is due to five causes and conditions: first, delighting in non-self;

second, having faith and delight in emptiness; third, deliberating upon worldly phenomena; fourth, contemplating the retribution of karmic actions; and fifth, reflecting on how one would have endured suffering in vain throughout incalculable kalpas.
As it is said:
"One who delights in the dharmas of selflessness and emptiness, and who further understands the retribution of karmic actions—
such as the eight worldly concerns of gain and loss— must inevitably experience these while dwelling in the world."
One should also reflect that in past lives one endured immeasurable suffering in vain;
how much more so for the sake of the Buddha-way—how could one not undergo it? Regarding "not abandoning anyone":
there may be sentient beings who are the most wicked and evil, possessing no merit and being beyond benefit; yet toward such individuals, the Bodhisattva never gives rise to a mind of abandonment.
Question:
If such evil persons are incapable of being saved, why does [the Buddha] not abandon them? Answer:
It is due to five causes and conditions:

first, because of the inferior nature of the dharmas of ordinary persons; second, because of the noble nature of the dharmas of great beings; third, out of fear of deceiving the Buddhas; fourth, out of gratitude for their kindness; and fifth, because one enters the supramundane for the sake of these mundane affairs.
As it is said:
"In order to deliver sentient beings, one gives rise to the mind that bears the heavy burden;
amidst evil enemies and thieves, the mind should never abandon its resolve."
To hold the lowly and small in contempt while esteeming the great and noble is a distinction based on size;
one should not, among sentient beings, allow the heart of compassion to cease.
Amidst all manner of urgent calamities, one should provide benefit without being asked.
When bearing a heavy burden, one must not grow weary or abandon it midway.
Even if one has resolved upon the unsurpassed mind, there may be occasions when one must forsake sentient beings,
or when one's own mind becomes exhausted by suffering, or when harmed by evil persons.
This would be to deceive and mislead the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time—
those World-Honored Ones who, for the benefit of sentient beings,
practiced various austerities and cultivated the path to Buddhahood.
Throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, the Buddha renounced his own happiness to perform meritorious deeds.
If one were to abandon even a single evil person, it would be to turn one's back on the Buddha’s grace;
therefore, one should not abandon evil sentient beings among them.
If a person, throughout immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas,
cultivates and accumulates the path to Buddhahood, great compassion is its root.
If one does so with a mind of craving desire, or with a mind of hatred and fear, [the path will not be realized].
To abandon even one person who can be saved is to sever the root of the Buddha-way.
Therefore, the path of wholesome karma enables those who do not abandon [others] to reach *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Regarding "those who deeply delight in the Buddha’s wisdom": if a person deeply delights in the Buddha’s wisdom, they will swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
There are five causes and conditions for deeply delighting in the Buddha’s wisdom: first, the Buddha’s wisdom has no equal;

second, the Buddha’s wisdom can cause one to become the most honored in the world; third, the Buddha uses his own Buddha-wisdom to deliver himself; fourth, the Buddha’s wisdom also delivers others; fifth, the Buddha’s wisdom is the dwelling place of all meritorious virtues.
As it is said:
"The wisdom of all Buddhas, throughout the heavens and the world, has no equal;
how much less could there be anything superior?"
By means of this wisdom, all Buddhas are venerated and paid homage by devas, asuras, and all people of the world.
Having crossed over themselves by means of wisdom, they likewise deliver others.
If one attains this Buddha-wisdom, which is a treasury of merit,

and delights in fully practicing throughout all the powers and sovereign dharmas of the Buddhas— where "fully practicing" means long-term cultivation, "the power of all practices" refers to the ten kinds of powers of wisdom, and "sovereignty" means acting according to one's will— [then one is a true practitioner].

If a person deeply delights in the Buddha’s ten powers and the qualities of mastery, and practices them exhaustively and universally, such a person will before long swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
For five reasons, one delights in the universal practice of the exhaustion [of suffering]:

first, out of respect for the Buddha’s instructions; second, because the Buddhas have great disciples; third, because they have personally realized all dharmas; fourth, because they gather in those who have fallen away; and fifth, because they are able to rescue those already fallen.
As it is said:
"The Buddha’s teaching is peerless; the sons of the Buddha consist of those of the fourfold, eightfold, sixfold, and threefold [vehicles], who are capable of being teachers for all the devas."
With the eye of Buddha-wisdom, he beholds all phenomena as they manifest before him—
those who commit逆惡 (heinous crimes), sever their roots of goodness,
and those who break the precepts. Such fallen persons he gathers in and delivers.
If a person acts with mastery throughout the powers of the Buddha,
Nirvāṇa and celestial blessings will always remain within that person's grasp.
In this regard, by means of their buddha-powers, all Buddhas are able to perform five kinds of deeds:

First, to cause sentient beings to study the Śrāvaka vehicle; second, to cause sentient beings to study the Pratyekabuddha vehicle; third, to cause sentient beings to study the Mahāyāna vehicle; fourth, to enable those with sufficient strength to attain liberation; and fifth, to enable those with inferior strength to abide in worldly happiness.
As it is said:
By means of their supernormal powers, the Buddhas cause sentient beings to feel weary of and detached from [samsara],
or lead them to study the Hīnayāna, the Madhyamayāna, and the Mahāyāna.
Those who possess the fullness of power cause them to attain liberation;
those who lack such power cause them to be born in heaven and enjoy worldly happiness.
Regarding "sovereignty," the Buddhas possess sovereignty over five matters:

First, mastery over the various supernormal powers; second, mastery within one's own mind; third, mastery within the cessation of perception and feeling; fourth, mastery within noble mental transformations; and fifth, mastery over the lifespan.
As it is said:
Mastery over flying and the like, mastery attained by one's own mind—
within the meditative absorption of cessation, it is as if entering and emerging from one's own house.
All that is pure and impure can be transformed according to the mind;
life cannot be harmed by others, nor is it exhausted by its own conditions.
Such mastery over these things applies equally to all phenomena.
Therefore, the Human Lion is called the Sovereign One.

He is able to destroy those with evil intentions—namely, those who have strayed from the Right Path, such as ordinary worldlings and the ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist outsiders. Briefly stated, those with evil intentions claim that the five aggregates (skandhas) are the self, or they say that the self possesses the five aggregates.
Some say that the self exists within the five aggregates;
some say that the five aggregates exist within the self;
and some say that there is a self apart from the five aggregates.
As it is said:
"If the five aggregates were the self, one would fall into annihilationism;
then, having lost the causes and conditions of karma, one would attain liberation without merit."
The remaining [categories] are of four kinds; they lack characteristics apart from the aggregates (*skandha*).
Since there are no phenomena (*dharma*) that possess characteristics, all should be refuted in this manner.

Furthermore, the five wrong views are called "evil intentions," namely: wrong view, the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), and the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). As it is said:
Having destroyed the false view of cause and effect, the twenty kinds of self-view,
and the views of existence and non-existence— regarding inferior matters as supreme—
they attain liberation solely through the power of their precepts.
As previously refuted regarding identity and difference, this view is likewise refuted.
When the right intention and the eightfold path are refuted [of such views], it is called attaining liberation.

Regarding those who protect the true Dharma of all Buddhas: if a person can protect what has been taught by all Buddhas—namely, the twelve divisions of the scriptures—and if their mind is able to believe in and accept them;
The ten paths of wholesome action can lead this person to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
For five reasons, one should cherish and protect the true Dharma:
first, because one knows how to repay the kindness of all Buddhas;
