He was well-versed in and fully mastered the scriptures, arts, mathematics, and incantations; he was skillful in discourse and capable of discerning their underlying meanings.
His ministers were complete in number and all possessed majestic virtue.
He constantly practiced the giving of material wealth, such that none could equal him. His thousand sons were handsome and dignified, like the sons of the gods;

they possessed majesty, virtue, courage, and strength capable of defeating powerful enemies. Their palaces, halls, pavilions, and towers were like the magnificent palaces of the Four Heavenly Kings or Śakra. The king’s instructions could not be subverted by anyone; throughout the four continents, only this king was fully endowed with such majestic signs, and thus none could surpass him.

The sound is deep and far-reaching, easy to hear and easy to understand; it is neither scattered nor confused, like that of the kalaviṅka bird—beautiful, soft, harmonious, and elegant, delighting the ears of those who hear it.
Their retinue is of one mind and cannot be thwarted or destroyed.
Wherever they dwell, there is no obstruction from earth, water, or space.
Their majestic power is fierce and intense, enabling them to undertake great tasks.
He is mindful of questioning the elders and does not deceive others.
His mind is free from envy and jealousy; he cannot endure what is contrary to the Dharma and harbors no malice or resentment.
His deportment is composed and serene, never frivolous or impulsive.
Their speech is truthful, and they never engage in double-tongued talk.
They practice giving and uphold the precepts, constantly cultivating a virtuous mind.
In their comings and goings they know the proper time, never failing in skillful means.
His countenance was serene and pleasant, and his speech was always accompanied by a smile; he never knit his brows or cast a malevolent glance at others.
He brought profit to those who had suffered loss, and ensured that those who already possessed profit understood well how to repay it.
Possessing a sense of shame and remorse, endowed with great wisdom, and majestic in his dignified presence, he is capable of enduring insults.
Having the marks of a great man, his nature is fierce and resolute, and he is able to swiftly accomplish whatever tasks he undertakes.

One should first deliberate thoroughly before acting; Your Majesty possesses the eye of Dharma, and your deeds are most excellent. One who deliberates well may be entrusted with affairs, but if one is not capable, you should seek out those who are wise and enlightened.
He has well accumulated merit and wealth;
he is pure and able to protect himself, never violating the prohibitions and precepts;
and he abounds in riches and treasures like King Vaiśravaṇa.

He possesses great power like Śakra, the Lord of Devas; he is as upright and lovely as the full moon; he can illuminate like the sun; he can endure like the earth; his mind is as deep as the ocean, and he is not shaken by pleasure or pain.
Like Sumeru, the king of mountains, it cannot be shaken by the winds.
It is the abode of all wondrous jewels and the locus of all virtuous merits; it is the refuge for all kinsmen of the world and for those afflicted by suffering.
He provides a refuge for those without refuge and a dwelling for those without a dwelling;
he can remove the fear of those who are afraid.
A Wheel-Turning Sage King possesses such characteristics as these.
They are able to transform those who break the precepts, causing them to abide in wholesome dharmas;
as for their other activities, they are as described in the First Ground.
Regarding "transforming those who break the precepts":
It enables sentient beings to abandon evil and practice goodness, thereby attaining matters of peace and happiness.

To cause them to abide in wholesome dharmas means to be able to transform the unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind of sentient beings, causing them to perform wholesome actions of body, speech, and mind.

This matter is as explained in the context of the First Ground (*prathamā bhūmi*): namely, the vision of all Buddhas and the attainment of various samādhis; however, while those [on the first ground] number in the hundreds, the distinction here is that they number in the thousands.
Daśabhūmivibhāṣā Śāstra, Scroll Seventeen.
